The *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi*, First Chapter:
(The auspicious invocation; the nature of Brahman; the causes that obstruct the knowledge of reality; and the nature of the Śabda-Brahman).
(The Nature of the Knowledge of Reality) (The Auspicious Invocation) Om, salutation to the Supreme Deity. Om, salutation to the Transcendent One.
Seated upon a swan-throne amidst a full moon shining from a thousand-petaled lotus, his body radiant with the luster of the moon,
he has two eyes and his lotus-like hands display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons; he is perfected in yoga.
May the God of gods, who sports within the lotus of the lineage, protect me. || 1 ||

1. Now, the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa, desiring to compose the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi*—which, like the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), reveals the secrets of the worship of Śrīvidyā for the sake of practitioners—performs an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) to ward off all obstacles that might hinder the completion of the work. And therein:

"From the Supreme Lord, who is the entirety of the manifestation of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, there arose Śakti; from that, Nāda; and from Nāda, the emergence of Bindu. (Śāradātilaka, Chapter 1, Verse 7). By such statements...

From the Unmanifest Supreme Lord, through the union of Śiva and Śakti, there arose the primordial Goddess, she who is Tripurasundarī herself. From her came Śakti; from that, Nāda; and from Nāda, the emergence of Bindu.

Thus, according to the statement from the *Pāñcarātra* cited in the *Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa-ṭīkā*, he first prays to Paramaśiva—the nature of the Śrī Guru—who is described as being the seed-form (*bījarūpa*) of the power of Tripurasundarī, the subject matter of this work: "Ten... and so forth.
[He prays to Him] who is shining intensely, blazing brilliantly, within that thousand-petaled lotus situated on the head.

The meaning is "in a mass of shimmering moonlight"; that is, he is situated within that full moon. Likewise, "situated within the haṃsa-pīṭha" means existing inside the seat consisting of the two syllables *haṃ* and *saḥ*. As it is said in the first chapter of the Mahākālī-tantra:
"Within the thousand-spoked [lotus], in the void, adorned with divine archways..."
"In the center of the lunar disc, upon two swan-colored syllables, [is the seed-syllable] resembling pure crystal, adorned with pure silk.
Here, situated within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus, are the syllables: *sa ha kha phreṃ ha sa kṣa ma la va ra yuṃ*.
According to another view, the abode of Paramaśiva is a twelve-petalled lotus distinguished by the twelve syllables consisting of the Guru and the Mantra. This is stated in the *Pādukāpañcakatīkā*:
"In the thousand-petalled lotus at the head, which is white in color and faces downward..."
"In that twelve-syllable lotus, adorned with all colors and possessing filaments as red as the young sun, within the hollow of its pericarp.
Likewise, concerning the thousand-spoked [lotus]:
There, within the hollow of the pericarp of that twelve-syllable lotus,
which is composed of light, [he resides] inside the pericarp, situated in the center of the lunar mandala.

"On the swan-throne consisting of the mantra, adorned with the three lines of *akathādi* and the three letters *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa*, [one should worship] one's own Guru in the form of Śiva. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Pādukāpañcaka-stotra*:
I worship the lotus of twelve syllables, eternally attached within the interior of the lake-lotus of the *brahmarandhra*, pure and wondrous, adorned with the stalk of the aperture of the *kuṇḍalinī*.
This has been specifically established by such passages as these. We shall clarify in the sixth chapter, the *Ṣaṭcakravivaraṇa*, that this is not the view accepted by Pūrṇānanda.
By this [it is meant] that [the deity resides] upon the seat of the *haṃsa* situated within the lunar disc in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head.

It is clearly stated that the state of Paramaśiva has been described. Regarding the status of the Haṃsa as a seat (pīṭha): "Upon the Haṃsa-seat, which consists of mantra, one should remember one's own Guru in the form of Śiva, preceded by his name and ending with the title 'Amukānandanātha'."
Thus it has been established by the words of the *Prapañcasāra*. Now, what is this that is called *haṃsa*? It is said:
the syllable *haṃ* is declared to be the *bindu*, and the *visarga* is remembered as *sa*;
the *bindu* is said to be *puruṣa*, and the *visarga* is remembered as *prakṛti*.
The *haṃsa* consists of the nature of both Puruṣa and Prakṛti; this entire world has that as its essence.

Thus, by the statement from the *Prapañcasāra*, the word "haṃ" denotes the Puruṣa (Spirit) and the word "saḥ" denotes Prakṛti (Nature); consequently, it is understood that the word "haṃsa" refers to the Inner Self (Antarātman), which consists of both Spirit and Nature.
[One should meditate on] the Supreme Inner Self situated in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus.

By such statements from the *Kālamālinī Tantra*, the existence of the inner Supreme Śiva— who is the inner self consisting of the Puruṣa and Prakṛti— is declared. Consequently, the phrase "the God of gods residing within the Haṃsa-pīṭha" is an epithet meaning that He dwells within the interior of that very Haṃsa-pīṭha, which is the inner self (antarātmā).
Regarding the phrase "himarucirucirāṅga": *himaruci* means the moon; he is one whose body (*aṅga*) is as beautiful (*rucira*) as that. In the first chapter of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*:
"He who is ever-auspicious (*sadāsiva*), ever-blissful (*sadānanda*), and an ocean of the nectar of compassion (*karuṇāmṛtasāgara*)."

Because his white complexion is established by such passages as, "The all-pervading Lord, white as camphor and the *kunda* flower, consisting of pure *sattva*" (1.6), and because there are three qualifying attributes— “having lotus-hands granting fearlessness and boons,” “complete in yoga,” and “two-eyed”— to indicate that he is the very nature of the venerable Guru. For instance:
Anointed with fragrant unguents, peaceful, with lotus-hands granting boons and fearlessness, his beautiful body is embraced by the Śakti stationed on his left;
he possesses the overflowing splendor of fullness and two lotus-eyes.
Thus, by the statement set forth in the sequence of worship—
"In the morning, [one should meditate on] the Guru with two eyes and two arms upon a white lotus at the head"—
and by the meditation described in the section on morning duties, his state of granting boons and fearlessness, his perfection in yoga, and his possession of two eyes are established.
Therefore, in the thirteenth chapter of the *Kulārṇava*:
"O Dear One, how can he who is Śiva—omnipresent, subtle, beyond the mind (*unmanā*), partless, immutable, of the form of space, unborn, and infinite—be worshipped? (13.51).
Having raised this question, it is said in that very same place:
"For this very reason, O Goddess, Śiva himself has directly assumed the form of the Guru; when worshipped with devotion, he bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
"I am Śiva, O Goddess; I have no form perceptible to the human eye.
Therefore, in the form of the venerable Guru, I protect righteous disciples."
"Bound with human skin, Paraśiva himself wanders secretly upon the earth for the sake of bestowing grace upon worthy disciples.
By such passages as these, it is shown that Paramaśiva himself, assuming the form of the venerable Guru for the protection of worthy disciples, moves secretly upon the earth.
Having established that [the Guru] dwells [in that state], it is said in that very same place:
"O Pārvatī, there is no difference between the Lord Sadāśiva and the venerable Guru; he who perceives a distinction between the two is a sinner. (13.61)

By such statements, the status of Śrī Guru is taught to belong to Paramaśiva alone. The essential point is that, in order to establish this very meaning, the venerable Paramahaṃsa Pūrṇānanda has employed three qualifying epithets beginning with *abhayavarakarābja*.
Regarding the term *kulakamalavilāsī*, the meaning of the word *kula* is stated in the seventh chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*:
"The individual soul, the principle of primordial nature, space, time, and ether, as well as earth, water, fire, and air—this is designated as 'Kula'. (7.97).
Then, he also speaks of the Kula-conduct in that very same place:

"And that conduct toward these [elements] which is free from conceptual construction, performed with the realization that they are Brahman— that alone is the Kula practice, O Primordial One, which bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa" (7.98). Consequently, by these two statements, [one should understand] the nature of being a living soul (*jīvatva*), the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛtitva*), the nature of the directions (*diktvādi*), and so forth, in regard to the categories beginning with the living soul and ending with the wind.

Family tradition (*kulācāra*) is precisely a specific conduct accompanied by a knowledge whose mode (*prakāra*) is "Brahman-ness," preceded by the abandonment of knowledge whose modes are [lower] categories.

It is thus stated that this brings about the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*), consisting of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. Consequently: *kula*—meaning the collection of principles beginning with the individual soul (*jīva*) and ending with *vāyvanta* (the wind-principle)—is itself the lotus; it "shines" there, meaning it sports by its own nature through ultimate reality (*paramārthasattā*).

This is the meaning of the term *kulakamalavilāsī* (the one who sports with the lotus of the lineage). By this, it is indicated that he possesses the capacity to accomplish the four aims of human life (*puruṣārthacatuṣṭaya*), and therefore, prayer directed toward him is entirely appropriate.
Here, by superimposing the nature of a lotus upon the lineage, just as the sun, through contact with its own radiance, [causes] the lotuses...

It manifests its own nature as expansion; likewise, it is indicated that the Supreme Lord also generates the cognition of Brahman within those entities—beginning with the individual soul (jīva) and ending with the vital air (vāyu)—which are denoted by the term *kula*. For this very reason:
[Salutation] to the one who has the form of the Supreme Brahman in human shape, the remover of ignorance.
"Salutation to that venerable Guru for the sake of illuminating the Kula-dharma" (5.32).

By this statement from the fifth chapter of the *Mahānirvāṇa-tantra*, his status as the illuminator of the Kula-ācāra is declared. Alternatively, "Kulakamalavilāsī" means he who sports (*vilasati*) in the "Kula-lotuses," which are the lotuses situated on the path of Kula. As it was said by Viśvanātha in the *Ṣaṭcakravivṛti*:
"In this regard, this southern hexad arises from the Kula, preceded by the Command (ājñā).
Now, in response to the doubt as to whether this Lord is with parts (*sakala*) or without parts (*niṣkala*), he says: "The God of Gods.
He is the eye of knowledge for the ignorant, destroying the dense and ever-increasing stream of passion.

I bow to the pair of lotus-feet of my initiation gurus— the root of bliss— which illuminate the beauty of the beloved of the forest of noble lotuses with the moonlight-like luster of their nails, and which are a flowing stream of pure, great merit shining from sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā and Kāśī. || 2 ||

The "gods" (devāḥ) are those such as Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and others who "play" (dīvyanti), meaning they sport by means of illusion (māyā) in the form of phenomenal expansion (prapañca). The "God of gods" (devadeva) is Paramaśiva;

the meaning is that he is the one who, through his own essential power (svarūpaśakti), brings about the activities consisting of engagement and withdrawal for them. This has been stated in the first chapter of the Śāradā-tantra:
"The eternal Śiva is to be known as both devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*) and possessed of attributes (*saguṇa*).

Devoid of attributes, he is other than *prakṛti*; possessed of attributes, he is remembered as the manifest whole (*sakala*). (1.6) 2. Having established, by means of the preceding verse, that the Supreme Śiva, who sports within the thousand-petalled lotus, alone possesses the status of the Guru, [the author now establishes] the identity of the initiating Guru with him...

He pays homage to that [Lord] with the words beginning "of the ignorant" (*ajñānām*). The words ending in the accusative case, such as "eye of knowledge" (*jñānanetram*), are adjectives qualifying the phrase "the pair of lotus-feet. For those who are ignorant—that is, those devoid of the knowledge of Brahman, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss—the Lord is the "eye of knowledge. Just as a person perceives all worldly objects by means of the eyes, so too does the practitioner [perceive everything].
Only through the power of initiation obtained from the succession of the grace of the lotus feet of the venerable Guru does one become a seer of Brahman. Therefore:
"Salutation to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance has been opened with the probe of the collyrium of knowledge."
By this, it is stated that the Guru alone is the one who opens the eye of knowledge. As it is declared in the first chapter of the *Rudrayāmala-uttarakhaṇḍa*:
"Merely through the grace of the Guru, there shall be great satisfaction of Śakti;
through the mere satisfaction of Śakti, the practitioner attains liberation. (1.224)
"The entire world has its root in the Guru; the supreme austerity has its root in the Guru.
By the mere grace of the Guru, the self-controlled one attains liberation.
(1.225) By such statements as these, it is declared that the grace of the venerable Guru alone is the bestower of liberation.

Possessing a radiance like the expanse of a dense, fresh *javā* blossom— meaning it has a luster like the redness of a thick, newly blossomed *javā* flower— and likewise, by means of the nets of moonlight from her nails, that is, the masses of their splendor.

The light of the splendor that is the beloved of the lotus-forest of the *kula*; the meaning of the word *kula* was demonstrated in the first verse. *Kula* is the supreme abode of the succession of the bliss of Brahman, possessing a fierce radiance that destroys the dense mass of the great darkness of the flood of ignorance regarding the principles (*tattvas*) such as the individual soul (*jīva*), and shining with the luster of ten million full moons.
May Śiva protect us—he who, seated upon a white lotus throne, most loftily grants the boons of fearlessness and excellence with his two hands, while resting his head [upon the moon]. || 3 ||

It is that which manifests the lovely and desirable splendor—the very lotus-forest—which is the manifestation of Brahman; such is it. Through the garland of moon-like rays from his toe-nails, the venerable Guru alone reveals the existence of Brahman, which resides within the categories of reality beginning with the individual soul (*jīva*) and ending with the wind (*vāyu*), yet remains beyond the scope of empirical knowledge. As it is said in the *Mahānirvāṇa Tantra*:
In the seventh *ullāsa*:

"Having obtained this knowledge, which is higher than the highest, through service to the true Guru, and having become devoted to the *Kulācāra*, [one should worship] the Mistress of the *Kula* with the five *tattvas*," and so forth. (7.101)

"Gaṅgā," and so forth. It means that which causes a mass of merit similar to the mass of merit shining forth at holy places such as the Gaṅgā and Kāśī to flow forth; that is to say, the kind of heap of merit that arises from bathing and other rites at the Gaṅgā and other sacred sites is exactly the same as that which arises from saluting the feet of the venerable Guru and so on. As it is said in the *Gurutantro* cited in the *Prāṇatoṣaṇī*:
"All rivers such as the Gaṅgā, all Gandharvas, the species of serpents, other beings—both stationary and moving—and mountains consisting of all elements;
these and others always abide within the body of the Guru. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the *Gurugītā* of the *Viśvasāra-tantra*:
"His residence is the sacred field of Kāśī, and the water from the feet of the Jāhnavī [is his drink].
The specific detail, however, is found in the twelfth chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Kulārṇava*:

"O Goddess, the remembrance of the supreme Śrīpādukā is superior to ten million recitations of mantras, O Goddess, to bathing at ten million sacred fords, and to the worship of ten million deities"—this and other such passages have declared this. Regarding the *Ānandakanda*: bliss is the nature of Brahman, according to the Vedic revelation; thus, bliss belongs to the Supreme Brahman.
The meaning is that the *kanda* is the root of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). As it is said in the twelfth chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Kulārṇava*:
"The root of mantra is the word of the guru; the root of liberation is the grace of the guru.
And likewise: "This great sequence of the supreme reality has its root in the favor of the guru" (12.17).
The meaning is: "I bow to the pair of lotus-feet of the initiation-gurus.
(3) Having prostrated before the initiation-guru with the previous verse, [the author now speaks] of those practitioners alone who have obtained the methods of worship through his compassion.

Since the worship of Brahman is possible [only for the most advanced], even there, because the worship of Paramaśiva— as described in the first verse beginning with "the full moon shining upon the thousand-petaled lotus"— is entirely difficult to accomplish for those of weak capacity, [the author],
setting forth the worship of Brahman with attributes (saviśeṣabrahmopāsana), states:

Having first worshipped Śiva, the worship of Śakti follows thereafter; indeed, one should offer some small portion of whatever articles of service belong to Him. (5.40) Otherwise, all the water of the Gaṅgā would become like urine.

Likewise, from the statement in the fifth chapter of the Toḍalatantra: "If one worships another deity in this manner and subsequently worships Śiva, the fruit of that worship is enjoyed by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas" (5.45), and so forth, it is heard that the worship of Śiva alone must be performed first; therefore, [one should worship] Śiva at the outset.
He clarifies [the meaning] with the words "by ignorance" (*ajñāna*). The flood of ignorance itself is a mass of dense darkness, because it veils the nature of Brahman, which is without distinction;
thus, it is essentially a thick heap of darkness. Upon its destruction—that is, its annihilation—it is like the sun of fierce radiance.
Just as the sun, having dispelled a thicket of dense darkness, brings the various categories of worldly reality within the range of people's knowledge, [so too does this wisdom].

The meaning is that Śiva likewise, having removed the veil of ignorance (*avidyā-āvaraṇa*), reveals the true nature of the Self as Brahman before his practitioners. He is the sole abode of the succession of Brahmānanda, the very essence of the support for uninterrupted Brahmic bliss.
Therefore, it is said in the first chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:
"Preceded by a smile, Mahādeva, the all-pervading Lord, consists of perfect bliss (*pūrṇānanda*).

By this, Śiva’s nature as perfect bliss is established. "Possessing the luster of ten million full moons"—meaning he is distinguished by a radiance resembling the light of ten million full moons. With his two hands, [he bestows] fearlessness and boons upon the worlds most exalted.

The meaning is that he bestows exceedingly abundant benefit. "Seated upon a white lotus throne on the crown" means situated upon the thousand-petaled lotus seat located at the head. Even for Sakala-Śiva, the thousand-petaled [lotus] alone is the locus. This is stated in the Gandharvamālikā-tantra as cited in the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa-ṭīkā:
"The thousand-spoked city of Śiva is beautiful and free from suffering.
Regarding this, the secret is as follows: according to such scriptural passages as, "The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon," etc.
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. (9.24) When the Supreme Brahman is realized, enough with all the observances.
"What need is there for a palm-leaf fan when the breeze from the Malaya mountains has been obtained?"—
by such words from the ninth chapter of the *Kulārṇava*,
one attains the formless state and reaches the stainless plane (*nirañjana-pada*).
O Queen of the Gods, by means of the formless [state], the practitioner has accomplished his purpose.
Thus, according to the statement in the ninth chapter of the Kubjikātantra:
"Understand that to be Brahman, from whose attainment there is no other attainment, from whose happiness there is no other happiness, and from whose knowledge there is no other knowledge."
That which has no other object of vision beyond itself, seeing which there is no further rebirth,
which fills all that is horizontal, upward, and downward— the imperishable, infinite, eternal, and unique Reality, Bliss, and Consciousness— determine that to be Brahman.

Thus, by the statement in the first chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*, the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahma-jñāna*) and the resulting fulfillment of all duties for practitioners are declared; however, since that is entirely impossible for weakly qualified living beings, the attainment of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahman*) occurs gradually through the worship of the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahman*). For this very reason, it is said in the thirteenth chapter of the *Kulārṇava*:
O Dear One, how can He be worshipped— He who is Śiva, all-pervading, subtle, beyond the mind, partless, immutable, of the form of space, unborn, and infinite?

Thus, Śiva’s question is justified. On this point, it has been well deliberated in the *Vedāntaparibhāṣā*: "Those of dull intellect who are unable to directly realize the supreme Brahman devoid of attributes are shown compassion through descriptions of Brahman with attributes."
"When their minds have been brought under control through the practice of Brahman with attributes (saguṇabrahma),
that very [Brahman] shall manifest directly, free from the conceptualization of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
To establish this very point, it is stated in the ninth chapter of the *Kubjikātantra*:
"O Great Goddess, one should meditate upon the formless by means of the formed;
O Goddess, without the formed, one does not perceive the formless. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Agastya-saṃhitā* cited in the *Haratattvadīdhiti*:
The Lord of All, consisting of all things, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
though formless by nature, assumed a form for the benefit of everyone.

Thus it has been stated. All this is now clear: through the corroboration of these successive statements, Paramaśiva—having manifested in various forms such as Śiva, Śakti, and so forth, for the sake of attaining the supreme human goal by those who are incapable of grasping His true nature due to their coarse faculties—grants grace to practitioners by becoming accessible through meditation and other means. Thus everything is explained.
Upon his stainless chest, which is more beautiful than the splendor of a rain-cloud, a pure pearl necklace is joined with the radiant gem named Kaustubha;
it bears a resemblance to the waters of the Yamunā mingling with the stream of the Gaṅgā as they flow into the ocean.
May that Dāmodara, who spreads splendor for me, extend auspiciousness to me. || 4 ||
The base of her feet is bathed by the streams of honey-drops falling from the garlands of mandāra flowers shimmering upon the heads of Brahmā, who bows in devotion;
she is served by Indra and the other hosts of gods through their most profound meditations alone.
May the lotus-eyed, divine Goddess Śambhu be for our auspiciousness. || 5 ||
4. Having propitiated Śiva with the preceding verse, he now propitiates Paramaśiva, who has manifested in the form of Viṣṇu, with the verse beginning "yasya" (of whom).

Regarding the phrase *ambhodharakāntisundaratare*: here, by the word *ambhodhara* (cloud), the extreme blackness of the cloud is indicated; since a cloud becomes white when its water has departed, a comparison of Dāmodara with it [in that state] is not possible. Rather, it is compared to the luster of a water-filled cloud. Even more than that—
Upon the stainless chest of that Dāmodara, which possesses a most charming luster, shines a pure pearl necklace—
meaning it is "saṃśuddhā," free from defects such as discoloration and thus transparent; this pearl necklace, a string of pearls,
is joined with the gem named the radiant Kaustubha, which is "bhāsvat," meaning luminous.

May that Dāmodara spread auspiciousness—he who, being present, spreads a splendor comparable to a stream of the Gaṅgā’s waters shining upon a single lotus blooming in the waters of the Kālindī (the Yamunā); [here,] "blooming" is to be supplied as the ellipsis for the lotus in the Yamunā's water, and he possesses such a likeness through that shining, beautiful stream of the Gaṅgā. Here...

It should be noted that because Dāmodara is dark-complexioned, he resembles the waters of the Yamunā; because the Kaustubha jewel is white, it resembles a lotus; and because the pearl necklace is white and hangs down, it resembles a stream of the Gaṅgā. Thus, although he is in reality formless, he assumes such a beautiful form for the sake of bestowing grace upon the multitude of practitioners.

With the intention that "May Dāmodara bestow auspiciousness," it is said: "May that Blessed One— who, though unbound, accepted even the most unbearable bondage by the cord for the sake of fulfilling his mother's desire, and whose compassion blossoms in delighting the minds of spiritual practitioners— surely grant welfare when propitiated by prayer."

5. Having thus propitiated the Blessed Śiva and Dāmodara, he now propitiates the venerable Tripurasundarī—the essential nature and power of Paramaśiva who, though formless, assumes a form out of a desire to bestow grace upon practitioners—saying "By devotion... By "devotion" (bhaktyā), he means through a particular intensity of affection for the venerable Tripurasundarī, the Mother of the Universe.

She whose vicinity of the footstool— that is, the area near her footstool— was bathed by showers, that is, by the masses of nectar-drops issuing forth from the garlands of Mandāra flowers shining upon the crown of the head of Viriñci, the humble Brahmā.
This is stated in the eleventh chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*:
"Her lotus feet are rubbed by the crest-jewels on the heads of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
By this, her status as one to be propitiated by Brahmā and the others is expressed; however, the method of practice for Indra and the other gods is not of such a nature.

Thus he says: She is worshipped by means of meditations—specifically those characterized by the weightiness of sovereignty—performed by Indra and the other eminent gods (*vṛndāraka*). Even the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), such as Indra and others who are lords of heaven and the rest, are unable to behold her true nature; out of a longing to behold her nature, they resort to the yoga of meditation and serve her.

May that lotus-eyed Goddess, the sovereign lady endowed with the sixfold sovereignty, the consort of Śambhu, the Supreme Śiva, whose nature is pure light—the illustrious Tripurasundarī—be for our welfare, for us practitioners.
Herein lies the secret: by the phrase "the Goddess of Śambhu," it is indicated that the agency for creation and so forth belongs to the Supreme Power (paraśakti), and [not to Him alone].
It is indicated that [the Goddess] is beyond the relationship with Śambhu. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"The Supreme Power (Parā Śakti) has the form of the sprout from the seed of the manifest union of Śiva and Śakti. Furthermore, in its commentary (*ṭīkā*), elsewhere it says:
"There is no Goddess without Śiva, and no Śiva without the Goddess."
There is no difference between the two, just as there is none between the moon and its moonlight.

Thus it has been stated. In the system of Tantra, existence (*sattā*) is accepted as being twofold: the existence of Light (*prakāśasattā*) and the existence of Reflexive Awareness (*vimarśasattā*). Among these, the existence of the Supreme Brahman, which is the Supreme Śiva together with His Power (*parāśakti*), is the existence of Light; whereas the existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth, is the existence of Reflexive Awareness. And therein, the Supreme Śiva, who is the Supreme Śiva together with His Power, whose nature is Light, [manifests] through His own divine play the entire [universe] which consists of Reflexive Awareness.
It manifests and withdraws the entire manifold of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañcajāta*) which resides within itself in a subtle state.

In that regard, the agency of creation and so forth belongs to the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*) alone by virtue of its being the substratum of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*); and that [agency] is accomplished by the Supreme Śiva through his being the substratum of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*). Consequently, in the absence of a relationship with the Supreme Śiva, even the Supreme Power would lack agency.
To indicate that [this] is not logically tenable, the authors of the treatise have stated: "The Goddess of Śambhu is the Great Māyā whose form is consciousness, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman;
for the sake of bestowing grace upon her devotees, she assumed various forms."
Thus, by the scriptural statement of the Goddess held within the *Haratattvadīdhiti*,
she alone is the fifth power (*pañcamī śakti*), whose nature is the Supreme Brahman;
she is that great cause of the worlds, whose form is supreme bliss.
The form of that Goddess is indeed devoid of rising and setting;
she possesses a gross form in her grossness and a subtle form in her subtlety,
shining within the center of the pericarp in the middle of the heart-lotus.

May that certain form, resting upon a joyful and auspicious bed, her lotus-feet shining with the preeminent pearls from the smiling crest-jewels of the best of gods and Śiva, protect me from the pit of delusion. (6)
The Lord Viśveśvara is the God who abides pervading the universe;
she alone is the Goddess Viśveśvarī, established as the all-pervasive one.

And by this statement from the third chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*, having established the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti as well as their assumption of various forms for the sake of favoring practitioners,
[it is stated that] her creation and dissolution occur again and again perpetually.
Therefore, power is primary, and this entire world is pervaded by power.

Thus, by this statement from the third chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*, Maheśvara declared that the agency for creation and other cosmic functions belongs to Śakti alone. And so, the intention is as follows: may she—who, when propitiated by Brahmā and others, as well as by Indra and others, assumes specific forms and bestows grace upon practitioners to accomplish their worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*)—surely grant us auspiciousness when she is invoked.

6. Having thus propitiated the Goddess, the author of the work, intent on the worship of this scripture, describes the form suitable for her worship and the place appropriate for that worship, as stated in the seventh chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra* beginning with the twelve-spoked *anāhata* lotus: [The text continues with the citation from the Nirvāṇatantra.]
O auspicious one, O Queen of the Gods, this Maharloka is a place of worship;
here indeed the best among those who know yoga performs the mental sacrifice.

By this statement, since it is declared that the heart-lotus alone is the locus for the mental sacrifice (*mānasayāga*), he says: "In the heart. Within the center of the heart-lotus, there is a radiant pericarp;

within that, situated in its interior, is the "bed of the joyful Śiva"—a bed whose nature is Śiva, who is delighted by the bliss of the touch of the Goddess's feet. Alternatively, the word "radiant" (*prollasantī*) is an adjective qualifying the form [of the Goddess].

In this context, although the sequence is such that there is the seed-vessel (*bījakoṣa*) in the center of the heart-lotus, from that the hexagonal mandala, and from that the wind-mandala—which is synonymous with Maharloka—it should nevertheless be understood that this has been stated in general terms.
[The phrase] "whose lotus-feet shine with the finest pearls from the smiles on the crowns of the lords of the gods" means: the finest pearls (*muktāpradhāna*) and the shining lotus-feet (*padābja*).

Regarding the phrase "of her," and the statement "adorned with pearls, gems, and corals at her lotus-feet"—which refers to a portion of the upcoming meditation—since the word *muktā* (pearl) is mentioned first among those things adorned by pearls, it indicates that although pearls, gems, and corals share the commonality of being foot-ornaments, the pearls alone hold primacy; this is expressed by the compound *muktāpradhāna*. [She is] smiling (*smerā*).
Neither drunk nor undrunk, neither limited nor unlimited, neither red nor unred, neither whitened nor unwhitened;
formless, eternal, devoid of the three qualities, the unborn and non-inert God.
I bow to that Self, the abode of the continuous flow of supreme bliss.

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "she whose lotus-feet shine with excellent pearls. Based on the statement in the upcoming meditation on Tripurasundarī, "she who has conquered the ocean of sweetness with a slightly smiling face," the word *smerā* (smiling) is an epithet of the Goddess.
Consequently, the phrase "she who resides upon the crest of Hara, the best of gods, and whose lotus-feet shine with excellent smiling pearls" is a *madhyapadalopin* (elliptical) compound.
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. May this certain form (*mūrti*) of such an indescribable nature protect me from the pit of delusion (*moha*).
Then, being freed from delusion, I shall complete the composition of this work without obstacles—this is the intention of the author.
(7) Now, for those seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) whose minds have been purified by the specific worship of the aforementioned deity, [the following applies]:
He describes the nature of Paramaśiva, which is the object of the final knowledge. In that regard:
He alone is the existent form, the true, non-dual, higher than the highest;
self-luminous, eternally full, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Unchanging, without support, without distinction, and undisturbed;
beyond the qualities, the witness of all, the self of all, the all-seeing, and omnipresent.
He is hidden within all beings, the eternal, all-pervading one;
he appears as the quality of all the senses, yet is devoid of all senses;
he transcends the world, is the cause of the world, and is beyond the reach of speech and mind.

This is because the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*, in its second chapter, describes the essential nature of Paramaśiva as being existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*), non-dual (*advaita*), changeless (*nirvikāra*), self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), and so forth; and because the author himself will state the same in the first chapter with the words, "There exists the supreme Brahman which is Truth," and so on.

He describes the nature of Paramaśiva, whose form is the undifferentiated Brahman, beginning with the words "not drunk," and so forth. Here, the "Self" (ātman) refers to the undifferentiated Brahman. Brahman cannot be defined as "drunk" because, in its aspect as pure light (*prakāśa*), it is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*); nor can it be defined as "not drunk" because, in its aspect of self-reflection (*vimarśa*), it possesses attributes (*saguṇa*). Therefore, it is said that Brahman is an indefinable essence, distinct from being drunk, not drunk, and so on.
It exists. This same logic should be applied to what follows as well.

If this is so, then what is the nature of that Brahman? He says: "formless" (*nirākāra*). To the question, "What is the proof for the existence of that which is not perceived by direct perception? he says: "eternal" (*nitya*). [This refers to] the term *sanātana* found in the previously cited verse from the *Mahānirvāṇa*.

(The Commencement of the Work) Now, indeed, there was one of supreme compassion, whose mind was fixed upon the self-knowledge of the entire multitude of sentient beings— who were distressed by being swallowed by the mass of flames from the fierce submarine fire of intense sorrow within the ocean of saṃsāra, which is otherwise endless, difficult to cross, and most terrible.

The Blessed One, the Supreme Śiva, is understood to be eternal through the words of numerous hundreds of millions of extensive tantras dedicated to expounding the secrets of the propitiation of the Supreme Deity. Now, one might ask: "How could He not be subject to pleasure, pain, delusion, and so forth, as we are? To this he says: "devoid of the three qualities" (*triguṇarahita*). If this were so, since activity would be impossible, He would be of no use to anyone; what then would He have to do with us? To this [he replies]:

He said: "The Lord (devam). Although the Supreme Self is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), He plays by resorting to His own inherent power (*svarūpa-śakti*), for the sake of delighting living beings, repeatedly emitting and reabsorbing the entire manifold world (*prapañca*) contained within Himself; thus, He is the "Lord" (*deva*). Alternatively, "Lord" means one whose nature is to shine (*dyotana-śīla*), that is, the illuminator of the universe. Now, one might object: playing (*devana*) is a quality belonging to sentient beings, whereas by the preceding qualifiers...

Since its nature as consciousness is not perceived [by that means], he says: "non-inert" (*ajaḍam*). This means its nature is consciousness (*caitanyasvarūpa*), because its nature as consciousness is understood from the term "characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss" (*saccidānandalakṣaṇa*) found in the previously cited *Mahānirvāṇa* scripture. By this, it is stated that its "sporting" (*devanam*) is merely a play (*līlāmātra*). Now, one might object: "Let Brahman have such a nature; nevertheless, since it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), it lacks the nature of bliss."
If it is argued that the arising of happiness is not possible for us because we have not attained His true nature, he says in response: "The abode of the stream of supreme bliss.
Even though He is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), His nature as bliss is understood from the phrase "characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss" (*saccidānanda*).
Now, one might raise the objection: "Bliss exists for us as well; what then is His distinction? To dispel this doubt, the word "supreme" (*parama*) is used in relation to bliss.

This is the qualification. The distinction is that supreme bliss, unmixed with suffering, exists therein. He states that even that bliss is uninterrupted by saying "santāna" (continuum). The bliss of those such as ourselves is momentary, whereas the bliss of Paramaśiva is continuous; this alone is the distinction. Therefore, for the sake of attaining the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), one should [realize] that Self, which is Paramaśiva.

"I pay homage"—this is the intended meaning. Here, this should be noted: the nature of Paramaśiva as described by the previously cited verses of the *Mahānirvāṇa-tantra*—namely, "Śiva encased in the body is the individual soul (*jīva*); Śiva free from the casing is Paramaśiva" (1.5)—and as stated in the *Paraśurāma-kalpasūtra*, is as follows: [The text here would continue with the specific description of that nature].
That very [reality] is what is called "non-dual Brahman" (*nirviśeṣabrahman*) in the Upanishads. By the first verse, its nature as the venerable Guru (*śrīgurusvarūpa*) is declared;

however, by the verse beginning with "na pītam," its nature as non-dual (*nirviśeṣasvarūpa*) is stated. The author himself will explain this nature of non-duality later in the text, starting with the words "What, then, is the reality of the Self?
(*kintāvadātmavastu*).

He presented the essential point. And therein, his mind being deeply agitated by the distress of the great multitude of people who were devoid of the pure awakening regarding the various systems and independent philosophical tenets— which are difficult to fathom even when immersed in continuous meditation— he [drank] the abundant nectar of the Vedas, which is the most secret of secrets, flowing from the lotus mouth of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Guru, Śrī Brahmānanda.
Tundilānanda Śrī Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa composes the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* in the year nine hundred and ninety-four of the Śaka era [1494 CE].
(The nature of the Supreme Self and the individual soul)

Now, what indeed is the reality of the Self? The supreme Brahman—the abode of the universe, devoid of gross and subtle forms, whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free; the illuminator of the manifold world of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth; transcending the three qualities (*guṇatraya*);

formless, uncontradicted, and lacking beginning, middle, or end—that alone is the reality of the Self. Its parts are known as individual souls (*jīva*), which are those very [parts] afflicted by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*).

Having taken recourse to a body, they undergo various kinds of experiences of pleasure and pain. Beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), which has that [body] as its locus and that [body] as its object—just as a dark chamber is the locus and object of darkness—attains the nature of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*) by virtue of having that as its locus and that as its object; it then veils that Self and projects [the manifold world]. Although ignorance is insubstantial (*avastu*), nevertheless, having attained the existence and manifestation (*sphūrti*) of the Self...

It appears as if it were a real object; just as the reflection of an object situated near a stainless mirror arises unimpeded, so too the immutable reflection of consciousness (kūṭasthacidābhāsa) is reflected in ignorance (avidyā), which consists of the three qualities (guṇas) such as sattva.
(In that context, the term "Lord" [īśvara] refers to that which is conditioned by sattva.)

Among those, that reflection of the conscious light (*cidābhāsa*) mirrored in the *sattva* portion which serves as the cause, through the firm superimposition "I am That," is called the Lord (*īśvara*). Because he has the quality of *sattva* as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), he possesses omniscience, lordship over all, and the agency for all effects.
(The term *jīva* is applied to that which is conditioned by *rajas* and *tamas*.)

When that reflection of consciousness— which is the primary cause consisting of the quality of *sattva*— is reflected through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the portions of *rajas* and *tamas* which are its effects, and when, by the power of the causes of karma, it assumes the threefold limitation of space, time, and substance, abandons its full essential nature,
and attains distinctions of the same class, of different classes, and internal, then the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of "I" and "mine" occurs; at that time, it is the *jīva*.

Thus it is said. Because this [intellect] has an effect as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it possesses insentience (*jāḍya*). Due to that, one thinks: "I am the agent, I am the enjoyer, I am happy, I am miserable;

I do not know myself. The Śruti also states: "This individual soul (*jīva*) has an effect as its limiting adjunct; the Lord (*īśvara*) has a cause as his limiting adjunct. This is the exposition of the creation of the world and so forth.
In the Vedānta, Īśvara is postulated.
(Regarding creation and so forth as performed by Īśvara:
Īśvara, through the differentiation of the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), appears in the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others, due to *avidyā*.
Having attained the two forms— obscuration and projection— it creates, sustains, and destroys the ninefold cycle of existence from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
(Here follows the objection:)

Now, one might object: how can obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*) be possible for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is solitary, unattached, indifferent, eternally liberated, pure, awakened, beyond all qualities (*guṇa*), and devoid of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), possessiveness (*mamakāra*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and effort (*prayatna*)—just like a human horn? Just as when it is said that "the sky-lotus is fragrant," the very sky-lotus itself is non-existent; so too [is the objection].
Whence comes this state of being fragrant?

(The resolution: It is true that all this is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*); its effects, consisting of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*), do not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality (*vastugatyā*).

However, for one who does not know the Self, this is established merely through delusion due to a lack of discrimination. When a person is situated in the state of dream, does his dream-activity not appear to him as true—just as it does for a magician? Furthermore, when the dream has ceased, and likewise when the magician’s illusion has ceased, everyone knows that everything was indeed false; this is established by the experience of all.

Similarly, prior to the arising of knowledge, one determines that [the world] is indeed real; immediately thereafter, when its falsity is known, ignorance and its effects—consisting of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*)—are all the more easily destroyed.
(This is the formal promise to describe the method of the means.)

Now, for the sake of the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), the methods of practice are being stated in order to remove the obstruction of beginningless ignorance (anādyavidyā) to the attainment of the human goal; for [it was previously shown] by means of reasons such as "non-attachment" (asaṅgatva) and so forth, starting with the word "nanu," that [liberation] cannot be attained prior to the performance of Vedic rituals.

Having established the impossibility of veils (*āvaraṇa*), projections (*vikṣepa*), and so forth in the Supreme Self, and having presented an illustration with the words "just as a sky-lotus," etc., he states the reply to the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) beginning with "It is true," etc. Regarding the phrase "or of a magician":
when a magician, through the performance of various actions such as waving a peacock-feather whisk, displays his skill in creating various diverse illusions such as illusory heads and the like;

He demonstrates this; the connection is as follows: at that time, does that activity of the magician not appear as true? Furthermore—"furthermore" (punarapi) means "but rather" (parantu). Regarding the phrase "ceased in a dream": for one situated in a dream, when the dream has ceased, [the objects] such as the golden palaces and dwellings experienced in the dream [cease]; and likewise, for the magician, when the magician's illusion has ceased.
The meaning is that one knows the illusory head and other such things experienced during the state of a magician's performance to be false.
Having thus presented the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he states the conclusion by way of showing the illustrated point (*dārṣṭāntika*): "In the same way" (*tadvat*).
Through the accumulation of merit and the destruction of sin, attachment and aversion are eliminated by means of the cessation of *rajas* and *tamas*. Just as the seed of a tree...

The tree is the cause of the seed, and the seed is the cause of the tree; likewise, passion and ignorance are the causes of the evil intellect, and the evil intellect is also the cause of passion and ignorance.
Because they are mutually dependent, the destruction of even one leads to the destruction of the other.
This, along with other matters, is now expanded upon in verse, following the authority of the Śrutis, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and the authentic tradition, in brief:

(The Nature of the Supreme Self and the Individual Self) The Supreme Brahman exists as the true reality; He is Śiva, partless, omniscient, the creator of all, the Lord of all, stainless, and non-dual. (1)

He is self-luminous, without beginning or end, changeless, higher than the highest, devoid of qualities, and is existence-consciousness-bliss; those who are His portions are designated as individual souls (jīvas). || 2 ||
Afflicted by beginningless ignorance, like sparks within a fire,
they are all indeed differentiated by limiting adjuncts through beginningless karmas.
Restrained by their own merits and demerits consisting of pleasure and pain,
stationary beings, birds, insects, animals,
and humans are born and die within this worldly existence, which is an ocean of suffering. (4)
(Regarding the excellence of humans among embodied beings:
Among all living creatures, human beings are the foremost;
for by becoming wise and steadfast, they may attain the fourfold liberation.
Human birth becomes fruitful when it falls within the scope of the sacred scriptures.
5. He states the reason for the preeminence of the virtuous human being: "The knower," and so forth. Regarding the fourfold liberation:
"Among the eighty-four lakhs of bodies belonging to embodied beings, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) does not exist elsewhere except in the human state. 6.
Human birth is sometimes obtained through the accumulation of merit;
human birth is difficult to attain, serving as a ladder to liberation. (7)
(Without a connection to a body, the attainment of the goals of human life does not occur.
Without a body, no one can obtain the goals of human life.
Therefore, having protected the body, one should accomplish the obligatory duties. || 8 ||
(An effort must be undertaken for the sake of protecting the self’s connection with the body and for the sake of turning away from what is harmful:
One should protect the self with all one's being; the self is the vessel of everything.
One should apply effort for the sake of protection; while living, one beholds auspicious things.
If one does not restrain oneself from what is harmful by means of oneself, who else is there to act for one's benefit? Who then will deliver oneself? (10)

(One must apply the remedy for sin even in this present life: "He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here—once he has gone to that region where no medicine exists, being afflicted by disease, what will he do? (11)
As long as this body remains, one should take refuge in the ultimate reality (tattva). || 12 ||
The meaning is that a Brāhmaṇa attains Nirvāṇa, a Kṣatriya attains Sāyujya, a Vaiśya attains Sārūpya, and a Śūdra attains Sālokya.
This has been stated in the second chapter of the Nirvāṇatantra:
"For the Brāhmaṇa there is great liberation (Mahāmokṣa), and for the Kṣatriya, Sāyujya."
"The Śūdra born from the thighs shares the same world as [the other castes]. Thus [it is said].
As long as suffering has not yet taken hold, as long as calamities have not arrived, and as long as there is no restlessness of the senses, so long should you take refuge in the highest good. 13.
Attachment to saṃsāra obstructs one's welfare; and time passes away through various activities arising from worldly existence.
One who partakes in the abundance of pleasure and pain does not recognize his own welfare.
Having drunk the wine of delusion, the world does not know its own welfare. || 15 ||
(The transience of prosperity and other things:
Prosperity is like a dream, youth is comparable to a flower, and life is as flickering as lightning; for whom, then, could there be stability except through ignorance? 16.
The life of embodied beings passes away in vain; a mortal lives for a hundred years, yet half of that is stolen by sleep.
Even that remaining half is fruitless, being consumed by the sufferings of childhood, disease, and old age. (17)

(Those who are deluded in their discernment of what ought and ought not to be done meet with ruin. Alas! What man is not destroyed by being indolent in what must be undertaken, slumbering when one should be awake, and placing trust in a situation of fear? 18.
With a body like a line on water or a wave of the ocean,
how can one remain fearless in this impermanent world of beloved things?

16. *Dhṛti* is contentment arising from ignorance—that is, from the absence of knowledge regarding the impermanence of worldly possessions. The meaning is that a fool takes excessive delight even in perishable riches. (The delusion of living beings.)
Though seeing, one stumbles; though hearing, one does not understand. Time is like a reflection; as it wastes away, it cannot be recovered. (20)
(Time destroys everything):
By this, the earth is consumed and even Mount Meru is shattered;
the waters of the ocean dry up—alas, what need is there to speak of the body? (21)
"My offspring, my wife, my wealth, and my kinsmen"—
thus do those devoid of intelligence lament, alas, at the will of Time, which is like a wolf.
In performing the task that leads to the highest good, it is improper to waste time.
One should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's work in the forenoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one's task is finished or not. 23.
Death is inescapable for all; it ordains the young, those in their prime, the elderly, and even those within the womb—for such is this world. (24)
The gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as all classes of living beings, head toward destruction here; therefore, take refuge in that which is supreme good.
(The causes for the exhaustion of lifespan:

Through accepting gifts from those who are devoid of their own caste, stage of life, and proper conduct, and through greed for the wives and wealth of others, the lifespan of men comes to an end. (26)
Through the neglect of the study of the Vedas and the scriptures, as well as by deceiving one's teacher, the lifespan of men shall diminish due to the lack of restraint over the senses. (27)
Attachment must be abandoned in every way;
liberation occurs only through detachment, for all defects arise from attachment.
Therefore, having renounced attachment, remain established in reality and be happy. 28.

(If that is impossible, association with the virtuous alone should be sought: "Association should be abandoned by all means; if it cannot be abandoned, it should be formed only with the virtuous, for the company of the virtuous is indeed the medicine. (29)
(On the excellence of association with the virtuous and discernment:
Association with the virtuous and discernment are the two stainless eyes;
how could that man who lacks them not be blind, and how could he not stray from the path? 30.
(The relationship of the individual soul even with its own body is momentary; what need be said of wives, sons, and the like?
O Mistress of the Family, this living soul departs even after abandoning its own body;
for what reason, then, [should one cling to] the relationship with wife, son, father, mother, and so forth? || 31 ||
(Who is happy, or who is miserable?
For cyclic existence is the root of suffering; he who possesses it is miserable.
He by whom its abandonment has been accomplished is happy—of this there is no doubt. (32)
(The nature of the renunciant: He who indeed renounces the fruit of action is called a renunciant;
the wise man should avoid the cycle of worldly existence, which is the abode of all evils. 33.
31. The statement consisting of the four quarters beginning with *svadeha* is seen in the first chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Kulārṇava*.

Therein, the address *kuleśvarī* is the Lord’s address to the Goddess. It is likely that the author of this work did not alter even the word *kuleśvarī*, as that very same statement has been reproduced here in its entirety.
(On the Rejection of Saṃsāra and the Acceptance of the Knowledge of Reality): This world is entirely suffering in its beginning, middle, and end.
Therefore, renouncing saṃsāra and being established in reality, be happy. 34.
(One who is established in reality has no connection with meritorious or sinful actions:
"Neither by a hundred horse-sacrifices nor by a hundred killings of Brahmins are those stained by merit or sin whose Brahman resides in their hearts. (35)
The dependence upon the functioning of the senses is itself the cause of actions; when that is abandoned, there is no arising of action.
Whatever actions exist on earth are caused by the tongue and the genitals;
one who has abandoned the tongue and the genitals—what will he do with action? (36)
(Who are those who go to hell?
Those people who do not know what is beneficial or harmful, who constantly follow the wrong path, and whose sole aim is the filling of their bellies, are remembered as denizens of hell. || 37 ||
(The excellence of the wise and the beast-like nature of those for whom mere enjoyment is the essence:
Sleep, fear, sexual intercourse, and food are common to all living beings.
One who possesses knowledge is called a human; one devoid of knowledge is a great beast. (38)
(Transmigrating beings experience incessant specific suffering due to the agitation caused by their respective duties:
"It is said that human beings are indeed afflicted by excrement and urine in the morning, by hunger and thirst at midday, and by passion and sleep at night. (39)
(But the deluded, attached to sense-objects, are subject to the continuous cycle of birth and death:
All living beings, entirely absorbed in their own bodies, sons, wives, and so forth, are born and they die; alas! Alas! They are utterly bewildered by ignorance. 40.
(For the attainment of the Self does not come about merely through the observance of the conduct prescribed for one's caste and stage of life:
All human beings who are devoted solely to the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life do not know the Supreme Brahman; being fools, they certainly perish. 41.
(“Some fools deceive the world with the ostentation of celibacy and other such practices, yet even through that, there is no attainment of the Self.
Some, devoted to the exhaustion of ritual actions and endowed with celibacy and other virtues, wander about as boatmen, their souls shrouded in ignorance. (42)
(For the Self is not attained by mere observances such as fasting:
"Enveloped by the Great Illusion, fools desire that which is beyond perception through rules such as eating once a day or fasting, which merely wither the body. (43)
What liberation can there be for the undiscriminating merely through the punishment of the body? (44)

(A type of deceivers: Attached to wealth, wives, and children, these lustful men who assume the dress [of ascetics] wander about in the world as if they possessed knowledge, and they cause other people to wander as well. (45)
A wise person should always avoid from afar one who is attached to worldly pleasures and claims "I am a knower of Brahman," as if he were a caṇḍāla.
(For one does not become a man of knowledge merely by sharing the common traits of a knower, such as living in a house or a forest, being devoid of shame, or being naked:
"In this world, donkeys and other animals live in houses or forests, are free from shame, and wander about naked; do they thereby become solitary [sages]? (47)
Do those who subsist on grass, leaves, and water, constantly dwelling in the forest, and even the deer and other wild animals, become ascetics? (48)
45. *Abhikāḥ* means lustful. *Veśadhāriṇaḥ* means those who assume disguises, wearing the attire appropriate for ascetics such as dyed garments, garlands, water-pots (*kamaṇḍalu*), and so forth.
They are indifferent to cold, wind, and heat, and likewise indifferent to what is fit or unfit to be eaten.
And do boars and other such animals remain [in that state], and do they become observers of vows? 49.
From birth until the end of death, those who dwell on the banks of rivers such as the Gaṅgā—chief among them frogs and fish—are they not observers of vows? (50)
(Knowledge alone is the direct cause of liberation, not action.
Therefore, [the verse beginning with] "tasmāt" states that action is merely a means for pleasing the world;
the direct cause of liberation is the knowledge of reality, and not otherwise. || 51 ||
(For self-attainment does not come through the mere study of the six systems of philosophy:
"Beings who have fallen into the great well of the six systems are always like cattle; constrained by the bonds of the beastly, they do not know the ultimate reality. (52)
(For even the words of one who knows the Vedas and so forth, if he does not know reality, do not lead to benefit.
He who knows the Vedas, Agamas, and Purāṇas but does not know the ultimate truth—even for such a person, all that is merely the chatter of a crow. (53)
(For those who are averse to the supreme reality, there is no attainment of the Self even through the constant study of scriptures:
"‘This is knowledge, this is the object of knowledge’—thus distracted by such thoughts, those who are averse to the supreme reality study the scriptures day and night. (54)
Knowledge of the scriptures and such is easily obtained, but knowledge of their intended meaning is not so.
The head bears the flowers, but the nose perceives the fragrance; people recite the Vedas and the Shastras, yet one who truly understands their inner spirit is rare. (55)
The study of the treatises is beneficial for the wise, but not for anyone else.
For one devoid of wisdom, reading is like a blind man looking into a mirror.
For the wise, the Dharma-śāstra is the cause of the knowledge of reality.
For one lacking wisdom, the treatises on Dharma lead to bondage;
they merely argue with one another, saying, "The reality is like this," or "It is like that. (57)
Desiring to hear all about this knowledge and this object of knowledge from every side, one does not reach the end of the scriptures even in a thousand years. (58)
(One should extract the essence from the treatises: "Logic and many other sciences are millions of obstacles to the short human lifespan;
therefore, one should discern the essence, just as a swan extracts milk from water. (59)
(The study of the scriptures has as its limit the knowledge of reality:
Having studied all the scriptures and having known the reality, the wise man should abandon all the scriptures, just as one seeking grain discards the straw. (60)
55. He is the awakener of dispositions and the knower of the divine, heroic, and animal states. And so it is said in the first chapter of the Rudrayāmala-uttarakhaṇḍa:
"Whether he be a great hero, a great sage, or even one established in the divine state..."
Alternatively, the practitioner situated in the state of a beast (paśubhāva) should cause [the disciple] to dwell in a sacred seat (pīṭha).
Likewise: "In the Kali age, those whose minds are constantly fixed upon it, being great devotees through the divine and the heroic [means], behold the supreme state of Mahāvidyā."
Likewise: The virtuous, who are of a silent disposition and always intent on spiritual practice, behold the lotus feet of my state through their divine-heroic nature.
Having thus expressed praise for the states of being such as the divine and so forth, a statement with a word-order almost identical to this one has been presented. For example:
"The tree bears flowers; the nose perceives fragrance."
"They study the Vedas and Śāstras, yet those that awaken [true] emotion (bhāva) are rare.
In accordance with this statement, although there is no distinction here, it should be understood that by the word "emotion" (bhāva), only divine and other such emotions are intended.
Just as there is no need for food for a dead body, it is certain that for one who knows reality, there is likewise no need for the web of scriptures. (61)
(Only knowledge is the cause of liberation, not the study of scriptures:
"Liberation does not come from the study of the Vedas, nor even from the recitation of the Shastras;
for liberation arises only from knowledge, and never otherwise. (62)
(The nature of liberation:
The wise declare that liberation is the cessation of infinite suffering.
(Regarding this, there is another opinion:)
"The destruction of craving is liberation"—thus do those who know the Tantras understand. || 63 ||

(Regarding this, my own view is as follows: "In the imperishable Supreme Self, which is a mass of pure bliss, the abiding of the individual self—that, in reality, is my conviction to be liberation. (64)
(If there is no connection with knowledge, means such as ritual action do not bring about liberation:
What is the use of bodily mortification or the extensive performance of sacrifices?
What is the use of conduct and reflection if knowledge is not attained? (65)
(The scriptures such as the Vedas are not the cause of liberation; knowledge alone is the cause of liberation.
The Vedas are not the cause of liberation, nor are the philosophical systems the cause;
likewise, all scriptures are not the cause—knowledge alone is indeed the cause. (66)
66. "All scriptures are not the cause of liberation"—this is the connection with what precedes. If one asks, "Then what is the cause of liberation?", he says:

"Knowledge" (*jñāna*). In the reading *jñānasyaiva*, the meaning is that all scriptures are the cause of knowledge alone, and not of liberation, because knowledge itself is the cause with respect to liberation.
(The two-fold nature of knowledge:
That very same knowledge is of two kinds, arising from discrimination and from scripture.
The Śabdabrahman consists of scripture, while the Parabrahman is born of discrimination. (67)
(The Nature of Śabdabrahman):
From the supreme *bindu*, as it was being differentiated, there arose a sound whose essence is unmanifest;
those proficient in all the scriptures call that "Śabdabrahman. (68)

67. In the preceding verse it was stated that knowledge alone is the cause; now he describes the divisions of that knowledge with the words "tadeva" (that very same). That knowledge is indeed of two kinds. Here, by the use of the restrictive particle *eva*, there is the exclusion of conventional cognitions of jars, cloths, and so forth, which are not conducive to liberation. The twofold nature of knowledge consists in its being possible through discrimination (*viveka*) and its being possible through scripture (*āgama*). He states that very point with the words "śabda... (through word...).

"Śabdabrahman" means sound whose essence is Brahman; that is, the knowledge of it. It is "consisting of scripture" (āgamamaya), meaning produced by scripture, because it is established by the *śruti* itself. However, the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahma*) is born of discrimination (*viveka*), since the attainment of the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman occurs through discrimination alone. 68. Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa says: he describes the origin of Śabdabrahman with the words "from that which is being divided" (*bhidyamānāt*), [referring] to the Supreme (*para*).

By the word "bindu" (the point), that which is the first *bindu* in the form of the state of *śakti* is meant; from that, the unmanifest essence—the indivisible *nāda* alone, devoid of specific qualities such as phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth—is produced. As it has been said by the Teachers:
"That sound is called *śabdabrahman* by those endowed with the power of hearing."

Thus, the meaning of *śabdabrahman* is that sound—which is the undivided, unmanifest, pervasive, and Brahman-natured essence consisting of *nāda* and *bindu*, being merely the first manifestation (*ullāsa*) of Supreme Śiva intent upon creation. And it has been said:
"It is the cause of both the word and its meaning for [the Power] whose primary attribute is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*)."
"From Prakṛti, who is of the nature of Bindu, the supreme Śabdabrahman arose.
This should be understood as follows: the Supreme Lord is both Niṣkala (partless) and Sakala (with parts). By the word *kalā*, Prakṛti is denoted;
He who is devoid of connection with that is Niṣkala, and He who is connected with it is Sakala. This very Prakṛti belongs to Paraśiva.

She is of the nature of the power of essential being (*svarūpa-śakti*); therefore, since she is the power of essential being of Paramaśiva, whose nature is *saccidānanda*, Prakṛti also possesses the nature of *saccidānanda*. In this regard, Paraśiva is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), and Parāśakti is likewise; thus, when the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*) arises in Paramaśiva by virtue of his divine play (*līlā*), Parāprakṛti also manifests as the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). As it has been said:
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"By the will of Śiva, the Supreme Power (parā śakti) attains oneness with the Śiva-principle;
thereafter, at the beginning of creation, she vibrates forth like oil from a sesame seed."
(The two views of the proponents of *sphoṭa*: Others know the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) as the meaning of the word, while still others know it as the word itself.
(The refutation of those two views.)
For the establishment of those two does not belong to them, because both are indeed insentient.
Also in the *Pāñcarātra* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"Having thus perceived at the beginning of creation [the Goddess] whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss,
and who is the substratum for the manifestation of the entire aggregate of principles..."
"The Supreme Person makes that eternal Prakṛti manifest.
Also, in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"Victorious is that primordial Śakti, whose nature is eternally incomparable and consists of her own bliss."
The seed of all that is moving and unmoving, a stainless mirror for the contemplation of the form of Śiva.

By this, it has been established that the Supreme Śakti is of the same nature as Paraśiva, that she is the cause of the universe, and that she also sustains the "I-consciousness" (ahantā) of Paraśiva. By this, it is stated that the creation of the phenomenal world arises from the mutual relationship between Paramaśiva and his Śakti.

And thus, although the Supreme Lord is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), by virtue of His connection with the power whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), He assumes the state of the *bindu*, which consists of the realization "I am full. The same applies to the supreme primordial nature (*paramā prakṛti*). As it was stated by Naṭānandanātha, the author of the commentary on the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*: "The Supreme Lord [is that] whose nature is the dissolution of the entire universe, which is His own limb..."

Having entered into the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*), it becomes the state of the *bindu*. Then, that power of reflective awareness also enters into the *bindu* consisting of light which is within itself; consequently, the *bindu* becomes swollen, and so forth.
By this, it is shown that the very state of power (*śaktyavasthā*) which is the first manifestation of Paramaśiva, whose nature is light, is that [very state].
The first *bindu* follows; by the phrase "from the supreme *bindu* as it is being differentiated," this very *bindu* is indicated.
With this very intention, Rāghavabhaṭṭa stated that by the phrase "from the supreme *bindu*" is meant the first *bindu*, which consists of the state of *śakti*.

69. Here Rāghavabhaṭṭa begins to refute the doctrine of the internal sphoṭa (āntarasphoṭavāda)—that is, the doctrine of sphoṭa consisting of both genus (jāti) and individual (vyakti)—with the words "śabda... etc. Some teachers declare that the word-meaning, which is the internal sphoṭa, is the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman). As it has been said: "The word-meaning consists of an indivisible, partless, eternal, and conscious nature."

Regarding the term "internal sphoṭa": other grammarians [hold that it is] the nature of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), which is awakened by the apprehension of the final word, aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of each respective word manifested by the utterance of each preceding phoneme.
It is my conviction that the consciousness of all beings is the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
(Manifestation of Phonemes):
Having reached that form of Kuṇḍalin situated within the bodies of living beings,
it manifests in the nature of phonemes through the distinctions of prose, verse, and so forth.
(An Examination of Duality and Non-duality) Some desire non-duality, while others desire duality; there are two states leading to bondage and liberation: "mine-ness" and "not-mine-ness. (72)

They declare that the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) is the word characterized as a sentence-sphoṭa (*vākyasphoṭa*), which reveals a single indivisible meaning. As it has been said: "The external sphoṭa—whether it be the individual-sphoṭa (*vyaktisphoṭa*) or the class-sphoṭa (*jātisphoṭa*)—is one, eternal, indivisible, and manifested by sentences. Thus, having presented two views on this matter, they have refuted them: some understand the Word-Brahman to be the very meaning of the word, while others [hold] that it is the word itself.
The connection is: "They know [it] as Śabdabrahman.

Thus, he refutes with the words beginning "na hi" both the previously mentioned view of the proponents of the internal sphoṭa—that the meaning of the word is Śabdabrahman—and the view of the proponents of the genus-sphoṭa and individual-sphoṭa—that the word itself is Śabdabrahman. Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa says: "Of those..."

In the view of those disputants, the establishment of those two—word and meaning—is not the establishment of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), because both of them are insentient (jaḍa). If either the word or the meaning were called the Word-Brahman, then the status of being denotable by the term "Brahman" would not be tenable; for the referent of the term "Brahman" consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda), whereas those two are insentient. As it has been said:
"Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the essence of sound, the imperishable syllable;
it manifests in the form of objects, from which the process of the world proceeds.
(70) He states his own view: "Consciousness," etc. The meaning is that consciousness alone is the Śabda-Brahman of all beings.
This has been stated in the *Prayogasāra* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"O Goddess, that Inner Self, being of the nature of sound (*nādātmā*), then sounds forth spontaneously.

By this, it is understood that the very same doctrine established by the passage beginning with "bhidyamānāt" (as it is being divided) is also expressed by the passage beginning with "caitanyam" (consciousness).
71. Having thus described the supreme creation of sound consisting of *nāda*, he speaks of the creation of phonemes (*varṇa*) with the word "that" (*tat*).

Here, Rāghavabhaṭṭa explains: the connection is that the consciousness in the form of the *kuṇḍalinī*—which resides within the bodies of living beings in the form of the *kuṇḍalinī*—manifests as the nature of phonemes through the distinctions of prose, poetry, and so forth. Having done what? Having reached the organs such as the throat.
The remainder [of the commentary]:
Having previously stated that the lower Brahman consists of scripture while the higher Brahman arises from discrimination,
and having established the nature of the Śabdabrahman;
Two positions have been set forth due to the distinction between ignorance (avidyā) and knowledge (vidyā). || 73 ||

Bondage and liberation are produced by actions consisting of ignorance and knowledge respectively. That action which leads to bondage is proclaimed as ignorance; that action which does not lead to bondage is declared to be knowledge. (74)
(Bondage and liberation exist precisely through the existence and non-existence of conceptual construction:
As long as conceptual construction itself exists, so long indeed is there bondage;
as long as that very thing does not exist at all, so long indeed is there liberation. (75)
(That action must be practiced until the knowledge of reality is attained:
Recitation, fire-offerings, worship, pilgrimage, the Vedas, the Shastras, the Agamas, and so forth—all these indeed remain necessary only as long as one has not found the ultimate reality. 76.
(Only steadfastness in reality is the cause for attaining liberation.
Therefore, if one desires liberation for oneself, the wise person should, with effort, remain steadfast in reality at all times and in all conditions. (77)
I shall describe its nature—the essence of the knowledge of reality—characterized by the Vedas and Agamas, according to its specific method. (78)
The one supreme Brahman alone is the eternal essence of rasa;
by means of Prakṛti, he is made manifest, and likewise, he is again made unmanifest by her.
Therefore, through the application of one's innate nature, one shall swiftly attain direct perception, just as light is the manifestor at the moment a jar is perceived. (80)

He states the nature of the Supreme Brahman with the words "some" (*kecit*). This refers to the proponents of Māyā (the Māyāvādins). "Others" (*apare*) refers to the Naiyāyikas and so forth. Here, by the terms "some" and "others," the lack of intrinsic validity in both systems is indicated. The meaning is that this is because the *Kulārṇava*, in its first chapter, states that the Supreme Brahman is distinct from both duality and non-duality, with the verse: "They do not know my true nature, which is devoid of both duality and non-duality. "Two steps" (*dve pada*)... [text continues].
The meaning is that the cognition "this is mine" leads to bondage, while the cognition "this is not mine" leads to liberation.
Just as a jar is not perceived unless it is conjoined with the property of "jar-ness," so too, even though it is being distinguished from others, [the Self] does not undergo differentiation. (81)
In the Puruṣa, there is no differentiation whatsoever without Śakti;
it cannot be [attained] through ritual applications, nor through cognitions, nor through the Vedas, nor through the lineage of gurus.
(Primordial Nature alone is the direct cause for the knowledge of reality:
Through Nature Brahma is known; through Nature the person is dissolved;
everything is presided over by Nature; the entire world is desired by Nature.
The knowledge of the equal flavor of these two is the reality of things, the supreme state. || 83 ||
There are many diverse means for knowing the eternal Brahman;
nevertheless, through the application of *prakṛti*, one may quickly attain direct perception of it. (84)
Just as a sea-faring merchant, having taken his ship to a foreign land, traverses various regions and only after a long time enters the great ocean; || 85 ||
Just as one takes a boat from one bank and returns to it in an instant, so too those [factors] that have come down in succession have indeed become the causes. 86.
