For those [other causes] are not the direct cause; rather, Primordial Matter (prakṛti) is the direct cause.
Therefore, I shall describe that Primordial Matter, preceded by the ritual procedure for initiation (dīkṣā). || 87 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Knowledge of Reality," in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the holy Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 1 ||

87 | Regarding "prakṛti": here, because "causality" (kāraṇatva) is the predicate, a compound with the word "prakṛti," which serves as the subject, would otherwise be improper; nevertheless, it is accepted out of fear of violating the meter. This is the second chapter.

(The Section on Initiation) Therein: the meaning of the word *dīkṣā*, the fruit of initiation, the varieties of initiation, the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple, the conduct of the disciple toward the teacher, an investigation into the wheels (*cakras*) such as Akatha and Hādi, an investigation into the days [of the week] for initiation, and therein [an investigation into] favorable and unfavorable months, lunar dates (*tithis*), and weekdays—
(The determination of constellations, ascendants, and so forth; the meaning of the word "mantra"; and the ten purificatory rites of mantras.
(Its utility for the determination of initiation:
Now, those who have not received initiation certainly possess no authority here.
Therefore, I shall now proclaim the initiation (dīkṣā) which bestows the fourfold aims of human existence.

1. Having stated in the previous section that the knowledge of Brahman is the means for accomplishing the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), in this section he introduces *dīkṣā* (initiation)—which establishes the qualification for the worship of the deity Śrī Tripurasundarī, who is the subject of this system—on the grounds that the knowledge of Brahman is rooted in *upāsanā* (meditative worship), and because scripture declares that those who have not been initiated lack the qualification for such worship. He begins with the word "atha" (now).
The *Gautamīya Tantra*, in its seventh chapter, states that the qualification for worship depends upon initiation (*dīkṣā*):
"Now I shall explain initiation, which bestows the accomplishment of all desires and goals;
without which a mantra will not be effective even after hundreds of years."

In the third chapter of the Bṛhannīlatantra, concerning initiation (dīkṣā), it is said: "O Great Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, without that [initiation], there is no authority over ritual action among any of the stages of life, among all beings, or among all the gods."
"O Great Goddess, without initiation (dīkṣā), everything for him becomes in vain.
The entire world has initiation as its root; initiation is the root of supreme austerity;
initiation is the root of great accomplishment (mahāsiddhi); therefore, one should perform initiation. Thus it is said.
And in the fourteenth chapter of the Kulārṇava:
"O Dear One, those who perform rites such as recitation and worship without initiation do not achieve results for them, like seeds sown in a stone."
(The etymology of the word *dīkṣā*):
Because it bestows divine knowledge and effects the destruction of sins, it is therefore called *dīkṣā* by the teachers who are knowers of the Tantras. (2)
(Another type of that [initiation]):
Alternatively, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is said by the virtuous to be the perfect consecration of the deity and the mantra by a Guru; it is the destroyer of all sins. (3)
Furthermore,
because it bestows a divine state here [in this world], because it exhausts karma consisting of illusion,
and because it yields the fruit arising from the four aims of life, it is therefore designated as *dīkṣā*.
(The Fruit of Initiation) Whatever sin has been committed over ten million lifetimes, whether done knowingly or unknowingly, flees at the mere reception of initiation; of this there is no doubt. (5)

Through the three initiations, a person destroys the sins of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, and other such major offenses, as well as hundreds of thousands of minor offenses (upapātaka).
(The differences in the fruits of initiation according to the distinction of caste:
An initiated Brāhmaṇa goes to the stainless world of Brahmā;
a Kṣatriya likewise goes to the world of Indra, and a Vaiśya to that of Prajāpati.
A Śūdra goes to the city of the Gandharvas through the power of initiation;
therefore, initiation is praised for all four castes.
O Goddess, for one devoid of initiation there is neither spiritual perfection nor a favorable rebirth;
therefore, with every effort, one should be initiated by a Guru.
This has been established by such statements as these. (The threefold nature of initiation): "In the Śiva-āgama, initiation is indeed of three kinds: the Śāmbhavī, the Śākta, and the Māntrī."
Initiation is taught as being threefold by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
(Therein, the Mantra-initiation:
Having directly realized the chosen deity according to the path of Mantra, the Guru instructs the disciple; that is called Mantra-initiation. (10)
(Another variety of that very [initiation] is called "accompanied by ritual action"):
Alternatively, it is performed by means of mantra, worship, meditation, yoga, and so forth, by the Guru through the path of yoga and in accordance with the scriptures. (11)
That [initiation] is the Mantrī, which is accompanied by ritual action and preceded by the sacrificial pit and the mandala.
(Another variety of the Mātrī:
Others, however, say that initiation by mantra consists merely of the instruction of the mantra. 12.
(This initiation by means of mantra is common to all castes and traditions. Indeed,
the initiation pertaining to mantra is traditionally held to be common to all within the various groups of mantras.
And it shall also prevail among the castes, beginning with the twice-born, as well as among the Śāktas and the Vaiṣṇavas.
9–17 | Regarding the term *śāmbhavī*: initiation (*dīkṣā*) is threefold—*śāmbhavī*, *śākteyī*, and *māntrī*.
By the word "threefold" (*tredhā*), it is indicated that other varieties of initiation, such as the *āṇava* and so forth, are included within these very categories.
Now, having here pointed out the three types of initiation in the sequence of *śāmbhavī*, *śākteyī*, and *māntrī*...

Regarding the passage beginning with "according to the path of Mantra" (*mantramārgānusāreṇa*), etc.: at the point of defining their respective specific characteristics, why is there an instruction given in reverse order as "the Mantric, the Śākta, and the Śāmbhava"? Or alternatively, [why is it said] "(the initiation is) Śākta"?
When success is achieved by observing one's own power, the initiation performed for a child through that power alone,
without any external means, is proclaimed as the Śākteyī initiation.
(The initiation consisting of knowledge itself is considered by some to be the Śākta initiation); now, others maintain that the initiation consisting of knowledge is the Śakti initiation. (15)
(Śāmbhavī Dīkṣā):
Without any prior intention on the part of either the teacher or the disciple,
the manifestation of Śiva-nature occurs solely through the grace of the Guru.
This is declared to be Śāmbhavī, which brings about the immersion into Śiva.
(Another variety thereof:
"By the mere sight of the Guru, or by touch, or even by conversation, consciousness arises immediately in the person; this is called the Śāmbhavī [mudrā] in the Āgama. (17)
"That initiation (dīkṣā) is threefold: the Mantric, the Śākta, and the Śāmbhavī.

Although this statement from the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra* provides a specific sequential order for the initiations, why is there here a presentation in reverse order? It is said: in the *Ṣaḍāmnāya-mahāratna* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa—
That initiation is threefold;
the first is the Āṇavī, the next is the Śākteyī, and the other is the Śāmbhavī, which bestows immediate liberation.
Having thus demonstrated the primacy of the *āṇava-dīkṣā*, [it is stated]:
"That initiation which is performed through mantra, worship, the seat, the location, meditation, yoga, and so forth,
by one who acts according to what is taught in the scriptures, is called *āṇava*."
Thus, since the characteristic of the *āṇava* initiation has been established, either as being performed together with that [initiation],
or as being performed through mantra, worship, meditation, yoga, and so forth—

because there is no difference from the characteristic of the *māntra* initiation described by Pūrṇānanda and others, the *kriyāvatī* (action-based) or *māntrī* (mantra-based) initiation is indeed the *āṇava* initiation.

And its primacy has indeed been established by the previously cited statement regarding the six great jewels of the Āmnāyas. Consequently, it is settled that the first is the Māntrī, the second is the Śāktī, and the third is the Śāmbhavī. For this very reason, in the Gandharvatantra, in the twenty-sixth chapter, referring to the sequence of the Māntrī, Śāktī, and Śāmbhavī:

The mantra-initiation (māntrī dīkṣā) is said to be that which is performed through the recitation of mantras, worship, the seat, the locus, meditation, yoga, and so forth, according to the procedures prescribed in the scriptures.
When the Siddhas, having perceived their own power, perform initiation for a disciple by means of that power alone and without external means, it is proclaimed as the Śākteyī initiation.
Without any prior intention on the part of either the teacher or the disciple, this Śāmbhavī initiation—
which brings about the manifestation of Śiva-nature solely through the grace of the Guru—
effects the immersion into Śiva.

The characteristics [of the initiations] have been defined accordingly. Thus, when a disciple has first gained entry through the initiation by means of mantra (māntradīkṣā) as prescribed by the rules according to the previously mentioned characteristics of those respective initiations, the second initiation is the *māntrī* initiation, which is the unfolding of the guru’s own power (*svaśakti*) who is perfected in mantra. Then, for the disciple whose power has been manifested, the third is the *śāmbhavī* initiation, which is the accomplishment of his state of Śiva-hood (*śivatā*).
"The term *dīkṣā* is understood [in this way]; such is the Siddhānta following the great jewel of the six Āmnāyas.
However, in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, it says:
'In the Śivāgama, there is the Śāmbhavī, the Śāktī, and the Māntrī [initiation].'"
Initiation is taught as threefold by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Having thus indicated:
"By the mere glance of the Guru, by touch, or even by conversation, consciousness arises immediately in the person; that is considered Śāmbhavī initiation."
The Śākta initiation, which possesses knowledge, is performed by the Guru through the path of yoga and with the eye of wisdom after entering the body of the disciple;
whereas the Māntrī initiation is ritualistic and is preceded by the preparation of the sacrificial pit and the mandala.

Thus, these characteristics have been established. In this ritual manual (*kalpa*), first, for the disciple whose soul is deluded by sense objects, there is the attainment of consciousness through the mere sight of the true Guru according to the respective characteristics previously mentioned; thereafter comes detachment from sense objects—this is the *śāmbhavī* initiation.

Then, for one who has been endowed with the state of Śambhu through this initiation, there is the second, the *śākta* initiation. And that is "possessed of knowledge" (*jñānavatī*); therefore, by means of it—

When knowledge arises through initiation, there is the third, the Mantric initiation (*māntrī dīkṣā*). This consists of ritual action (*kriyāvatī*) characterized by the predominance of rites, preceded by means such as the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the mandala; it is for the disciple who has been brought into the state of Śambhu by the two previously mentioned initiations and in whom knowledge has arisen, and which takes the form of the bestowal of mantras.
With this very intention [it was said]:
"The great initiation (mahādīkṣā) and likewise the initiation (dīkṣā), and thereafter the instruction (upadeśa);
in every age it must be performed, but in the Kali age, the instruction [is what must be done]."

Thus, even by this statement from the *Viśvasāra* cited in the *Tantrasāra*, having established that the three initiations must be performed in every age, it is declared that the initiation consisting of oral instruction (*mantradīkṣā*) is the final one. Here, because of the expression "after that" (*tataḥ param*), it is understood that the performance of the three initiations themselves is required.

Because the instruction regarding internal sacrifices and other rites— which depend on the knowledge of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) and so forth— can by no means enter the mind of a disciple that is clouded by powerful ignorance,
[this is the meaning of the term *āgama*.]
Having emerged from the mouths of Śiva and entered the mouth of Girijā, it was then received by Vāsudeva; therefore, this is called Āgama.
(The Characteristics of the Guru) Now I shall describe the characteristics of gurus as indicated in the Tantra:
he is the best of Brahmins, capable both of uplifting and of destroying. (19)
Contemplating with his intellect the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra,
he should recite it with one-pointed mind from the morning until midday.

Furthermore, because the cultivation of the identity between the deity, the guru, and the mantra as taught in the twenty-eighth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra* would otherwise be untenable, it follows that instruction regarding ritual action (*karma*) is only appropriate when the disciple’s heart has been purified by knowledge (*jñāna*). It should be noted that for the purpose of demonstrating these two views, the venerable Paramahaṃsas have provided the definitions of the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣākrama*)—namely the Śāmbhavī, Śāktī, and Māntrī—in a reverse order. Likewise:
Furthermore, the conclusion here is that the characteristics of both types of initiation have been indicated by the venerable Paramahaṃsas through the words "or else" (*athavā*) and so forth.
19. Both the teacher and the disciple, out of delusion, [proceed] without examining one another.

Since the fourteenth chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava* states, "By giving instruction or receiving it, both may incur the state of a *piśāca*," thereby prohibiting the transmission and reception of mantras between teacher and disciple without mutual examination,
and since such examination depends upon knowledge of their characteristics, the characteristics of both teacher and disciple must now be stated.

He states the characteristics of the Guru as they follow in sequence, beginning with the word "atha" (now). Likewise, in the third chapter of the Bṛhannīlatantra: "One who wears irreproachable attire, free from deceit, possessed of proper conduct, and intent upon the propitiation of Mahāvidyā."
One who is devoted to the conduct of that kalpa is called a Guru;
the knower of Kaula wisdom, the great yogi, is indeed the Guru and the deity.

"O beautiful one, he alone who is of noble birth, the giver of all mantras among all [beings], and the master of initiation is the Self; no other, even if he has mastered the Vedas. Thus it is specifically stated in the thirteenth chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*:
O Supreme Goddess, the glorious Guru is elegantly attired and captivating;
he is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with the beauty of every limb.

One who knows the reality of mantras and yantras, a knower of their vital points and secrets, one who has performed the preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa), an adept, and one who knows the application for the attainment of mantra-siddhi. || 20 ||
He knows the true meaning of all scriptures, he is conversant with the application of all mantras,
he causes the delusion of the world, and his appearance is as pleasing as that of a god.
He has a pleasant countenance, is easy to approach, pure, and the destroyer of delusion and doubt;
he understands gestures and facial expressions, is wise, skilled in reasoning and refutation, and is radiant.
With the internal as the object of focus and the gaze directed outward, he is omniscient and knows time and place;
he possesses the perfection of command, knows the three times, and is capable of both restraint and grace.
He is a piercer [of ignorance], an awakener, peaceful, and devoted to compassion for all living beings;
he has mastery over the movement of his senses and is capable of conquering the group of six [internal enemies].
Foremost among the assembly, profoundly deep, and discerning between those who are worthy vessels and those who are not;
a saint equal to Śiva and Viṣṇu, he was a reviler of the dull-witted.
Stainless, eternally contented, independent, and possessed of the power of mantras;
affectionate toward true devotees, steadfast, compassionate, and whose speech is full of smiles.
He is fond of devotion, eternally generous, profound, and a practitioner of refined conduct;
he is ever eager to worship his chosen deity, his guru, his elders, and women.
Dedicated to blameless actions— whether obligatory, occasional, or performed for specific desires—
he is free from attachment, aversion, fear, affliction, hypocrisy, and egoism.
Devoted to the practice of his own knowledge, he is an acquirer of dharma and other virtues;
satisfied with whatever comes by chance, he discerns between qualities and defects.

Unattached to women, wealth, and the like, as well as to evil associations and vices; endowed with the sense of universal "I-am-ness" (sarvāhaṃbhāva), free from the pairs of opposites, and firm in his vows.
For he is free from greed, impartial toward those without preconceived notions, discerning, and one who does not sell wealth, learning, or the like, nor mantras, yantras, tantras, and so forth.
Free from attachment, free from conceptual construction, having ascertained the ultimate meaning, and supremely righteous;
equal toward blame and praise, observing silence, indifferent to worldly concerns, and free from affliction.
"O Dear One, the Śrī-guru is said to be endowed with such characteristics as these.
Also, in the twenty-sixth chapter of the Gandharva-tantra: "The Guru is endowed with all virtues, his mind untouched by defects," and so forth.
Thus it should be understood in other places as well.
One who is a giver, self-controlled, tranquil in mind, whose body is utterly at peace, a knower of the supreme self, a celibate student, and of noble birth—such a person is called a guru. (21)
(The Characteristics of a Disciple) Handsome, pleasant-faced, pure, wise, and of firm resolve;
free from greed, steady-limbed, observant, and having conquered the senses. (22)
A disciple should be one who possesses faith and firm devotion toward the guru, the mantra, and the deity; one who is otherwise causes suffering to the guru.
(Before initiation, the disciple should serve the guru);
first, service to the guru must be performed with body, speech, mind, and wealth. || 24 ||
(The Manner of Serving the Guru):
On an auspicious day, having performed his bath and worshipped Gaṇanāyaka, Sūrya, Hari, Śiva, Durgā, Vāṇī, and Kamalālayā; 25.

22. He states the characteristics of the disciple with the words "handsome" (*sundara*). Also, in the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*: "One who is endowed with the aforementioned suitable qualities, who is exceedingly pleasant in speech, whose body and face are pure, who wears white garments, and is clean."
He was averse to censuring others and to visiting the shrines of deities;
he was free from longing for women and for the oppression of the earth.
Endowed with compassion for all people, acting with discernment, having conquered the senses,
being a believer, devoted to the guru, pure, and of very firm resolve;
Free from greed, possessing steady friendship, taking the words of the guru as authoritative,
and always maintaining firm devotion toward the guru, the mantra, and the deity.

"A disciple of such a kind [is acceptable], whereas any other causes suffering for the guru. As for the characteristics of the perfected guru and disciple, the author of this work has not included them; therefore, we have also omitted them. Their detailed exposition, however, should be sought in the *Kulārṇava* and other such texts.
Having bowed to his mother and father and having satisfied the brahmins,
he took fruits, flowers, excellent food, and other offerings, filled with devotion.
To attain the goals of human existence, a true disciple should take refuge in a guru;
he should worship with devotion, as if he were Śiva himself, that teacher who illuminates the knowledge of Śiva.
Having circumambulated him three times, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff;
then, rising and kneeling with both knees upon the earth, one should make one's request.
Having joined his palms in reverence and prostrated again before the guru,
and having received the guru’s permission, he should desist according to the prescribed rule.
When the words were being spoken by the Guru, he then spoke these words: "Be gracious, O Lord, O God! And he, showing due respect, replied, "So be it."
One should never, even in thought, do anything that is disagreeable to one's guru.
One should constantly perform salutation with body, mind, and speech toward one who dwells in the same village, regarding him as Nārāyaṇa.
In the morning, one should remember the Guru on a white lotus upon the head— two-eyed, two-armed, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and peaceful— preceded by his name.
One should never address the Guru by name except at the time of recitation;
in debate or during spiritual practice, one should call him "Śrīnātha," "Devam," or "Svāmī. (34)
(On the Fruit of Service to the Guru) Whatever fruit one may obtain from worshipping Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the other deities,
that same fruit one attains by saluting the guru every day. (35)
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru alone is the peaceful one who carries one across the ocean of worldly existence, the supreme goal.

(Prohibition of worshipping another human being in the presence of the Guru) If a man, while the Guru is present, should worship another human being, he falls into a miserable state; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. || 37 ||
(Regarding the teacher: to be dissatisfied with him there leads to fault.
But he who, having accepted a teacher, acts contrary to him out of delusion, is cooked in hell for ten million eons; of this there is no doubt. (38)
(Non-observance of the guru’s command leads to hell:
Those most sinful and lowest of men who do not carry out the guru’s command—there is no way whatsoever for them to escape the sufferings of hell. (39)
(The Fault of Reviling the Guru, etc.
Those who, out of delusion, revile their guru and speak harshly to him, will surely be born as pigs for even hundreds of lifetimes. (40)
(The Consequence of Betraying the Guru) Those fools who betray their guru and are constant evildoers—
there is no doubt that for them, whatever merit or demerit they may possess [shall perish]. (41)
(The Role of Devotion to the Guru as the Means to Liberation) For those whose devotion to the guru is steadfast, liberation rests in the palm of their hand.
Day and night, one should carry out his command like a servant. (42)
(The conduct of the disciple toward the teacher):
He should avoid that which is unbearable, inauspicious, and likewise excessive speech;
he should not harbor pride on account of his wealth, caste, stage of life, and so forth. (43)
One must never consume the property of the guru if it has not been given by him;
if it is given, it should be accepted as a favor, and never out of greed. (44)
One should directly avoid non-duality, worship of deities, the recitation of mantras, sacrifices, hymns of praise, and so forth, as well as jesting and idle chatter in the presence of the Guru. (45)
One should not step over, nor even touch with one's feet, the sandals, the meditation belt, and other such emblems of the Guru; one should always bow down before them. (46)
Sitting on a wooden seat, as well as mounting a vehicle or the like,
sleeping on a couch, and likewise stretching out one's feet;
One should not perform stretching of the limbs or playful gestures in the presence of the guru. || 47 ||
Having prostrated before the sandals of the Guru, one may go and come;
having reflected, one should perform one's duties, being graced by the word of the Guru. 48.
One should not step over the teacher's shadow, nor should one walk ahead of the teacher;
one should depart from the teacher's house behind him after having prostrated.
One should not exercise influence or gather disciples in the presence of the guru.
(The teacher’s satisfaction is the means to achieve the desired goal, and his anger is the obstacle to that attainment):
When the teacher is pleased, Śiva is pleased; when Śiva is pleased, the three worlds are pleased.
When Śiva is angry, the teacher is the protector; when the teacher is angry, there is no protector at all. (51)
(Conclusion: Therefore, with every effort, one should not provoke the anger of the guru.
In this manner, according to the prescribed rule, one should perform service without weariness.
(Regarding the castes, which one becomes fit for discipleship through service to the guru, and after how much time?
A Brāhmaṇa becomes fit after one year, a Kṣatriya after two years, a Vaiśya after three years, and a Śūdra after four years of service to the guru. (53)
(The duties of the Guru:
The Guru, for the sake of his own purification, should satisfy his disciples;
having reflected for a long time with effort, he should carefully consider which mantras are to be given. 54.
(The Akathahacakra; the drawing of the lines therein): One should draw five lines with their tips pointing eastward, and likewise [five] with their tips pointing southward.
Then, by means of four sets of four [lines], there shall be four squares.
53. Regarding the phrase "by one year" and so forth, it is stated in the second chapter of the *Tantrarāja*:

"Having considered the fitness [of the disciple] for one, two, three, four, or five years, as well as their qualities endowed with devotion, according to the sequence of the castes and the mixed castes (*saṅkara*)."
One should recite the Vidyā with undistracted mind according to the sequence just described;
otherwise, if one should recite it differently, the teacher, along with his disciple, shall meet with destruction.

By these two statements, having specified the time for examination for the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa according to the aforementioned sequence, a distinction is observed in that the examination of those of mixed castes (*saṅkaravarṇa*) is stated to be after five years.

(55) In the preceding statement it was said, "one should investigate the mantras to be given"; since the *cakra* is required in the sequence for investigating those mantras, [the following is stated].
For the sake of the meaning of the Great Wheel of Speech, [this is] the most supreme among all supreme wheels;
by the mere contemplation of which, a man may become one who takes any form at will.
Thus, according to the statement in the fifth chapter of the *Rudrayāmalottarakhaṇḍa*:
"O Bhairava, having carefully deliberated upon the great wheel (*mahācakra*) consisting of the letters 'A', 'Ka', and 'Tha' within the Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and Devī-mantras."
He who takes up the great mantra is Śiva; there is no doubt about this.
And by this statement from the third chapter of the *Rudrajāmalottarakhaṇḍa*, [it is established that] the *akathaha* wheel is the most supreme among all wheels:
"The four squares situated in the northeast, and likewise four in the southeast;
the four squares situated below those, and likewise those situated to their left. (56)
(The designations of the squares: Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, and Ripu are proclaimed [as the names of the four directions]. (57)
(Therein is the sequence for the placement of the phonemes): In their first squares, then in the second,
thereafter in the third, and in the fourth, again in successive order through rotation.
Because it is established [as the primary] and because it is determined to be the producer of specific fruits, he first defines that very [mandala] with the words beginning "pūrva" (eastern).
In that regard, five lines should be drawn from west to east, and five lines from north to south.
When this is done, sixteen squares are produced.

56. And a fourfold division of those sixteen squares must be made. Among them, there is the group of four squares in the northeast (aiśāna), the group of four squares in the southeast (āgneya), the group of four squares in the southwest (nairṛta) situated below that [southeastern] group of four squares, and the group of four squares in the northwest (vāyavya) situated to the left of that [southwestern] group of four squares.
He says "one should imagine" by means of the previous statement, "in four ways each.
57. Among those, the first tetrad is designated as *siddha*, the second tetrad as *sādhya*, the third tetrad as *susiddha*, and the fourth tetrad receives the name *ari*.
58. Regarding the phrase "of these": this means in the first four cells among these sixteen, situated in the northeast (īśāna);

in the second [set] in the southeast (āgneya), in the third in the southwest (nairṛta), and in the fourth in the northwest (vāyavya). These are to be obtained according to the previously mentioned sequence of placement (*nyāsa*) within the four sets of four cells beginning with *Siddha*.
The connection with the subsequent text is that one should write the syllables to be described hereafter, moving clockwise in rotation.
In this regard, although neither a clockwise nor a counter-clockwise rotation has been specifically mentioned by the phrase "by sequence and rotation," nevertheless:
"In all houses, however, having written [the letters] from 'a' to 'kṣa' in a clockwise order, one should then count them. (5/5)

By this statement from the fifth chapter of the *Rudrayāmala*, the clockwise circumambulation (*dakṣiṇāvṛtti*) is clearly understood. For this very reason, the *Tantrasāra* states: "The wise man should write the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with the visarga; then he should write those beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma'.
Having written those beginning with 'ya' and ending with 'sa', he should then write the consonants (*hal*) and the syllable 'kṣa'. (59)

It has been stated that "the wise man should write the letters in the square according to the method of clockwise rotation. Rāghavabhaṭṭa also stated in his *Śāradā-ṭīkā* that this is done "in a clockwise direction"; such is the conclusion.
(59) He states those letters as follows: "beginning with 'a' and so forth," etc.; [meaning] from the letter *a* up to the visarga (*ḥ*), and then from *ka* up to *ma*.
Then, from the letter *ya*, one should write the letters ending in *sa*, and thereafter the three letters *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa*.

By this, the following is meant: in the first square of the first group of four, the letter *a*; in the first square of the second group of four, the letter *ā*; in the first square of the third group of four, the letter *i*; and in the first square of the fourth group of four, the letter *ī*.

Thus, in the second [position] of the first tetrad is the vowel *u*; in the second of the second tetrad is *ū*; in the second of the third tetrad is *ṛ*; and in the second of the fourth tetrad is *ṝ*. Likewise, in the third of the first tetrad is *ḷ*; in the third of the second tetrad is *ḹ*; in the third of the third tetrad is *e*; and in the third of the fourth tetrad is *ai*. Thus...

One should write the letter *o* in the fourth [square] of the first tetrad, the letter *au* in the fourth of the second tetrad, the letter *aṃ* in the fourth of the third tetrad, and the letter *aḥ* in the fourth of the fourth tetrad. This is the sequence for the placement of the vowel-syllables (*svaravarṇanyāsakrama*). In this same manner, one should write the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*. Thus, in the first square of the first tetrad—

One should write the letter *ka* [in the first position]; the letter *kha*, which is the first of the second tetrad; the letter *ga*, which is the first of the third tetrad; and the letter *gha*, which is the first of the fourth tetrad.
In this manner, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the other letters, beginning with *ṅa* and ending with *kṣa*, should be performed by repeating them again and again in a clockwise direction. Here—
The wise one should write the letters starting from 'a' and ending with 'ha', beginning from the central square,
by following a clockwise rotation within the squares.
Thus, by the statement from the *Viśvasāra* cited in the *Tantrasāra*, the arrangement of the letters from *a* to *ha* within the wheel (*cakra*) is taught;
however, this would result in a contradiction with the statement from the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi*: "Then one should write the consonants (*hal*) and the vowels (*akṣas*).
Furthermore, in the fifth chapter of the *Rudrayāmala*, in the section on the *Akathaha-cakra*: [The text continues with the description of the cakra.]
"Having written [the letters] from the letter *a* up to the letter *kṣa*, one should then count them.
And in the first chapter of the *Tantrarāja-tantra*:
"In this manner, one should write [the letters] within four squares, ending with the letter *kṣa*."

Thus it has been said; these two statements as well support only the arrangement of phonemes beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'. If one does not accept it as such in the present context, it would be impossible for those seeking initiation (dīkṣā) to investigate the mantras by means of names beginning with 'la' and 'kṣa'. Therefore, [the sequence] from 'a' to 'kṣa'—
We understand that the statement of Viśvasāra, which has the form "iti," exists in the form "i" (from *a* to *ha*) within modern Tantrasāras, having been modified. And it is not the case that—
having excluded the four neuter vowels (*ṣaṇḍa*) and the two letters *la* and *kṣa*— [the remaining consonants] constitute the phonemes of Apabhraṃśa.
One should purify each letter of the name together with the syllables of the mantra.

It should not be argued that the previously cited statement from the *Tantrasāra* is contradictory because the *Piṅgalāmata*—as quoted by Rāghavabhaṭṭa in his *Āgamatattvavilāsa*—is seen to exclude two hundred [letters]; for the aforementioned statement from the *Piṅgalāmata* concerns the purification of each individual syllable within names and mantras that are distinguished by vowels and consonants. For this very reason, Rāghavabhaṭṭa [states] in the *Piṅgalāmata*:

The counting of the *siddha* and other groups is stated for every single syllable. One should separate the letters therein according to the distinction between vowels and consonants, including the name given by the mother and father as well as that bestowed by the kinsmen.
In that same manner, one should then begin the purification of the seed-syllables of the mantra—
those arising from the *bindu*, the double *bindu*, the *upadhmānīya*, the tongue, and the feet—
as well as those obtained through combined pronunciation and those consisting of additional syllables.
Having begun thus and stated "the Apabhraṃśa syllable" and so forth, [it says]: "One should purify consonants with consonants alone, and likewise vowels with vowels;
having purified the first [consonant] with the first, and the second with the second."

By such statements, its status as a distinct ritual procedure (*kalpāntara*) consisting of the purification of each individual syllable is declared. Furthermore, in the statement from the *Piṅgalāmata* beginning with "apabhraṃśa" and so forth, the phrase "the group of four neuter vowels" serves as proof for its status as a distinct ritual procedure, as it prescribes the exclusion of even the neuter phonemes known as *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*. Consequently, in this ritual procedure which prescribes the purification of the initial syllables of name-mantras (*nāmamantra*) and the like—
Thus, it is entirely clear that taking two hundred thousand [recitations] is indeed appropriate.
In the first chapter of the *Tantrarāja Tantra*:
"One should arrange those [mantras] in sequence by dividing them into groups of four."
In the first of the first [sections], however, it is the first; likewise in the first of the second.
One should conceive of a second [syllable] from another source, and likewise another;
one should write each respective fifth syllable in those various squares. In this manner, one should inscribe them in the four squares up to the letter *kṣa*.

By such statements as these, this very same sequence for establishing the letters is described. This has been clarified by Subhagānandanātha in his commentary on the first chapter of the *Tantrarāja*:
"When written in this manner, there are four syllables—*a*, *ka*, *tha*, and *ha*—in the first square of the first group of four."
(Therein is the sequence for counting the mantra):
The practitioner of mantra should count from the square in which the first letter of his own name is seen, up to the first letter of the mantra. 60.
Then, one should write in the Sādhya square, in due order: Siddha-Siddha, Siddha-Sādhya, Siddha-Susiddha, and Siddha-Ari. || 61 ||
The wise man should count, in due order within the *susiddha* [category], the *sādhyasiddha*, the *sādhyasādhya*, the *sādhyasusiddha*, and the *sādhyāri*. (62)
First, Susiddhasiddha and Susiddhasādhya;
then Susiddhasusiddha, and after that, Susiddhāri. (63)
The one who knows mantras should avoid these four: the *ari-siddha*, the *ari-sādhya*, the *ari-susiddha*, and the *ari-ari*.
In its second square are the three: *u*, *ṅa*, and *pa*. In its third square are the three: *ḷ*, *jha*, and *ma*. In its fourth square are the three: *o*, *ḍa*, and *va*.
In the first square of the second group of four are the four syllables: *ā*, *kha*, *da*, and *la*. In its second square is *ū* and *ca*.
In the first [group of four], there are three: *pha*, *ba*, and *bha*. In its third cell are three: *ḷ*, *ña*, and *ya*. In its fourth cell are three: *au*, *ḍha*, and *śa*.
In the first cell of the third group of four are four: *i*, *ga*, *dha*, and *kṣa*. In its second cell are three: *ṛ*, *cha*, and *va*.
In its third cell are three: *e*, *ṭa*, and *ra*. In its fourth cell are three: *aṃ*, *ṇa*, and *ṣa*.

In the first square of the fourth group are the three letters: *i*, *gha*, and *na*. In its second square are the three: *ṛ*, *ja*, and *bha*. In its third square are the three: *ai*, *ṭha*, and *la*. In its fourth square are the three: *aḥ*, *ta*, and *sa*. When written in this manner, the letters above those in the squares of the first group appear respectively in the squares of the second group.

With this much of the text (verses 60–64), having thus explained the sequence for the placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*), he states the sequence of calculation, beginning with the word "nijā" (one's own). Among the sixteen previously mentioned squares, in whichever square the first letter of one's own name— that is, the first letter of the practitioner’s name— [occurs...]

The first letter is seen; from that square up to the first letter of the mantra—in the manner stated in the *Viśvasāra* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*, "one should count by the very same [method] by which one performs the writing"—one should count until the square in which the first letter of the mantra's constituent syllables is seen. [This applies to the categories of] *siddhasiddha* and so forth, which will be described below.

The phrase "siddha, sādhya, and so forth" is to be understood as the ellipsis. An enemy who is *siddha* (accomplished) will kill one's daughter; an enemy who is *sādhya* (to be accomplished) will kill one's daughter-in-law; an enemy who is *susiddha* (well-accomplished) will kill one's wife; and an enemy of an enemy (*aryari*) will destroy one's impurity. || 65 ||
A *siddha-siddha* [mantra] is effective as described; a *siddha-sādhya* is so through two qualities;
a *siddha-susiddha* is effective from half the recitation; but a *siddha-ari* destroys one's kinsmen.
If it exceeds [the length] by two units, it is *sādhyasiddha*; if it exceeds by two units, it is *sādhyāsādhya* and is useless.
If it exceeds by two units, it is *sādhyasusiddha*; but a *sādhyāri* destroys those born in the lineage.
He teaches that very sequence of counting with the words beginning with *siddha* and ending with *aryariñcaiva*. This is what is meant:

in whichever four-square grid one's own initial letter falls, that is the *siddhasiddha* square; then, in the three squares following it in that same four-square grid, moving clockwise, one should count *siddhasādhya*, *siddhasusiddha*, and *siddhāri*. If the initial letter of the mantra also falls within this same four-square grid...

In that case, it would be established by this very calculation: if the first letter of one's own name is in another [position], and the first letter of the mantra is in the second group moving clockwise, then starting from whichever square in the first group contains the first letter of the name, the sequence for counting as "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya), "accomplished" (siddha), and so forth, is the same in the second group as well—so says Rāghavabhaṭṭa. Thus...
This applies to the third tetrad and so forth as well.

Thus, that which is joined with the first letter of its own name is *siddhasiddha*; in relation to that, the second is *siddhasādhya*, the third is *siddhasusiddha*, and the fourth is *siddhāri*. By the phrase "in this very order," this same meaning is indicated.

"Regarding the section beginning with *sādhyakoṣṭha* (the compartment of the 'to-be-accomplished'): according to the previously stated sequence, the first compartment of that which is called *sādhya* is *sādhyasiddha*;

the second is *sādhyasādhya*; the third is *sādhyasusiddha*; and the fourth is *sādhyāri*. By the phrase 'in this very sequence' (*krameṇaiva*), the meaning is that this calculation also follows the same order of calculation as previously stated."

He states the third [set] with the words "susiddha" (well-accomplished). According to the method previously described, for that which is named *susiddha*, the first is *susiddhasiddha*, the second is *susiddhasādhya*, the third is *susiddhasusiddha*, and the fourth is *susiddhāri*.
He states the fourth [set] with the words "atho" (now). In relation to that, the first square of the fourth group is named *arisiddha*.
The second is named *arisādhya*, the third is named *arisureddha*, and the fourth is named *āryārya*; thus, the distinct names of the sixteen squares should be inferred.
He states that the four enemy-squares obtained through calculation must be avoided: "The knower of mantras should avoid the quartet."
65 | He states the reason for avoidance: "arisiddha" and so forth. The meaning is that the very fact of producing such undesirable results is the reason for its avoidance.
[A mantra] "susiddhasiddha" is accomplished by half the recitation; "tatsādhya" is accomplished by more than double.
One who is well-perfected [in this] becomes, in an instant, a destroyer of enemies who are themselves well-perfected;
thus has the great wheel of Akatha been described according to the path of the Tantra.

69. Having [discussed] the *akathāca* wheel, he states the *ṛṇadhana* wheel—beginning with "In a previous birth" (*pūrvajanma*).
(In this regard, there is the method for drawing the lines and the sequence for placing the numbers of the *sādhya* and *sādhaka*: A line of twelve units from east to west.
Likewise, one should place the five [syllables] situated from south to north; indeed,
one should write the syllable of the *sādhya* above the center, and the syllable of the *sādhaka* below it, starting from the northeast (Īśa).
(The sequence for the placement of the phonemes: Two vowels each in five compartments, and the remaining six vowels, one by one, in six [compartments].
Then, one should write the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*, placing each letter individually in eleven locations.
(Therein, the method of multiplication preceded by the placement of the names of the person to be protected and the protector:
Multiply the persons to be protected by eight, nine, eight, five, three, six, four, three, two, twelve, fifteen, six, and four.
70. The wheel of debt and wealth (*ṛṇadhanacakra*) is of three kinds. Regarding that, he states the sequence for drawing the lines in the first [type] with the words "from the east" (*pūrva*):
twelve lines should be drawn from east to west, and likewise five lines from south to north.
Regarding the phrase "the number to be calculated" (*sādhyāṅka*): it refers to the uppermost part, in the external upper region above the five lines running north-south.

One should write the target-numbers (*sādhya-aṅka*) to be described below, one by one in sequence, above the eleven squares produced by the intersection of twelve lines running east-west. In the forty-four central squares, one should write the syllables to be described below.
The meaning is that one should write the practitioner-numbers (*sādhaka-aṅka*) to be described below, in sequence, beneath the five lines running south-north.
71. Therein, he first states the sequence for the placement of the letters (varṇanyāsa): "two by two.

One should write two vowels each in the first five squares of the forty-four compartments produced by the previously mentioned lines. By this, it is stated that the ten vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *ḷ* are to be placed in the first five squares.

It occurs as follows: "The remaining" means that one should write the vowels beginning with *e* and ending with the *visarga* one by one in the six remaining squares of the first row. "The letters beginning with *ka*" means that one should write the consonants from *ka* to *ha* one by one in the thirty-three remaining squares. The phrase "in eleven" is stated with reference to each individual row.
Then, multiply the letters of the practitioner by ten, one, seven, eight, four, eight, seven, four, six, three, and fire (three) respectively. || 72 ||
(The method for determining the debt or credit status of mantras, and their specific results:

Having determined the remainder of the "elephant-eaten" [calculation] from the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *jha*, the greater of the two remainders shall be either a debt (*ṛṇa*) or a credit (*dhana*).
However, when a mantra is both debt-bearing and auspiciously fruitful, or both inauspicious and wealthy, it is declared by the lords of sages to be equal and thus yielding an even result. (73)

72–73 | Regarding "Indra" and so forth: according to the stated sequence beginning with "the number of the *sādhya* above," one should write down the letters of the *sādhya* multiplied by these numbers—14, 27, 2, 12, 15, 6, 4, 3, 5, 8, and 9—which are reached by the words starting with Indra, respectively, in the spaces above the first through eleventh squares; this is done according to the sequence stated as "the number of the practitioner below."

The meaning is that one multiplies the letters of the practitioner (sādhaka) by these numbers— 10, 1, 7, 4, 8, 3, 7, 5, 4, 6, and 3— which are denoted by the words "direction" (dig) and so forth. Having reached the collection of letters consisting of the vowels and consonants that form the names of both the object to be accomplished (sādhya) and the practitioner, divided according to their distinctions as vowels and consonants, and comprising eleven and eleven syllables respectively starting with 'a', 'ka', 'ṭha', and 'va', one multiplies them by the numbers beginning with "Indra" (indra), "constellation" (ṛkṣa), and so on.

Having understood the letters of the *sādhya* (the object to be accomplished) multiplied by the directions (*diś*) and so forth, as well as the letters of the *sādhaka* (the practitioner), the meaning is that whichever is greater between the two—the *sādhya-aṅka* and the *sādhaka-aṅka*—will be the remainder, whether it be a debt (*ṛṇa*) or a wealth (*dhana*). Thus says Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "In this regard, the method is as follows: the name-letters of the practitioner and the mantra to be accomplished, distinguished by vowels and consonants..."

One should set them apart. Then, having divided the *mātṛkā* into four groups of eleven syllables each—consisting of the letters *a*, *ka*, *ṭha*, and *va*—one should multiply the mantra-syllables, separated by their nature as vowels and consonants, by the numbers beginning with Indra (1, 2, 3, etc.).
One should multiply the syllables of the practitioner’s name, separated by their nature as vowels and consonants, by the numbers beginning with the directions (10, 8, 6, etc.). In that regard:

The method of multiplication: whichever letter is in a particular position, one should multiply that letter by the number corresponding to that position; the meaning is that one should multiply it by the numerical value of that place. For example, the letter in the first square is *a*; one should multiply it by fourteen.
There, the number one multiplied by fourteen remains fourteen itself. Likewise, the letter in the second square is *i*; one should multiply it by twenty-seven.

One should multiply by that; thus, twenty-seven multiplied by two becomes fifty-four. In this way, the letter *u*, situated in the third position, when doubled, becomes six. Likewise, one should also multiply the letters of the practitioner's name by ten and the other [factors].

The meaning is that it is the remainder of what is left after being divided by eight, which was previously consumed by the elephant. In this regard, it should be noted that if the quotient is greater [than the divisor], it is a debt (ṛṇa), and that which is less is a credit (dhana). He states the result of such a procedure as follows: "If the mantra is in debt," and so forth. If the mantra is in debt—that is, if it has a higher numerical value—then it yields auspicious results and is a bestower of well-being.

If the creditor has a lower numerical value, then it produces an inauspicious result; this is the meaning. When the final figures of the mantra-practitioner and the subject are equal, then the result is neutral; that is to say, it bestows neither good nor evil. This is the sequence for the *ṛṇadhana-cakra* (the wheel of debt and wealth) as approved by the *Mantraratnāvalī*.

it was said that "births and so forth [occur] again and again," and he says that very thing with the words beginning with "birth. The meaning is that the results are to be inferred in this manner: that [names] which bestow results equal to themselves are "prosperities" (*sampad*) because they produce prosperity, while those which produce calamity are "calamities" (*vipat*). He states this point clearly:
In the *Nibandhatantra* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"The [houses] of six, eight, nine, and the auspicious ones (three), as well as those occurring in pairs and double-pairs, are auspicious;
the others are not auspicious and should be avoided by the wise."

By this, it follows that those [birth-stars] which are favorable, friendly, or supremely friendly, and which bring security and prosperity, are to be accepted, while others are to be avoided. For this very reason, the author of the *Tantrasāra* has also stated that the third, fifth, and seventh birth-stars from one's natal star are to be avoided.
Here, this should be noted: the twenty-seven previously mentioned birth-stars are of three types, distinguished as human (*mānuṣa*), demonic (*rākṣasa*), and divine (*daivata*).
Thus it is stated in the Nibandha-tantra as cited in the Tantrasāra:
"The three [asterisms] beginning with Pūrva and the three beginning with Uttara, as well as Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, and Rohiṇī—

Birth, prosperity, adversity, security, enemy, achiever, death, friend, and great friend—these [twelve] bestow results corresponding to their names. (90)

(91) Having thus described the circle of constellations, he speaks of the circle of zodiac signs (*rāśicakra*) with the words: "having drawn the circle of zodiac signs.
Regarding the sequence of drawing it, [the author] states in the *Āgamakalpadruma*, which cites the *Tantrasāra*:

"One should draw two lines from east to west, and from their midpoint, two lines toward the south and the north; then one should draw [lines] toward the northeast and the southwest, and toward the southeast and the northwest; thereafter, one should write the syllables. The meaning is that one should draw four lines in each of the four corners starting from Īśāna (the northeast). When this is done, twelve squares for the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Aries are produced.

(92) Regarding those squares beginning with Aries, he states the sequence for the placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*) as follows: "Vedāgnī" etc. By this, [it is shown that] *a* and *ā* [are placed] in the square of Aries.

In the house of Aries (Meṣa) are the four syllables: *i*, *ī*, *u*, and *ū*. In the house of Taurus (Vṛṣabha) are the three: *ṛ*, *ṝ*, and *ḷ*. In the house of Gemini (Mithuna) are the three: *ḹ*, *e*, and *ai*.

In the house of Cancer (Karkaṭaka) are the two: *o* and *au*. In the house of Leo (Siṃha) are the two: *aṃ* and *aḥ*. In the house of Virgo (Kanyā) are the five: *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, and *ṅa*. O auspicious lady, one should count them sequentially, starting from the first letter of the name, in order through the signs beginning with Aries and ending with Taurus, writing them out one by one.
By this statement, he describes the placement of each individual letter in a clockwise direction (*dakṣāvarta*). Now, he states the sequence of counting: "from Aries" (*meṣāditaḥ*).

By the phrase "from Aries to Pisces," counting is indicated in a counter-clockwise direction (*vāmāvarta*); however, by the inclusion of the word "also" (*api*), the meaning that counting may also proceed from Pisces to Aries is obtained, thereby teaching counting in a clockwise direction as well.
96. He explains the sequence for purifying the mantra used to construct this wheel with the words "of the reciter" (*japtuḥ*).

This means that from the first letter of the name—meaning from the first letter of the practitioner's own name—up to the first letter of the mantra, one should repeatedly count the *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* [categories] by moving clockwise and counter-clockwise. When the counting has been performed in this manner, however many houses...
Regarding those [names] designated as *siddha* and so forth, the third chapter of the *Rudrayāmala* specifically states:
"The *siddha* is in the ninth, first, and fifth; the *sādhya* in the sixth, tenth, and twelfth;
the *susiddha* in the third and seventh; and the *ripu* (enemy) in the fourth, eighth, and twelfth. Thus it is said.
Thus, it is concluded that the first, fifth, and ninth [letters] are *siddha*; the second, sixth, and tenth are *sādhya*;
the third, seventh, and eleventh are *susiddha*; and the fourth, eighth, and twelfth are *ari*. This is the *A-ka-ḍa-ma* wheel.
(Conclusion of the akaḍama-cakra, and the promise to investigate the kulākula-cakra:
The akaḍama-cakra has been explained; now the kulākula is investigated. || 98 ||
(The Kula-Akula Wheel) (Therein, the drawing of lines and the placement of phonemes): One should draw six lines extending from east to west in succession.
The castes consist of the five elements, divided into five groups of five. || 99 ||

99. Having thus described the *akaḍama-cakra*, he describes the *kulākūla-cakra*: "In the east," and so forth. Five short vowels and five long vowels, ending with the *bindu* (ṃ), arise from the junctions (*sandhi*).

The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṣa*, *kṣa*, *la*, *sa*, and *ha* are declared to be in groups of five. 100. [The verse continues: "Extending from east to west... [The text proceeds to describe the arrangement of these phonemes within the diagram.]
By the drawing of six lines, five houses (squares) are formed. These consist of the five elements. As for the fact that the phonemes consist of the five elements:
"Since Mātṛkā has arisen from the cause of the five elements..."
Then the phonemes, consisting of the elements, are fivefold according to their fivefold division.
This is to be understood from the statement in the second chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*: "In those houses, one should arrange the letters beginning with 'a' by dividing them into groups of five.
(100) He states those very letters [as follows]: "The five short vowels," and so forth. Consequently, in the northwest house [are] *a* and *ā*; in the southeast house...

*i* and *ī* in the house of Bhauma (Earth); *u* and *ū* in the house of Vāruṇa (Water); *ṛ* and *ṝ* in the house of Ākāśa (Ether); and *ḷ* and *ḹ* in the house of Ākāśa—thus two letters each are to be placed in every house, according to Āpātataḥ. Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that because those arising from sandhi are mentioned separately, there is no inclusion of the technical short (*hrasva*) and long (*dīrgha*) vowels [as defined by the Prātiśākhyas]. As for the phrase "those ending in the *bindu* (anusvāra) arise from sandhi," the term "ending in the *bindu*" is an epithet of "arising from sandhi."

This is the qualification: those phonemes produced by euphonic combination (*sandhi*) that have a *bindu* (anusvāra) at their end—namely those designated as *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*—are called "ending in a *bindu*" (*bindvantāḥ*). Rāghavabhaṭṭa has demonstrated the nature of these phonemes as being produced by euphonic combination;
how they arise from *sandhi* has been stated by the Teachers (*ācāryas*) as follows:
Through the union of *a* and *kāra*, the phoneme *e* is desired;
through the further union of that very *e* with *kāra*, the syllable *ai* then arises.
"When joined with *u*, that very [consonant] becomes the vowel called *o*;
when joined with *ū*, that same [consonant] becomes the vowel called *au*.
These four diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) are mantras that accomplish all aims. Thus it is said.

Regarding the reason for not counting the *visarga* here, despite its inclusion among the sixteen vowels, Rāghavabhaṭṭa states: "The *sarga* (emission), which is of the nature of *prakṛti*, is not counted here among the elements because it is produced from the *mūlādhāra*, arises from the effort born of the desire to speak, is impelled by the vital breath (*prāṇapavana*), and—without reaching another location—emerges directly from the throat. Likewise, it is stated in the *Kādima-tantra*:
"The creation called the power of Māyā is the Lord consisting of all beings;

therefore, its placement here within the self of Śiva is not in a single location. Here, "creation" (sarga) means emission (visarga). Having thus described the placement of vowels and letters, he states the placement of the consonants [beginning with *ka*] starting with the words "in groups of five" (*pañcaśaḥ*). These are the letters beginning with *ka*.
The designations for those colors are, in sequence: wind, fire, earth, water, and space. (101)
(The procedure for purifying the mantra used in constructing this wheel:

If the practitioner first knows the syllable of his own [mantra] and likewise the syllable of the [target] mantra, and if they have the same deity as their presiding divinity, then that indeed belongs to his own family (kula). 102.
The meaning is "five by five. The suffix *śas* is used here in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). The meaning is that there are five letters each, beginning with *ka*.

By this, the five groups (*varga*) starting with *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*, as well as *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and *śa*, are obtained. To the question of what kind of letters these beginning with *ka* are, he says:
"ending with *ṣa*, *kṣa*, *la*, *sa*, and *ha*."

In this context, it is indicated by the instruction of five groups of five— namely, the five short vowels, the five long vowels, those ending with the bindu (anusvāra) arising from sandhi, the five consonants beginning with *ka*, and the five beginning with *pa* (i.e., *kha, ga, gha, ṅa*)— that each of these pentads corresponds respectively to air (*vāyu*) and the other elements. And thus:

A, ā, e, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, ṣā—these ten belong to the wind (vāyavya). I, ī, ai, kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pha, ra, kṣā—these ten belong to fire (taijasa). U, ū, o, ga, ja, ḍa, da, ba, la, lā—these ten belong to earth (pārthiva).
*ṛ*, *ṝ*, *au*, *gha*, *jha*, *ḍha*, *dha*, *bha*, *va*, *sā*—these ten belong to Varuṇa (*vāruṇa*).
*ḷ*, *ḹ*, *aṃ*, *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, *ma*, *śa*, *hā*—these ten belong to the ether (*nābhasa*).
In this manner, it should be understood that the phonemes possess the nature of air and the other elements. As for what is stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
The number of syllables in the *varṇa* meters is proclaimed to be forty-five;
however, among the five beginning with *pārthiva*, the *gaṇa* should be known as consisting of nine syllables.

By this statement, it is declared that the nine vowels constitute the group beginning with Vāyu; therein, Rāghavabhaṭṭa has resolved the point by stating that the long vowels are included by means of the short ones alone, thus [the group consists of] nine. Therefore, the usage "by nine" is intended to mean "by ten," and thus there is no contradiction whatsoever.
102. By this [verse], beginning with "of the practitioner" (*sādhakasya*), he states the method for the purification of the mantra. This should be noted:

here, by the terms *kula* and *akula*, one's own *kula* (*svakula*) and the other's *kula* (*parakula*) are designated; it is precisely because it explains these that this is named the *Kulākula-cakra*.
To the inquiry, "What then is one's own *kula*? he replies: "of the practitioner. [This refers to] the name of the practitioner and the mantra that preceded it.

If the first syllable should have a single elemental deity, or if among these [elements] such as wind there is only one element— [according to the established system of mutual enmity and friendship among the letters]: the Maruta [element] is friendly toward the Pārthiva and Vāruṇa, and also toward the Āgneya.
While the letters of the earth-words remain in a state of enmity, the letter of the wind remains established. || 103 ||
Water is the enemy of fire, and wind is the enemy of water; however, that which belongs to the ether is non-opposing to all the elements. (104)

The meaning is that one should know that [mantra] to be one's own *kula* (family) if its deity is the same. Regarding the term *ekabhūtadaivatyam*, the analysis of the compound is: "that which has a single element (*bhūta*) as its deity (*daivatyam*)," meaning its deity is one. Thus, if the first syllable of the practitioner’s name belongs to a certain elemental deity, and the first syllable of the mantra also falls within the letters belonging to that same elemental deity, then it is one's own *kula*; however, in the opposite case, it is another's *kula*. For this very reason:
If the first letter of both the mantra and the practitioner is an earth-element (pārthiva) letter, then that is declared to be his *kula*; one should observe the others in the same manner.

Thus, in the statement from the *Piṅgalāmata* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, by the phrase "one should observe among others," it is established that even for other mantra-practitioners, their own lineage (*svakulatva*) exists when their initial letters [of the name] belong to a single deity.
(103–104) Now, he describes the arrangement of enemies, friends, and so forth regarding letters belonging to different elemental deities— beginning with the Earth element (*pārthiva*).

From the passage beginning with "ityādinā" up to "mārutaṃ ripuḥ," by this [text], the mutual enmity, friendship, and neutrality of the letters belonging to the four elements starting with air— excluding those of the nature of space— are established. This is clearly stated in another Tantra cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
I shall describe the division of colors established in four measures:
one's own family, the friend, the neutral, and the enemy as the fourth.
The [elements] of Vāyu, Agni, Varuṇa, and Earth are proclaimed;
their results are, respectively, success, equality, disease, and death.
Having approached them here through the understanding of counsel, ministers attain success;
it is declared that success is found with a friend, but nothing at all with one who is neutral.

Death, disease, and enemies [result from unfavorable positions], while supreme success is found within one's own family. One should draw the initial letters of the names of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and the practitioner (sādhaka) respectively, positioned one above the other, and determine the *aṃśaka*. Thus it is said.

Wherein lies the friendship, enmity, neutrality, or kinship of anyone toward another? That too has been specifically demonstrated in that very place [the *Phala*]: "Where there is the coexistence of mutually contradictory castes..."
That mantra kills the practitioner; it does not become propitious in any way. || 105 ||
One should know that the fiery element is a friend in the northwest, the watery element is neutral,
the earthy element is an enemy, and the airy element is one's own kin.
The watery [element] is the enemy of the fiery, while the earthy is neutral;
the airy is declared to be the friend, and one's own kind is again the fiery.
One should know that the earthly element is a friend, the airy element is neutral,
the fiery element is an enemy, and the watery element is one's own kin.
The Varuṇa element is a friend to the Pārthiva, while the Taijasa is said to be an enemy;
the Vāyava is neutral, and one's own family is again Pārthiva.

Now, an objection is raised: since the statement "the Māruta [group] stands as the enemy of the Pārthiva [group] letters" here denotes a mutual enmity between the Pārthiva and Māruta letters, it contradicts the previously cited statement from another Tantra which says, "The Vāyava [group] is neutral. It is replied:

In the third chapter of the *Rudrayāmala* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*, regarding the passage beginning with "the Māruta [is the enemy] of the Pārthivas," the phrase "of the Pārthivas" (pārthivānāñca) is used.

From the word "ca" (and), according to the commentary of Śrī Kṛṣṇānanda which states that fire is the enemy of earth elements, it is established that there is enmity between both the airy (*vāyavya*) and fiery (*taijasa*) classes and the earth (*pārthiva*) ones. Furthermore, since fire destroys the earth elements along with their roots in a manner that the wind does not, here [the author] treats fire as the primary enemy.

This is the designation. To establish this very point, other systems (tantra) have described the air element (*vāyava*) as being neutral (*audāsīnya*), whereas the fire element (*taijasa*) is described as an enemy. Since neutrality is not mentioned in the *Rudrajāmala*, the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi*, and other such works, the letters of the air element are likewise categorized as belonging to the side of the enemy, just like those of the fire element; such is the summary.
Having thus stated the essential nature of the four [elements], he explains the arrangement of the colors belonging to the ether (nābhasa) with the words "of all" (*sarveṣām*).

The meaning is that the ether-born color, which arises from the class of letters presided over by the deity of the sky, is compatible with all [the others] and is a friend. As stated in the third chapter of the *Rudrayāmalatantra*:
"The ether-born [color] is a friend to all; one should never practice what is hostile."

Because friendship is clearly expressed by this [verse], [the author] states the result after having thus described the arrangement of the letters (varṇavyavasthā): "paraspara... etc. Where there is the "establishment" (saṃsthitiḥ) of those previously mentioned letters—such as earth, air, and so forth—which are mutually opposed, within a mantra, specifically in the first syllable of the mantra; [therein lies the result].
The wind is the mutual wheel of the *kulākula*.

That indeed is the wheel of the classes.
Now the procedure for the wheel of groups (vargacakra) is described, preceded by the initial letter of each name, for the purpose of purifying the collection of mantras. || 106 ||

It should be understood that this contradiction depends upon the first letter of the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*); thus, "that mantra kills the practitioner," and so forth. Regarding the statement "it is not propitious in every way," the reading preserved by Rāghavabhaṭṭa—*kiṃ vā nāsya prasīdati* ("or rather, it is not propitious for him")—is the correct one. For even when there is mutual opposition between letters, there is not necessarily a state of being a killer in all cases.

Furthermore, because other undesirable results are also mentioned— such as "the attainment of ever-higher perfection, equanimity, disease, and death," and likewise, "nothing at all [occurs] in the indifferent, while death and disease [occur] in the enemy"— according to the previously cited statement from the *Piṅgalāmata*, here too, as in the words of Rāghavabhaṭṭa, it is not propitious in every respect.
"Another result" means that one does not become clear-minded; this is the meaning of verses 106–107.

Having thus defined *kulākula*, he states the wheel of classes (*vargacakra*) with the words "Now," etc. [This includes] the construction of the grid based on the initial letters of names and the placement of the syllables therein.
Having drawn eight squares, one should write the eight groups [of consonants] in sequence.
(The designations of the groups:
Birds, cats, lions, dogs, snakes, mice, and elephants;
and the ram—these, in order, are based upon the eight groups beginning with the letter 'A'. (108)
(The fruit of purifying the mantra by means of this wheel:
One should always ascertain the mutual affection between the practitioner and the subject [of the rite] according to their birth. 109.

The meaning is that, beginning with this, the procedure for the wheel of classes (*vargacakra*) is now set forth for the purpose of purifying the collection of mantras. He states its sequence as follows:
"eight," etc. The meaning is that having drawn eight squares—four situated above and four situated below—one should write the eight classes beginning with *a* in them in due order.

108. He states their designations as "bird" (*pakṣin*) and so forth: bird, cat, lion, and dog are the designations for the four [groups] above; snake, mouse, elephant, and ram are the designations for the four below.
The meaning is that these, beginning with the bird, are situated by resorting to the eight groups of consonants starting with *a* in sequence. For instance, the first is the bird.

The first enclosure consists of the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *visarga*; therefore, these vowels are designated as "birds. The second is the "cat," which takes its support from the *ka*-group (*kavarga*). The third is the "lion," which takes its support from the *ca*-group (*cavarga*). The fourth is the "dog," which takes its support from the *ṭa*-group (*ṭavarga*).

The fifth is the "serpent," which takes its support from the *ta*-group (*tavarga*). The sixth is the "mouse," which takes its support from the *pa*-group (*pavarga*). The seventh is the "elephant," [consisting of] *ya*, *ra*, and *la*.

The eighth is Aries (Meṣa), which is based on the letters *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa*. By this, it is established that these [signs] also possess their respective designations. (109) He states the result: "In the case of the *sādhya* and *sādhaka*... When the initial letters of the names of the *sādhya* (the object to be determined) and the *sādhaka* (the determiner) are of the same class (*sājātya*), there is affection; when they are of different classes (*vaijātya*), there is no affection, nor is there a lack of affection. It should be understood that in the case of eternal enmity (*śāśvatika-vaira*), there is enmity. Eternal enmities include those such as between birds and snakes.
The enmity between the cat and the mouse, the lion and the elephant, and the dog and the sheep is well known.
(The Circle of Groups) Bird.

Ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa are Siṃha;
ca, cha, ja, jha, ña are [the next group].
The dog: ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa; the serpent.
