The elephant, the letter *ya*, the letter *ra*, the letter *la*, the letter *va*, and the ram.
Śa, Ṣa, Sa, Ha, La, Kṣa (the sequence for removing the previously mentioned defects of mantras):
in all these cases of defects, one should everywhere insert Māyā (I) or Kāma (E).
And having first cast [the oblation], one should bestow prosperity for the sake of liberation from each respective defect.

110. Having thus explained the sequence of the wheels (*cakraparipāṭī*), he now describes the method for remedying the defects—such as enmity and so forth—that arise within the mantras obtained through the investigation of the various wheels heard in various places, beginning with the *akatha* wheel. He says "in these" (*eṣu*).

"In these" refers to the defects such as enmity residing in the mantras obtained through the aforementioned investigation of the *akatha* and other wheels. By the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*), it means whoever [is affected].
It is indicated that even a mantra defiled by the faults previously mentioned becomes free from those defects through the remedial measures to be described hereafter.

For this very reason, the *Muṇḍamālātantra*, as cited in the *Tantrasāra*, states: "Those mantras which are declared in the Tantra to be defiled by defects such as being 'cut' (chinnā) and so forth..."
They all attain perfection through the power of the syllables of the Mātṛkā.
By these and other such statements, the faultlessness of all mantras corrupted by defects has been established through this method.
Alternatively, even a defective mantra is perfected when encapsulated by the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*).
(Another method.)
Whichever mantra one has devotion for, that very mantra will bring success for him. || 111 ||
(Another method:
By means of a garland of syllables arranged in both direct and reverse order,
the mantras joined with each individual syllable, when recited, shall bestow all accomplishments.
Even the spells of enemies and other mantras of men [are ineffective], how much more so [other spells]? || 112 ||
(On the differences in the fruits of mantras according to their state, such as being established in a place, etc.):

Mantras established in a [sacred] place grant boons, and those established in meditation bestow fruits; however, those devoid of both place and meditation are enemies, even if they are well-perfected. 113.
(An examination of the sixfold locus:
In this very context, I shall describe that locus in detail. (114)

Śiva has declared the sixfold state to be: the differentiated (sakala), the undifferentiated (niṣkala), the subtle (sūkṣma), as well as the differentiated-undifferentiated (sakalaniṣkala), that which is not distinct from the parts (kalābhinna), and that which transcends the parts (kalātīta). || 115 ||
(The nature of the sixfold abodes:
Know that the Sakala [Brahman] resides in the *brahmarandhra*, and that which is below it is the Niṣkala.
That which is called Sūkṣma resides in the mind, while the Sakalaniṣkala resides in the heart. (116)

111. He states another method: "Tāraḥ" (the Savior). This means encapsulated by the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), that is, joined with the *praṇava* at both the beginning and the end. He states another method: "Yasya" (of whom). *Bhaktiḥ* is supreme devotion.
112. He states another method: "Anu" (following). The mantras joined with each individual letter [refer to] the individual letters constituting the mantra.

The meaning is that by encasing [the mantra] with the letters of the *mātṛkā* in both direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*viloma*) order— encasing each individual letter of the mantra with the letters from *a* to *kṣa* and from *kṣa* to *a* through recitation— even corrupted mantras become bestowers of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
That which resides in the Bindu is differentiated by the Kalās, while that which transcends the Kalās is situated above it.
That very Kalā is Kuṇḍalinī; she is declared by Śiva to be the power of Nāda.
Mantras situated in these locations are proclaimed as "situated in their place" (*sthānastha*).
[Regarding specific mantras, there is no requirement for purification such as *siddha* and so forth.
Now, the procedure for the classification of mantra-clusters (*mantrakūṭa*) is being declared. (118)
One should not examine the success (siddhi) and other qualities of mantras that consist of syllables with *sapiṇḍa* vowels. || 119 ||

In the case of a single-syllable mantra, a peak-syllable (kūṭa), a garland-mantra, or a three-seed mantra—whether obtained in a dream or given by a woman—one need not deliberate over its success or other qualities. 120.
And among the Vaiṣṇava tantras, some Tantrikas maintain this view. || 121 ||
The practitioner should likewise [purify] Kālī, Tārā, and Chinnamastā;
however, regarding the excellent mantra of Sundarī, one should not purify the Siddhas and so forth at all.
(Selection of Months for Initiation) Having reflected thus, the wise man should purify the months and so forth.
An initiation in Caitra leads to suffering; in Vaiśākha, there is an accumulation of jewels. (123)

116–117 | "The whole," and so forth. "Situated in the *brahmarandhra*" means residing in the thousand-spoked [lotus]. "Below that" means situated in the upward-sounding resonance (*nāda*) of the downward-facing *praṇava*. "Situated in the mind" means residing in the *ājñācakra*. "Situated in the heart" means residing in the twelve-spoked [lotus]. "Situated in the *bindu*" means situated in the *bindu* above the first *nāda*. "Above that" means situated in the *nāda* above the *bindu*—thus according to manuscript B.
Sub-commentary (Pādaṭīkā).
119. Of mantras consisting of single syllables and mantras consisting of conjunct syllables.
123. "Caitra," and so forth. This has been stated in another Tantra cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
Failure, success in one's stage of life, death, the loss of kinsmen,
increase in lifespan, the destruction of offspring, prosperity, and the accumulation of jewels.

"The attainment of auspiciousness, the destruction of one's position, delusion, and subjugation—these are to be known as the results for those beginning in Caitra and the subsequent months; one should avoid the intercalary month (malamāsa).
Regarding this: "The commencement of mantra practice in Caitra bestows all human goals."

By this statement from the fifth chapter of the *Gautamīya Tantra*, the excellence of the month of Caitra regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*) is declared; however, that refers specifically to Viṣṇu, because the *Gautamīya Tantra* is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu. For this very reason, the authors of the *Tantrasāra* have stated: "The [mention of] Caitra refers to Gopāla, because it belongs to the *Gautamīya [tradition]. Initiation in the month of Madhu (Caitra) leads to suffering and death," as cited from the *Yoginīhṛdaya*. Therefore:

Pūrṇānanda stated that initiation (*dīkṣā*) should not be performed in the month of Caitra because it would lead to suffering, since this text is devoted to the exposition of the worship of Śakti. Rāghavabhaṭṭa also said:
"The commencement of mantra practice in the month preceding Vaiśākha [Caitra] is very difficult to endure."
In Vaiśākha it causes financial loss, and in Jyaiṣṭha it becomes a bringer of death.
In Āṣāḍha, there is the attainment of a son; in Śrāvaṇa, it is considered the bestower of land. In Bhādrapada, the loss of knowledge is proclaimed by the wise.
In Āśvina, there is the accomplishment of all goals, and Kārttika bestows the perfection of knowledge.
Mārgaśīrṣa brings about the path of auspicious deeds; Pauṣa bestows suffering;
in Māgha there is an increase in intelligence; and in Phālguna, there is mastery over all.

By such statements, the very sequence of time for initiation (*dīkṣā*) as declared in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* has been established. However, in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi*, other tantras, and so forth, it is stated that the month of Āṣāḍha yields undesirable results, such as the destruction of one's kinsmen. But here, in the citation provided by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, its capacity to grant desirable results is expressed by the phrase "for the sake of obtaining a son in Āṣāḍha."

This is the distinction. However, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, it is established that even among those months previously mentioned as auspicious, there are superior, inferior, and middling qualities. As it says:
"Initiation during the autumn season and in Vaiśākha bestows the most excellent fruit."
And initiation in Phālguna, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Jyeṣṭha is middling.
"Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Māgha are the youngest months esteemed by the virtuous;
whereas Caitra, Pauṣa, and Bhādrapada are likewise censured.
Thus, according to the Mūla [text], the prohibition of Jyeṣṭha and the others follows precisely from their inclusion within the "inferior" category.

This is understood from the intention of Rāghavabhaṭṭa; likewise: "In the first half of Āṣāḍha, in [the month of] Āṣāḍha, and in Mārgaśīrṣa, a wise man should not perform initiation; however, he may perform it in other months."

Thus, even in the statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, the prohibition of Mārgaśīrṣa is due solely to its not being included among the "excellent" months. "If death occurs in Jyeṣṭha, there is the loss of kinsmen in Āṣāḍha;
in Śrāvaṇa there will surely be prosperity, and in Bhādrapada there is ruin. (124)
In the month of Āśvina, it bestows the fruit of all desires for living beings;
in the month of Kārttika, there shall be knowledge; and in Mārgaśīrṣa, great wealth. 125.
In Pauṣa there is the destruction of ignorance; in Māgha there shall be an increase of intelligence;
in Phālguna all success shall be attained; one should avoid the intercalary month (mala-māsa).

(The Excellence of Initiation at the Equinoxes and Other Occasions) Initiation should be performed with great effort during the equinox, the two solstices, the solar transits, the festival of Madana, the Pavitra rite, and on the festivals of the Guru. (127)
In the *Kālottara* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "The procedure for the rite of initiation is traditionally prescribed for the conjunction of autumn and spring;
in their absence, it is recommended at other times, except during the rainy season."
In this context, since it is stated "without the rains," the lack of excellence for Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa is established;

furthermore, by the previously cited statement from the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, their inferiority is determined. Thus, by the statement in the root text that "in Āṣāḍha there would be the destruction of kinsmen," the total avoidance of Āṣāḍha is indicated, whereas by the statement in the root text that "prosperity is surely in Śrāvaṇa," [the excellence of] Śrāvaṇa is established.
Even though it has been prescribed, its lack of excellence is understood through a careful examination of the preceding texts.

(127) He states the specific days recommended for initiation (*dīkṣā*)—namely, "the equinoxes" (*viṣuva*) and so forth: at the two equinoxes (*viṣuvadvandva*), that is, during the *jalaviṣuva* and *mahāviṣuva* solstices; at the two solstices (*ayanadvandva*), that is, during the *dakṣiṇāyana* and *uttarāyaṇa* transitions; and at the [other] transits (*saṃkrānti*).

On common [occasions], on the Madanotsava (the thirteenth day of Kāma), or on the Kāmacaturdaśī—so say some; or on the "Guru-parvan" as will be mentioned later, such as the sixth day of Bhādrapada and so forth. Here, although the equinoxes and solstices are already included by the mention of "saṃkrānti," their separate specification in various places [is for a specific purpose].
This is for the purpose of indicating a specific result. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Gandharva-tantra*, in the twenty-sixth chapter:

"During the equinoxes or solstices, during the month of Āṣāḍha, during the festival of Madana (the spring festival), or during an eclipse of either the sun or the moon—that day shall be the bestower of that [specific] fruit."

In this context, the mention of only the equinoxes and solstices among the *saṃkrāntis* is solely for the purpose of indicating that they produce results equal to those generated by initiation (*dīkṣā*) performed at the same time as a lunar or solar eclipse. Likewise—
(the praise of initiation on the festival days of the gods).

The sixth day in the month of Bhādrapada, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in Īṣa (Āśvina), the ninth day of the bright fortnight in Kārttika, and the third day of the bright fortnight in Mārgaśīrṣa. || 128 ||
In Pauṣa, the ninth day of the bright fortnight; in Māgha, the excellent fourth;
in Phālguna, the ninth day of the bright fortnight; and in Caitra, the thirteenth day known as Kāmatrayodaśī. || 129 ||
During the conjunctions of planets and constellations, at the equinoxes, during festivals,
and at all solstices, a union [with a preceptor] bestows the accomplishment of all goals.

Thus, in the *Kālottara* verse cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, although the equinoxes (*viṣuva*) and solstices (*ayana*) each occur in pairs, the use of the plural in various instances is solely intended to indicate that they produce an excellence of fruit.
"The festival of Madana" refers to the fourteenth day of the month of Kāma. "The festival of the Guru" means the festival of the deity to be described hereafter.

128–129 | Here, in the *Tantrasāradhṛtaratnāvalī* verse which shares the same sequence [as the one cited], the reading "fourteenth" (*caturdaśī*) is seen where [the other text] has "thirteenth" (*trayodaśī*). Regarding that, Śrīmat Kṛṣṇānanda stated, "Some say 'thirteenth'. Furthermore, in the third chapter of the *Bṛhannīlatantra*, the reading is likewise "Kāmatrayodaśī" in the month of Caitra. Consequently, [the practice applies] to both the fourteenth and the thirteenth.

Since the *Tantrasāra* and the *Bṛhan-nīlatantra* respectively designate [the thirteenth and fourteenth days] as being praiseworthy, here the thirteenth day is obtained by the phrase "the Kāma-thirteenth" (*kāmatrayodaśī*), while the fourteenth day is obtained by the previously cited statement, "on the Saṃkrānti, during the Madana festival.
Although the previously cited statement does not specifically specify [the date] by the term "Madana festival," because it is specified here as "Kāma-thirteenth," [it follows that] in that case—

By the term *madanotsava* (the festival of Madana), the fourteenth day of Madana (*madanacaturdaśī*) is understood; this should be noted because such a festival of Madana is impossible at other times.
As stated in the *Tantrasāra*:
"The thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, and the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha..."
The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in Jyeṣṭha, and the fifth day of the dark fortnight in Āṣāḍha, known as Nāgapañcamī.
The eleventh day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the eighth day of Bhādrapada conjoined with Rohiṇī,
and the highly meritorious Mahā-aṣṭamī in Āśvina are all bestowers of desired fruits.
"The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, likewise the sixth and fourteenth days of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa,
the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa and Māgha,
and the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna— such is the determination of the times."
In Vaiśākha, the Akṣayā is praised; likewise, the Daśaharā in Jyeṣṭha;
the fifth day of the bright fortnight in Āṣāḍha; and the fifth day of the dark fortnight in Śrāvaṇa. (130)
On these festival days of the gods, one obtains the fruit of ten million holy fords (*tīrtha*).
(Regarding the excellence of initiation during a solar eclipse or at the sun's transit, and the independence from considerations of the *lagna* and so forth:
Initiation is declared to be auspicious even during forbidden months, as well as during an eclipse. (131)
There is nothing on earth equal to the time of a solar eclipse;
whatever action is performed there, one shall obtain infinite fruit from it. (132)
131. He states the excellence of initiation during an eclipse of the moon or sun: "Even in censured [months]," etc.

By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even in censured [months]," it should be understood that initiation is indeed auspicious in praiseworthy months such as Vaiśākha and others; furthermore, even in censured months such as Caitra and others, it produces the desired fruit. Regarding "auspicious during an eclipse": this refers to both solar and lunar eclipses.
"At the solstices, at the equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun"—thus [it is stated] from the *Yoginīhṛdaya* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*.
(132) Regarding "at the time of a solar eclipse," one might object: [Is this not so?]
One should not perform a Śākta initiation during an eclipse of the sun,
nor should one perform a Vaiṣṇava initiation if there is an eclipse of the moon.

If it is argued that, because of the prohibition of Śākta initiation during a solar eclipse according to the statement in the *Tantrasāradhṛtarudrajāmala*—"At the two solstices (*viṣuva*), at the two equinoxes (*ayana*), during the month of Āṣāḍha, and during the festival of Madana"—then how can the passage beginning with "at this time of the solar eclipse" and so forth be justified? It is replied: the aforementioned statement from the *Rudrajāmala* pertains to matters other than the *Śrīvidyā*.
[The exceptions are: "At the two solstices, at the two equinoxes, during the month of Āṣāḍha, and during the festival of Madana."
During an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, that day shall yield its fruit.
Thus, from the words of the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Gandharva Tantra*, which expounds the *Śrīvidyā*:
"The seed-syllables of Śrī Parākalī and the mantra of Lopāmudrā and Aghora,
when obtained during a solar eclipse, bestow the fruit of liberation upon men."
Thus, from the *Jāmalavacana* cited in the *Ratnāvalī*, which is itself embraced by the *Tantrasāra*:
"At the time of a solar eclipse, however, nothing else need be sought.
And from the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, which expounds the *Śrīvidyā*: [the same]. Therefore, the specific mention of the solar eclipse in the root text is indeed significant.
It should be understood that this is for the purpose of establishing a specific excellence [of the time].

Furthermore, during the sun's transit (saṃkrānti) and likewise during an eclipse of the sun, no consideration whatsoever of the ascendant (lagna) or other such factors should be made in any way. (133)
(Independence from considerations such as the purity of time on the Great Eighth Day):

On the Great Eighth Day, specifically for the sake of accomplishing dharma, desire, and wealth, there is here no requirement for the purity of time and so forth, nor is there any need for the purification of the lunar mansions. 134.
(When the venerable Guru desires to initiate out of compassion, there is no dependence on considerations of time or season in Kāśī and other such places:
In the presence of the venerable Guru who manifests compassion, as well as in Kāśī, Prayāga,
at sacred bathing-places, in sacred fields, and in the four seats of the Goddess—
Likewise, on Śrīparvata, the practitioner of mantra should not distinguish between the proper and improper time. || 135 ||

134. Regarding the phrase "on the Mahāṣṭamī": the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, in its fifty-ninth chapter, describes the Mahāṣṭamī as follows: "That lunar day which falls on the eighth of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina is called the Mahāṣṭamī; it is the supreme [day] that brings great delight to the Goddess."
Regarding the specific details, the *Viṣṇujāmala*, as cited in the *Tantrasāra*, states:
"Beginning from the awakening of the Goddess (the first lunar day) up until the ninth lunar day,
initiation performed by the wise during these days bestows all desired fruits."
Especially during the bright fortnight, and particularly on the eighth lunar day;
and even there, when the goddess Śāradī Durgā is present in every household.
In that case, the initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed; one need not examine the month, the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), and so forth.
Likewise, in the awakening of Durgā, one need not examine whether the time is auspicious or inauspicious.
On this day, the eighth is called Aśokāṣṭamī, and likewise the ninth is called Rāmā.

Thus, by this [statement], it is declared that from the Bodhanavami until the Durganavami, initiation (dīkṣā) is highly commendable regardless of considerations regarding the lunar day, the weekday, the time, or its inappropriateness. Furthermore, because a specific excellence of fruit for initiation on the Mahāṣṭamī is heard [in scripture], she alone is mentioned in the root text.
135. Regarding the phrase "of the venerable Guru": the meaning is that when the Guru, out of compassion, calls the disciple and desires to bestow the mantra.
This has been stated in the *Samayātantra*, cited in the *Tantrasāra* [concerning the restriction of days for initiation]:
(dīkṣāyāṃ vāraniyamaḥ) [The restriction of days for initiation]...
On Sunday there will be wealth; on Monday it bestows peace;
on Tuesday it destroys longevity; therefore, one should avoid initiation on that day. (136)
If it is bestowed by the Guru out of compassion upon his disciples, then at that time,
one should never consider the astrological ascendant or other such factors.
"All the *vāras*, all the planets, all the *nakṣatras*, and the *rāśis*—on whichever day the Guru is pleased, they all bring about auspiciousness.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding "meritorious" (*puṇya*) and so forth, it is stated in the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
The fields of merit are described; listen to me according to their primary importance:
a riverbank, a cave, and a mountain peak are fields of merit.
Sacred sites, the confluence of rivers,
purifying forests, secluded gardens, the foot of a bilva tree, and the slope of a mountain.
A grove of Tulasī, a cow-pen, a temple of Śiva devoid of a bull,
the roots of an Aśvattha or Āmalakī tree, a cow-shed, and the midst of water.
"A temple, a riverbank, and one's own home—
these places are praised for the practice of mantras by practitioners.
And in the *Tantrasāra*:
Now I shall describe, according to the tantras, the locations for initiation:
in a cow-pen, in the house of the guru, in a temple, in a shrine of Śiva, in a sacred field, as well as in a garden or on a riverbank— these are the places for one who knows the mantra.
"Near the Dhātrī and Bilva trees, on mountain peaks, in caves, or even on the banks of the Gaṅgā, [the merit] shall be multiplied by ten million times ten million.
Regarding "Devī": the four seats of the Goddess (devīpīṭha) are—Kāmagiri-pīṭha, Jālandhara-pīṭha, Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha, [and Uḍḍiyāna-pīṭha].

And Uḍḍīyāna-pīṭha. The author himself will explain this in the fifteenth chapter during the discussion on the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa); therefore, it is not elaborated upon here. The meaning is that in these locations, there is no consideration of whether the time is auspicious or inauspicious for receiving initiation (dīkṣā).
As it was said by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"At the holy pilgrimage site of Kurukṣetra, at the four Devī-pīṭhas, at Prayāga, Śrīgiri, and Kāśī, one need not distinguish between the auspicious and inauspicious times.
(136-137). Regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), he restricts the days that are prescribed and those that are prohibited, beginning with the word "ravi" (Sun): here...
Under Mercury one attains beauty, while under Jupiter there shall be knowledge;
under Venus one attains good fortune, but under Saturn there is loss of fame. (137)
(The rules regarding the lunar days for initiation:
The fourth, the ninth, the fourteenth, and likewise the eighth;
the full moon, the fifth, the second, and likewise the seventh. (138)
The thirteenth and the tenth lunar days are praised as bestowing all accomplishments. (Regarding the restriction of the fortnight:
Initiation is auspicious during the bright fortnight; in the dark fortnight, it is also permitted up until the fifth day. 139.
(Therein lies this distinction:
those desiring liberation [should perform it] during the dark fortnight, and those desiring prosperity always during the bright fortnight;
on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the rite of initiation bestows auspiciousness.
(The Rule of the Constellations:
One attains happiness under Aśvinī; under Bharaṇī, death is certain;
under Kṛttikā, one becomes miserable; and under Rohiṇī, one becomes a lord of speech. 141.

The reading "duḥkham" (suffering), as held in the *Pādaṭippanī*, is erroneous; for the reading "tantrasāre ravivāre bhaved vittam" (in the *Tantrasāra*, it says wealth shall be obtained on Sunday) is observed, and because of the statement in the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*: "It should be performed on Sunday, Thursday, Friday, Monday, or Wednesday," and [the variant]: "It should be performed on Sunday, Thursday, Friday, Monday, Wednesday, or Venus [day]."
Furthermore, because the *Gautamīya-tantra*, in its fifth chapter, declares the excellence of initiation on Sundays;
and as stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, the author of the *Tantrasāra*:
"Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, initiation is auspicious everywhere."
Having relied upon this statement from the *Kālottara*, he states the distinction regarding the excellence of both positions, beginning with the word "mukti.
Therefore, it should be understood that the arrangement of the two positions in initiation (*dīkṣā*) depends on the aforementioned difference in aspiration.
(Verses 141–145) He points out the auspicious and inauspicious lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) for initiation, beginning with the words "in Aśvinī," as stated in the *Nīlatantra*.
In the sixth chapter:
Under Mṛgaśīrṣa there is the attainment of happiness; under Ārdrā, the destruction of kinsmen;
under Punarvasu, one becomes miserable; and under Puṣyā, one becomes wealthy. (142)
Under Aśleṣā one may become ill, under Maghā one attains liberation,
and indeed, under both Phalgunīs, there shall surely be an increase in fame.
In Hasta there will be loss of wealth; in Citrā and Svātī one shall become happy;
in Viśākhā there is happiness, and in Anurādhā the destruction of kinsmen. (144)
In Jyeṣṭhā there shall be an increase of sons; in Mūlā, the enhancement of fame;
and in both Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā, they shall be bestowers of renown. (145)
"Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, Dhaniṣṭhā, the three Uttaras,
Puṣya, and Śatabhiṣā are said to be the asterisms for initiation (dīkṣā)," according to the *Kāraṇa* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
Pauṣṇa, Rohiṇī, Āditya, Śravaṇa, and likewise Aśvinī;
Sāvitra, Tvāṣṭra, Vāyavya, Aindra, and Nairṛta as well.
"Tiṣya (Puṣya), the three [asterisms] following Uttarā-Ārdrā, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), and the birth asterism of the disciple—
these asterisms are praised for the rite of initiation, O lady of good vows. Here, Pauṣṇa is Revatī, Āditya is Punarvasu, Sāvitra is Hasta, and Saumya is Mṛga.
The commentary of Rāghavabhaṭṭa: Citrā belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ, and Svātī belongs to Pavana.
However, Rāghavabhaṭṭa, by means of the following verse from the Ratnāvalī, states that there is inauspiciousness when the lunar day (tithi) and the asterism (nakṣatra) are in mutual conjunction:
as follows—
The first lunar day (pratipad) with the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā, as well as the fifth with Kṛttikā;
the sixth with Pūrvābhādrapadā, and likewise the tenth with Rohiṇī.
The twelfth lunar day when conjoined with the Sarpa (Āśleṣā) asterism, and the thirteenth when conjoined with Aryaman (Punarvasu)—
these are known as "asterism-deprived" (nakṣatraluptā), and they bring destruction even to the gods.

Thus, he states that the defectiveness of the lunar day (*tithi*) and the asterism (*nakṣatra*) resulting from their conjunction with other factors is to be understood from the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). And so it is said:
"Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā bestow fame;
under Śravaṇā one becomes miserable, and under Dhaniṣṭhā there is poverty."
One’s intellect will flourish under Śatabhiṣā, and one shall become happy under Pūrvabhādrapadā. (146)
There is happiness under Uttara-bhādrapadā, and an increase in fame under Revatī. || 147 ||
(The Rule for the Ascendant, Moon, and Stars):
One should undertake the commencement of initiation when the ascendants are Taurus, Leo, Virgo, Sagittarius, or Pisces, and when the moon and stars are favorable. (148)
The Moon situated in the third, eleventh, sixth, or tenth house is declared auspicious for the natal Moon, provided it is not the Moon of birth itself. (149)
In the bright fortnight, however, the second, the fifth, and likewise the ninth [are auspicious]. || 150 ||
If the planets are in their proper domains, even the Moon, though conjoined with malefics, is auspicious;
likewise, the Moon situated between benefics shall bestow good fortune. (151)
One should avoid performing auspicious rites during the third, seventh, sixteenth, eighteenth, nineteenth, twenty-first, twenty-third, and likewise the twenty-fifth lunar mansions. || 152 ||

Thus, although Pūrvāṣāḍhā is praised by this [statement], because the first lunar day (pratipad) yields undesirable results— as stated in the *Tantrasāra*: "Initiation performed on the first lunar day leads to suffering and death"— therefore, when conjoined with that [day], even Pūrvāṣāḍhā, though otherwise auspicious, [is not recommended].

[This refers to] the state of being defective. Thus, even when the fifth [lunar day] is auspicious, it becomes inauspicious due to its conjunction with the inauspicious Kṛttikā constellation. Even where both the lunar day and the constellation are auspicious, their conjunction produces an undesirable result according to the previously stated rule—as, for example, in the case of the conjunction between the tenth lunar day and Rohiṇī, despite their inherent auspiciousness.
Both of these indeed result in undesirable consequences. The same applies elsewhere as well.
(It was previously stated that the purification of months and so forth pertains solely to mantra-initiation:
"For the purification of the month, lunar day, weekday, and so on, has indeed already been explained."
That [initiation] should be understood by the best of practitioners as being primarily concerned with mantra-initiation (mantradīkṣā). || 153 ||
(However, in the case of the initiation into the Vidyā, there is no requirement for the purification of the lunar day, the weekday, and so forth:
There is no purification of the lunar day or weekday whatsoever beyond the initiation into the Vidyā;

(An Etymological Explanation of Mantra):
Because it protects through contemplation and because it brings about the realization of non-duality, as well as through the empowerment of Śiva, it is correctly called "mantra. (156)
Because it is secret, because it is contemplated (manana), and because it protects (traṇa), it is called "mantra" by the teachers who are knowers of the tantras. (157)
154. Also in the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"Listen to the special occasion for initiation even without a [specific] lunar day:
when the rare opportunity of meeting true gurus occurs but once."
"When his permission has been granted, that is the great occasion for initiation.
Whether in a village or in the forest, in a sacred field by day or by night—whenever the Guru arrives by destiny, then the initiation shall take place. Thus it is said.

(The tenfold consecration of mantra): The ten consecrations of mantra are now described according to the path of the Tantras:
birth, vivification, and thereafter striking, as well as awakening; (158)

Now, consecration (abhiṣeka), purification (vimalīkaraṇa), nourishment (āpyāyana), satiation (tarpaṇa), illumination (dīpana), and concealment (gupti)—these ten are the purificatory rites for mantras. (159)

(Therein, the first consecration is called "generation"): On a pedestal smeared with saffron or perhaps with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and the like, or smeared with cow dung, one should draw a lotus. (160)
158. In the fifteenth chapter of the *Kulārṇava*: "O Dear One, the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) that remove defects in mantra are now being told.
Since this indicates that the purificatory rites of the mantra to be described hereafter serve to eliminate defects in the mantra, [the following applies].
Just as weapons sharpened on a whetstone indeed become keen,
so too do mantras attain their full power through the ten consecratory rites.
Thus, because this [treatise] specifically effects the manifestation of the mantra, he promises to describe the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the mantra with the words "of the mantra.

Consequently, by means of the purificatory rites performed according to the method that will be explained, even mantras corrupted by defects such as being "cut" (*chinna*) and so forth produce auspicious results; those defects, however, are described in the second chapter of the *Śāradā-tilaka* by the verse beginning, "cut, obstructed, powerless," and so on.

O observer of excellent vows, [one may do so] with Kāśmīra sandalwood paste or even with ashes.
"Saffron is prescribed for the consecration with power (*śakti*), sandalwood for the Vaiṣṇava mantra,
and ashes are declared for the Śaiva [mantra], as well as for the drawing of the *mātṛkā* yantra.
Here, because of the mention of "the *mātṛkā* yantra,"...

"The extraction of mantras from the *mātṛkā*-yantra is known as their 'birth' (*janana*)," according to the statement in the *Tantrasāra*. Therefore, in the present context, it should be understood that by the word "lotus" (*kamala*), the syllable *ma* which constitutes the *mātṛkā*-yantra is intended.
The *Tantrasāra* describes the *mātṛkā*-yantra as follows:
One should draw two groups of eight petals; on the eastern side, one should arrange a pair [of letters], beginning with 'ka' on the seven petals, and 'la' and 'kṣa' on the eighth petal.
The extraction of mantras from those syllables is traditionally known as their "birth."
[One should meditate on] the lotus whose pericarp is the syllable *caṃ*— the sky, moon, earth, and water— whose throbbing filaments are the pairs [of consonants],
whose radiant petals are the unfolding of the [consonant] classes, which is encircled by the abode of the earth (*vasumatīgeha*),
and which is surrounded in the three directions by the city of the earth (*kṣauṇīpura*) joined with the plow-shaped [consonant] ending in *la*.
"The Yantra, which consists of the body of letters, is declared to be the bestower of good fortune and prosperity.
Likewise, in the *Gautamīya* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*:
"One should place the five groups of consonants, beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma', in the directions starting from the east."
"One should place the letters from *ya* to *anta* (ya-va) and from *śa* to *ha* within the *la*-lakṣmī;
[one should draw] a square with four doors in the cardinal directions and *vaṃ* and *ṭhaṃ* in the intermediate directions.
Thus is the sequence for drawing the yantra. First, he describes the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the lotus:

Regarding the phrase "having the sky, the moon, the vowel *au*, and the letter of the tongue as its pericarp": "sky" (*vyoma*) is the letter *ha*; "moon" (*indu*) is the letter *sa*; from that [comes] the vowel *au*; and the "letter of the tongue" (*rasanārṇa*) is the visarga. The analysis of the compound is:

that which has the sky (*ha*), the moon (*sa*), the vowel *au* (*auḥ*), and the letter of the tongue (*ḥ*) as its pericarp. By this, the meaning is that *hsauḥ* is to be written in the pericarp. He describes the filaments: "that whose filaments are radiant with the pairs of vowels (*acām*). By this—

The meaning is that one should write the sixteen vowels, from *a* to *au*, in pairs upon the eight filaments starting from the east. Next, he describes the petals: "having petals shining with the groups" (*vargollāsivasucchadam*). Those which shine by means of the groups are "shining with the groups" (*vargollāsinaḥ*); that which has eight petals (*chadāni*) characterized by these groups is "having petals shining with the groups. Thus, having written the eight petals, one should place the *ka*-group on the eastern petal, the *ca*-group on the south-eastern, and the *ṭa*-group on the southern.

The meaning is that one should write the *tavarga* in the southwest (*nairṛta*), the *pavarga* in the west, the four letters consisting of *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* in the northwest (*vāyavya*), the four letters consisting of *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* in the north, and the two letters *la* and *kṣa* in the northeast (*īśāna*). Furthermore, it is enclosed by the "abode of Vasumatī," which is the *bhūpura* (earth-fortress), joined with the letter *va* ending in *la* (i.e., *vla*) and the plow-shaped letter *ṭha* in the cardinal directions and the intermediate corners (*astri*) respectively.

Regarding the phrase "with the *kṣauṇīpura* and the four gates," the *Āgama-tattva-vilāsa* explains it as such. However, in the ancient manuscript of the *Tantrasāra*, the explanation "with the *kṣauṇīpura* and the *anusvāra*" is observed. According to that view, the word "*kṣauṇīpura*" appears to be intended for the purpose of joining the *anusvāra* with the letters *va* and *ṭha*. Thus, one should write "va" at the gates of the four directions and "ṭha" in the corners. It is said:
The sequence for the *mātṛkā* diagram:

Here, in this lotus, one should proceed according to the sequence taught in the *Tantrasāra*.
Regarding the establishment of the phonemes (varṇasthāpana), [the author] says:
(The second is called "Life")—
the wise practitioner should recite the syllables of the mantra with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) interspersed between them.
The Tantrikas call this "living" (jīvana), and they perform it one hundred times.
