Having written the syllables of the mantra on birch bark, one should strike each one a hundred times with the wind-seed-syllable (*vāyubīja*), and likewise the mantra itself with sandalwood water. (164)
(4. Awakening):

Having written the mantra on birch bark with *karavīra* flowers, one should perform the awakening by striking it with the syllable *repha* (*r*) as many times as there are letters in that mantra. (165)

Regarding the passage beginning with *dviraṣṭa* and so forth: the term *dvir-aṣṭaka-kesare* means "in the petals of two eights. The word *dviḥ* is used in the sense of repetition (*vārārthe*), as indicated by the suffix *suca*. Thus, the meaning is that one should write the syllables in pairs, having placed two [syllables] each upon the petals starting from the east. Regarding the phrase *tadakṣarāt*: this refers to the ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*) called "birth" (*janana*), which is the extraction of the syllables that constitute the mantras from those specific letters. Accordingly, Rāghavabhaṭṭa says: "On an auspicious pedestal (*pīṭha*) and so forth..."
Having drawn the *mātṛkā* lotus with saffron, yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), and so forth, each individual syllable of the mantra to be given should be extracted from that *mātṛkā* lotus;
this is [verse] 163. Regarding the word "praṇava": the meaning is that one should recite the constituent syllables of the mantra separated by the *praṇava*, that is, interspersed with the *praṇava*.
For example, when the mantra is *hrīṃ*, the sequence of interspersing with the *praṇava* is: *ha oṃ ra oṃ īm*. One should recite [in this manner].
The meaning is "one hundred times. As stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "One should recite the syllables of the mantra together with the *praṇava* one hundred times; that is declared to be its life-force.
(164) Regarding the word "bhūrja": [it is purified] by the seed-syllable of Vāyu, namely *yama*. The formula for the striking is: "of such-and-such a mantra..."
"I strike such-and-such a syllable"—thus [ends] the *Āgama-tattva-vilāsa*. The striking may be performed a hundred times or ten times. As it is stated in another Tantra cited in the *Tantrasāra*:
"One should cause all the syllables to cross over [to liberation] by means of sandalwood water through the act of striking."
"Or one may awaken the mind a hundred times or even ten times thereafter. Thus [it is said]. In the Viśvasāra:
"Listen, O Goddess of gods, to what is proclaimed as the tenfold striking. Thus.

165. Regarding the phrase "the mantra": having written the mantra to be bestowed upon a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*), one should strike it with red *karavīra* flowers equal in number to the syllables (*varṇa*) contained within that mantra, using the fire-seed-syllable (*vahnibīja*) "ram". As stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "In this [leaf], the written mantra..."
(The fifth [chapter], called the Consecration:
The wise practitioner of mantras, having written the mantra on birch bark using jasmine buds or the root of kuśa grass,
[should perform the rite] according to the number of syllables in the mantra.
One should consecrate the mantra with the sprouts of the aśvattha tree for the sake of purification. || 166 ||

(Chapter Six, titled "Purification") The mantra-practitioner should burn away the three impurities—known as the innate, the adventitious, and the illusory—by means of the light-mantra; thereafter, that mantra shall become pure. 167.

It is stated that the "awakening" (*bodhana*) [of a mantra] is performed with *karavīra* flowers according to the number of its syllables, using the formula "I slay [the syllable] by means of the fire-seed (*vahni-bīja*).
Here, because of the expression "by those [flowers] equal in number to the syllables of that mantra," it is indicated that the awakening of one mantra-syllable is performed with one flower.
The sentence for the awakening is: "I slay such-and-such a syllable of such-and-such a mantra"—thus says the *Āgama-tattva-vilāsa*.

166. Regarding the word *mālatī*: having written the mantra on a birch leaf with *mālatī* buds or with the roots of *kuśa* grass, one should then consecrate that mantra with as many leaves of the *aśvattha* tree as there are syllables in the mantra. The meaning is that the mantra thereby becomes purified. This is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
Having placed the syllables upon the pericarp with *mālatī* buds,
one should perform the consecration with pure *aśvattha* sprouts equal in number to the syllables of that mantra, according to the procedure prescribed in the *Svatantra*.

But in the second chapter of the Śāradātilaka: "The practitioner of mantra, according to the procedure taught in the Svatantra-tantra, should consecrate the mantra with asvattha shoots as many times as there are syllables in the mantra, for the sake of purification."
Regarding the statement "by the procedure prescribed in one's own independent [tantra]" found here, Rāghavabhaṭṭa has explained it as follows:
according to the Śiva-tantras for a Śaiva mantra; according to the Śakti-tantras for a Śākta mantra; and according to the Vaiṣṇava-tantras for a Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Rāghavabhaṭṭa has stated that the consecration consists of one hundred and eight [verses], and that one should perform the consecration according to the path enjoined in one's own tantra.

This is the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) for a mantra written on birch bark with *pippala* sprouts, performed one hundred and eight times. Regarding the formula for the consecration, Rāghavabhaṭṭa states: "I consecrate such-and-such a letter of such-and-such a mantra; *namaḥ*. However, in the *Āgamatattvavilāsa*, it ends simply with "I consecrate. In that regard, it is stated that the consecration is performed either one hundred times or ten times for each [letter].

167 | Regarding the term *sahaja*: the practitioner (*mantrī*) is one who knows the secret of mantra. That which is called *sahaja* (inborn), *āgantuka* (adventitious), and *māyā* (illusion)—namely, the *sahaja*, the *āgantuka*, and the *tāra*—is considered the *bindu* at the end of *śiva*, *agni*, and *tāra*; this is the *jyotirmantra*.
(The seventh is named *āpyāyana*.)
One should sprinkle water over each syllable of the mantra with kuśa-grass water that has been consecrated by recitation.
Having written this one hundred and eight times on birch bark, this is considered the nourishment [of the mantra] through that very mantra, performed according to the rules. (169)
The connection is that one should burn the three impurities of the mantra, which are illusory in nature, with the *jyotirmantra*. As it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"One should burn the [impurities] known as the innate (*sahaja*), the adventitious (*āgantu*), and the illusory (*māyā*) with the *jyotirmantra*."
"The practitioner of mantra, having thus purified the three impurities within the mantra, shall then become stainless.
However, in the *Tantrasāra*, it is said: "Having mentally contemplated the mantra at the root and middle of the *suṣumṇā*..."
The ascetic should duly burn away the three impurities with the Jyotir-mantra.
Having thus defined the nature of purification, [the text] states "the three impurities" (*malatrayam*), namely: the *māyika*, the *kārmaṇa*, and the *āṇava*.
In the *Prapañcasāra*:
"The *māyika* impurity arises from woman; the *kārmaṇa* impurity is that which pertains to the person."
"It is said that those two belong to the *āṇava* [nature], and that triad of impurities (*mala*) is prohibited.

By the word "mantrin" (the practitioner), Rāghavabhaṭṭa explains that one should raise the Kuṇḍalinī from the *mūlādhāra* and, by means of that, burn away the defects. For this very reason, the author of the *Tantrasāra* also stated: "from the middle of the root of the *suṣumṇā*."

It was stated that one should burn [the obstacles] with the *jyotirmantra*; he now states that *jyotirmantra*: "The *tāra*," and so forth. The *tāra* is the *praṇava* (oṃ); *śiva* is the letter *ha*; *agni* is the letter *ra*; the end of the *tāra* is the vowel *au*; and the *bindu* is the *anusvāra*. Thus, *hrauṃ* is the *jyotirmantra*. It is also stated in the *Śāradā-tantra*: "The *jyotirmantra* is considered to be the *tāra*, followed by *vyoma* (ha), *agni* (ra), and the *manu-yuga* (au), ending with the *daṇḍī* (*anusvāra*). However, by the author of the *Āgama-tattva-vilāsa*:

One performs the burning twenty-five times with the flame of fire produced from the *jyotirmantra*, while reciting the formula: "I burn such-and-such impurity of such-and-such mantra. (168–169) Regarding the word "kuśa": having written this mantra on a birch-bark leaf, one sprinkles it with water from *kuśa* grass over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times.

The connection is as follows: for each syllable, that is, for every letter, one should perform one hundred and eight sprinklings with that *deya-mantra*; this is called "nourishment" (*āpyāyana*). However, some [interpret it] as meaning "with that *jyotiḥ-mantra*" because the *jyotiḥ-mantra* was mentioned previously;
[this is the eighth [rite], known as "satiating" (*tarpaṇa*)].
Satisfying with water accompanied by a mantra is considered "tarpaṇa" performed with a mantra. || 170 ||

(Chapter Nine, titled "The Illumination") Having first applied the seed-syllables *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā* to the beginning of the mantra, one should recite the mantra seven times; this is declared to be the "illumination" (*dīpana*). || 171 ||
They offer this interpretation. Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa has investigated it as follows: some explain "by that mantra" (tena tanmantreṇa) to mean "by the Jyotis-mantra";

that is incorrect because it contradicts other texts. As it is said: "The nourishment [of the mantra] should be performed syllable by syllable with water and *kuśa* grass over which one's own [mantra] has been recited.

Thus, the meaning of "over which one's own [mantra] has been recited" (*svajaptaiḥ*) is "with those [substances] over which one's own mantra—that is, the specific mantra in question—has been recited," using water and *kuśa* grass. However, in the present context, it is "by that [mantra] having been recited."

It should be understood that the sprinkling is performed with that very [water]. For this very reason, Rāghavabhaṭṭa, by stating that the word "tena" (by that) is connected to both [instances], has presented the authority of the Piṅgalāmata as favorable to the support of his own view, as follows:
"The pure water of kuśa grass, obtained from one hundred and eight [draws]..."

"The mantra shall become nourished if it is sprinkled syllable by syllable. Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that the sprinkling is performed seven times. As for the formula for the nourishment (*āpyāyana*), it is stated in the *Āgama-tattva-vilāsa*: "I nourish such-and-such a letter of such-and-such a mantra."

170. "With the mantra" means: the libation (*tarpaṇa*) which is performed with water over the mantra written [on the vessel], or with the mantra that is to be offered—that alone is the *tarpaṇa*, meaning the consecration (*saṃskāra*) known as *tarpaṇa*. Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that this too should be one hundred and eight times.
In the *Tantrasāra*:
For the Śakti-mantra, libation with honey is prescribed; for the Vaiṣṇava, with water mixed with camphor; and for the Śaiva, with ghee or milk—this is declared to be the proper method of satiation.
"With water containing camphor" means with camphor-water.

171. Regarding "Tāra": *tāra* is the *praṇava* (Oṃ), *māyā* is *hrīṃ*, and *ramābīja* is *śrīṃ*. The word *bīja* (seed-syllable) is to be connected with each [of these]. The phrase "of the mantra" means of the mantra to be bestowed. On this point, it is stated in both the *Tantrasāra* and the *Śāradā*:
It has been stated in general that "the kindling of the mantra occurs through the conjunction of the *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā*. Furthermore, in the *Viśvasāra* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*:
"The best of practitioners should kindle the mantra by reciting it one hundred and eight times, encapsulated by the seed-syllables of *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā*."

By this [verse], he states that the "kindling" (*dīpana*) consists of the recitation one hundred and eight times of the mantra to be given, encased within the seed-syllables *tāra* and *māyā*. In the present context, however, "concealment" (*gopana*)—the tenth [limb]—is the non-disclosure of the mantra being recited. (172)
(The Application of the Ten Purificatory Rites): Ten purificatory rites have been proclaimed, which are kept secret in all tantras;
by performing these and bestowing the mantra, the practitioner of mantra shall obtain his desire. (173)
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 2 ||

The application of the *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā* seed-syllables at the very beginning of the mantra, along with a sevenfold recitation, contradicts the previously cited statements from the *Viśvasāra* and *Śāradā*. This is thus deliberated: in the root text beginning with "tāramāyā," because of the connection of the word "ca" (and) with the word "ādau" (at the beginning), the meaning understood is that they are to be applied both at the beginning of the mantra and at the end; thus, the application of the seed-syllables such as *tāra* is understood to occur at the end as well.

Furthermore, since the author of the text also intends the application of the *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā* seed-syllables at the beginning and end of the mantra, there is no contradiction with the statements in the *Viśvasāra* and other works. The conclusion is that the arrangement between the hundred and eight recitations and the sevenfold recitation is determined by the distinction between those who are capable and those who are incapable.
The Third Chapter: The Section on Initiation (*Dīkṣāprakaraṇam*).
(In this section: the prescribed locations, the purpose of determining the location of the lamp, and the tortoise-diagram [*kūrmacakra*].)
(The Vāstuyāga, the sixty-four-square Vāstu-maṇḍala which is its constituent part, and the offering mantras); [and] (the excellent locations for initiation).
Now I shall describe the location for initiation according to the Tantras:
1. Now I shall describe the location for initiation in accordance with the Tantras.
The knower of mantras [should practice] in a cow-pen, in the house of a guru, in a temple, in a grove, in a sacred field, as well as in a garden or on a riverbank.
Near the Dhātrī and Bilva trees, on a mountain peak, in caves,
or by the Gaṅgā or its banks, [the merit] shall be multiplied ten million-fold.
(The procedure for recitation and other rites at the lamp-site:
Having taken recourse to the lamp-site, one should perform recitation, sacrifice, and so forth. (The promise to describe the tortoise-diagram [kūrmacakra]:)
Therefore, I shall explain the Kūrmacakra, which is the cause of spiritual accomplishment.
4. By means of the passage beginning with "In a cowshed" (*gośālāyām*), the author has described those places praised for initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Now, in order to make known the point that even in those places, the recitation of mantras (*japa*), sacrifice (*yāga*), and so forth must be performed specifically relying upon a location for the lamp (*dīpasthāna*), he describes the location for the lamp immediately after the description of the locations for initiation, starting with "The location for the lamp" (*dīpasthānam*). This is precisely the location of the mouth of the tortoise (*kūrma*) which is about to be described.

The location of the lamp will be explained further on. Since that location of the lamp depends upon the knowledge of the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmacakra*), he makes the formal declaration to explain the tortoise-diagram with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
(In this regard, there is the sequence for drawing the lines and the ritual placement of the syllables.)
First, having made a circle, one should fashion nine compartments;
one should likewise draw the central compartment as consisting of nine parts, starting from the east.
One should write the seven groups of consonants beginning with *ka* in the eight squares surrounding the *la* and *kṣa*,
and in the middle eight squares, one should write the vowels in pairs.

5. Herein is the procedure for constructing the tortoise diagram (kūrmacakra): First, one draws a circular shape in the form of a tortoise; in its center is a square; and in the center of that, two [lines] extending eastward and two extending northward. Thus, nine compartments are formed within the circle.
Of these nine compartments, the central one is designated as the "middle compartment" (madhyakoṣṭha), while those situated outside it are designated as the "outer compartments" (bahiḥkoṣṭha).

He says "divided into nine parts" (*navabhāgam*) in order to explain [the layout]. Regarding that wheel, he states the placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*) with the words "in the same way" (*tathaiva*). This is intended to indicate that, just as there are nine internal squares, the placement of the consonants (*vyañjana*) should be performed in the external squares.
(6) Regarding "the *ka*-group and so forth": thus, in the external eastern square is the *ka*-group, and in the southeastern square is the *ca*-group.

The method for filling the outer compartments is as follows: the *ṭa*-group in the southern compartment, the *ta*-group in the south-western compartment, the *pa*-group in the western compartment, the four letters beginning with *ya* in the north-western compartment, the four letters beginning with *śa* in the northern compartment, and the two syllables *la* and *kṣa* in the north-eastern compartment. This very point is clearly stated in the verse cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"In the eastern square, the five [consonants] of the *ka*-group [are placed] in order from the center;
likewise, the *ca*-group is placed in the same manner from the center elsewhere, namely in the south-eastern [square].

Thus he describes the procedure for the inner squares with the words "in the centers" (*madhyeṣu*). Accordingly, starting from the central square of the eastern direction, one proceeds clockwise through each square.
The meaning is that one should write the sixteen vowels in pairs, sequentially. Thus Rāghavabhaṭṭa says:
"In the area in front of the central square, one should write two *a*s;
one should know there are two *i*s in the southeast, and one should write two *u*s in the south," and so forth.
Also in the *Tantrasāra*:
"Having divided the ground into a square, one should draw a group of nine squares. Starting from the eastern square, one should write the seven groups [of consonants] in successive order."
In the central square of the Lakṣmī diagram, one should write the vowels in pairs according to their sequence.
In the central square is the excellent wheel called Kūrma, which contains the name of the field;
in whichever square the first letter of the field's name occurs, that is traditionally held to be its mouth. (The determination of the mouth and other limbs.)
By this, this very sequence for establishing the phonemes (*varṇasthāpanā*) has been described. However, in the third chapter of the *Rudrayāmala-uttarakhaṇḍa*, it is stated:
"The vowels are on the head; the *ka*-group is on the right foot;
the *ca*-group is proclaimed on the left foot; and the *ṭa*-group is on the lower foot. (73)

By means of these and other [verses], the mantra-practitioner, having written the seed-syllable of Śakra, the letter *kṣa*, upon the tail and in the middle of the phallus, should count the wheel that removes the impurities of the Kali age. (74)
By this much, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters in the *kūrmacakra* has been described in another way.

(7) "In the central square" means that one should write the name of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) in that ninth square which lies within the previously mentioned eight squares. As for the sacred field, it is precisely that place where the practitioner sits and recites [mantras]. Among those, the auspicious fields are, for example, a cowshed.
These [locations] were already mentioned at the very beginning of the *Prakāśa* with the words "in the house of the Guru," and so forth.
Also, in the second chapter of the *Śāradā*:
"A sacred field, the bank of a river, a cave, or a mountain peak..."
The regions of sacred fords and the confluences of rivers are great purifiers.
"Solitary gardens, the foot of a *vilva* tree, and the slope of a mountain—
these places are praised for the practices of practitioners (*mantrins*).
Thus it is stated elsewhere as well.

Now, since the mouth itself is the location of the lamp, one might wonder what the mouth of the tortoise is, given that the knowledge of the lamp’s location depends upon it. Anticipating this doubt, he defines the mouth with the words "in which": "In which [square]... Among the previously mentioned inner squares of the tortoise, in whichever square the first letter of the name of the field [is located]...
The meaning is that the first syllable of the name of the place suitable for practice is considered its "mouth. This is stated in the second chapter of the *Śāradā*:
"In whichever direction, starting from the east, the first syllable of the name of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) is situated..."
One should know that his face is [as follows]... [and so forth].
Thus it is established that the face of the tortoise should be indicated according to the first letter of the *sādhana-kṣetra*.
On both sides of the face, there should be a pair of hands;
the region of the belly is the pair of feet, and at its end, the tail is said to be located. (8)
(The differences in results based on reciting while resting upon various limbs of the tortoise:
"If [the mantra] is recited while resting on the mouth, undertakings succeed; if on the hand, one encounters hardship;
if on the belly, there is excessive suffering; and for the feet, loss is declared."
In the tail there will be loss of wealth; the location of the lamp is known as the mouth.
(The fault in performing initiation and other rites elsewhere than at the lamp-site:
"Indeed, whoever performs initiation, fire-offerings, and so forth without the lamp-site, one should know that very act to be fruitless; it conduces to malevolent magic. (10)

8–9 | Having thus indicated the face, he describes the hands and other limbs of the tortoise with the words beginning with "mukhasya" (of the face): the two compartments situated on both sides of the face constitute the pair of hands; the two compartments situated on both sides [of the hands] constitute the region of the belly;
the two compartments on both sides below that constitute the pair of feet; and the compartment below that is the tail—this is the meaning. This is according to the divisions of the face and so forth.
He states that recitation, sacrifice, and so forth produce desired and undesired fruits, beginning with the words "In the mouth" (mukhe) and so on.
Regarding the phrase "the location of the lamp" (dīpasthāna), Rāghavabhaṭṭa, having stated here that the meaning of the word "lamp" has been explained elsewhere, says:
"I shall now fully explain the lamp as it was taught in the *Brahmajāmalatantra*."
By this, palaces, villages, houses, and so forth are to be known as auspicious or inauspicious.
"The letters from *ka* to *kṣa* are known as 'lamps' (*dīpa*).
The sixteen vowels should be understood as the 'seats' (*pīṭha*) by the best of mantra-practitioners.
Likewise: "The vowels are designated as the seats, while the consonants are indeed the lamps."
The place where the lamp-syllable resides within a particular square shall be that "lamp-place";
this is undoubtedly the lamp-place in the tortoise-diagram (kūrmacakra).

And thus it has been said: by this it is understood that the compartments of the directions (*dikkoṣṭha*) consist of consonants and serve as the locations for lamps; whereas the eight internal compartments (*antaḥstha*) consist of vowels and are designated as the seats (*pīṭha*). Consequently, by this [statement], the exclusion of the vowels is declared on account of their nature as seats; likewise, in the present context, Śrīmat Pūrṇānanda stated: "In the belly, suffering is excessive."
By stating this, it has been declared that vowels and consonants situated within the abdomen are to be avoided; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
(The necessity of performing the Vāstuyāga during initiation:
Now I shall describe the initiation preceded by the Vāstuyāga, which is an ancillary part of the rite.
By performing which [rite] according to the prescribed rule, one shall obtain the fruit of initiation (dīkṣā). || 11 ||
(The determination of the offering to the fifty-three deities presiding over the limbs of the site):
Having slain the Rākṣasa named Vāstu and having occupied his body, the gods remain there; one should first offer a bali-oblation to those fifty-three.
In the second chapter of the *Śāradā-tilaka*, the teachers of the *lakṣaṇa* state: "One should know that its face is [in the center], with two hands situated on both sides;
the two compartments are the two flanks, the two feet are the remaining [parts], and the tail is said to be [the rest]."

Having thus instructed on the determination of the mouth and other features according to the first letter of the name of the *kṣetra*, one should divide even that which stands in the center by means of this sequence.
By this [statement], [it is shown that] for the vowels situated within the eight central squares as well, one should proceed according to the method previously described.
It is understood that the conceptualization of the "mouth" and other [parts of the face] has been stated.

Regarding this, the contemplation of enmity, friendship, and so forth between the first letters of the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the field (*kṣetra*), and so on, has been explained in detail by Rāghavabhaṭṭa;
however, as it is not mentioned in the present context, it is not demonstrated here.

11. Having thus determined the location for the lamp, he begins to describe the *vāstuyāga* (sacrifice to the site-spirit) with the word "atha" (now). Regarding the phrase "an auxiliary of initiation" (*dīkṣāṅgam*), Rāghavabhaṭṭa, citing the *Mayamata*, states that the *vāstuyāga* is an auxiliary to initiation:
"In auspicious rites, in initiation, in the construction of a pavilion, and likewise in the rules for building houses and so forth..."
An offering to the site (vāstuvali) should be performed for the sake of pacifying demons and obstacles and for the attainment of prosperity.
Thus, regarding the phrase "preceded by the Vāstuyāga," the meaning is that the Vāstuyāga is the precursor to that which consists of the constituent parts of initiation (dīkṣā),

namely the collection of the constituent parts of initiation. Consequently, by the term "constituent parts of initiation" (dīkṣāṅga), there is the inclusion of the preparation of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), the consecration (adhivāsana), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the mandala, and so forth.
12. Regarding the term "rākṣasa": Rāghavabhaṭṭa describes the origin of the Vāstu deity as follows:
"Siṃhikā, the wife of Kaśyapa, gave birth to two sons, Rāhu and Vāstu;
the elder had his neck severed by Hari, and the younger was struck down by the gods."
In the thirtieth chapter of the *Tantrarāja*:
"A certain asura of square form, the destroyer of all, [arose];
for the very sake of slaying him, all the gods made an effort."
Having prepared to strike him down, they found him invulnerable due to a boon;
to dispel that [threat], he then spoke to me, saying, "Come to us."
Now tell us how that pride of the Vāstupuruṣa was quelled;
for because of it, the entire world had been oppressed.
When they had spoken thus, I said to them: "His death is difficult to accomplish;
having dug him into the earth, one should likewise place his body there."
And constantly, for the sake of overcoming the fifty-three [deities] who are devoid of movement,
those among them who are averse to worship— by them indeed [are these acts] performed.
They would take away their merits and perform evil deeds;
therefore, one should always perform their worship every day.
"Only auspicious things arise quickly, and not even a mention of anything inauspicious.
And in the Mahākapilapañcarātra as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"Formerly there was Mahānugra, the terrifier of all beings."
Slain by the gods, he fell to the earth; he is known as the Vāstupuruṣa.
As long as the earth remains stable in the world, so long does Vāstu, the asura, remain;
but at the time of dissolution, he goes to absorption along with the gods, all the planetary deities, and the rest.
Extending for a hundred crores of yojanas all around,
that person stands pervading the earth, lying face upwards and black in color.
"The knees, elbows, and the sides [of the chest] are located at the directions of fire and wind;
this [form] has the feet and hands of the Pitṛs and the head of Īśa; with palms joined at the heart, hair standing erect, very stout, with round eyes, it has the form of an asura. Thus [it is said].
In this context, the upward-facing orientation of the *vāstu* (the site) has been described; however, its downward-facing orientation is also observed, as Rāghavabhaṭṭa states:
"Indeed, the demon named Vāstveśa, who possessed a massive body and had received boons from the gods in ancient times, remains worshipped;
he always lies upon the earth, having stretched out his feet and hands, with his face turned downwards."

Even though such a contradiction exists regarding the downward and upward orientations, its resolution has been established by Somaśambhu as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "The site (vāstu) with its hands drawn in is upward-facing, while that shaped like a demon is downward-facing."
In acts of worship, one should remember your face as being turned downward when situated on a wall or similar surface. (Regarding the rite of offerings, the Vāstu-maṇḍala:
I shall now describe the offering-circle (vali-maṇḍala) for these [deities], which destroys all obstacles. (13)
(The squareness and the hand-measure of this maṇḍala:
The mantra-practitioner should prepare a square plot of ground measuring one cubit.
(The measure of one cubit:)
Those who know the tantras understand a cubit (hasta) to be twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula) plus one.
(The measurement of the *mānāṅgula*): The length of the middle joint of the middle finger of the maker’s right hand is declared to be the measure of the *mānāṅgula*. (15)

(Another sequence for that same [measurement]): The middle finger of the performer of the rite, measured across the width of his own thumb, is this "measured finger" (*pramāṇāṅgula*); others, however, hold it to apply to all ritual acts.

By this [it is meant]. And thus, while in the construction of houses and the like the site (vāstu) is face-downward, in the present context it is indeed face-upward. "They remain" means that the fifty-three deities remain presiding over their respective bodies; the sense is that even after killing, they have not departed by abandoning those bodies.
This has been established in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"One should worship all the gods residing in the site (vāstu) for one's undertakings;
by that he prospers, otherwise he rises up at the command of Mādhava.
And thus, having slain the Rākṣasa named Vāstu according to the manner previously described, the fifty-three deities presided over his body.

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "one should offer the *bali* to those who abide with the characteristics to be described hereafter, prior to the initiation (*dīkṣā*)," and "in the manner that will be described.
(13) Now, he begins to explain the *vāstu-bali-maṇḍala* with the verse beginning with "the *bali*," etc.

Regarding this, he says: "Square" (caturasrām). The meaning is that one should make the ground square with the measurement of a *hasta*. To the question, "What is the measurement of a *hasta*? he replies: "Twenty-four" (caturviṃśati).
Since the knowledge of the measurement of a *hasta* depends upon the knowledge of the measurement of a finger (*aṅgula*), he states the various measurements of the *aṅgula*.
—By the words "the agent of action" and so forth.
(Another sequence for that same [measurement]:
That subtle dust which is seen when the sun shines through a lattice window.
First, among the measures of length, the *trasareṇu* is declared. (17)
Eight of those atoms (paramāṇu) are to be known as one mote of dust in a sunbeam (trasareṇu); eight of these motes of dust are traditionally said to constitute one particle of dust (reṇu). || 18 ||
Eight of those dust particles are known by the wise as a "hair-tip" (bālāgra);
eight hair-tips are known as a "nit" (likhyā), and eight nits are known as a "louse-egg" (yūkā).

17. Now, what is the nature of the *mānāṅgula* (measuring finger-breadth) by which the measure of a *hasta* (cubit) is determined? To this he says: "The *jāla*" and so forth. And thus: eight *paramāṇus* (atoms) make one *trasareṇu*; eight *trasareṇus* make one *reṇu* (dust mote); eight *reṇus* make one hair-tip (*bālāgra*); eight hair-tips make one *likhyā* (nit); eight *likhyās* make one *yūkā* (louse-egg); eight *yūkās* make one barley-corn (*yava*). Eight barley-corns [make one *mānāṅgula*].
"Aṅgula" means the measurement of a finger-breadth.

Here, although it is established by all schools of thought that the atom (*paramāṇu*) alone possesses the status of the primary measurement, the fact that the statement beginning with "firstly, those atoms... identifies the *trasareṇu* as the primary measurement is [intended to show]... [the process of aggregation].
It should be understood that this refers to the first dimension perceivable by the senses.
However, in the seventh chapter of the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*, it is stated:
"A *rathareṇu* (dust mote) is proclaimed to be formed by eight *paramāṇus* (atoms)."
Eight *rathareṇu*s are proclaimed to constitute one *trasareṇu*.
Eight of those [translucent particles] make one *vālāgra* (the tip of a hair); eight of those are known as a *likṣā*;

eight of those *likṣās* are called a *yūkā*; eight of those make a *yavamadhya* (a middle barley grain); eight barley grains make one *aṅgula* (finger-breadth); and twenty-four *aṅgulas* make one *kara* (cubit), and so forth. (2–4)
According to this view, one *trasareṇu* consists of sixty-four atoms (*paramāṇu*). Thus, in other contexts, various different methods for defining measurement are observed.
They say that eight lice-motes (*yūkā*) make one barley-corn (*yava*), and eight barley-corns make one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
Furthermore, the measurement of the *mānāṅgula* has been declared by the wise. (20)
(Another method for this same [measurement]:
Eight horizontal barley-corns and three rice-grains with straight tips—some tantrikas maintain that this is the measure of the *mānāṅgula*. 21.
(The scope of the previously mentioned cubit measure: The measure of one cubit is prescribed for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). || 22 ||
(The sequence for the division of the squares of the site mandala):
Now, the mantra-master should divide that [site] into sixty-four squares as follows. (23)
22. "The *sruk* and *sruva*," and so forth. Also, in the seventh chapter of the *Hayaśīrṣa*, having defined the measurement of the cubit (*hasta*) according to this same sequence, it says:
"With these cubits, one should construct a temple, a sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), as well as an image, a pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), and even a mandala."
Those who desire to attain the fruits [of their merit] should never construct an archway, a banner, or a vessel rich in qualities that is devoid of honor.
Thus it has been stated. However, in the Mahākapilapañcarātra as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, it says:
"For houses, palaces, wells, pavilions, and water-reservoirs, a Vāstu-maṇḍala measuring eight cubits should be prepared, and not otherwise."

By this, he states that the mandala measures eight cubits (*hasta*). However, since it was specified here as being "by the measure of a cubit" (*hastapramāṇataḥ*), it is established that in the *vāstuyāga*, which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to initiation (*dīkṣā*), the *vāstu-maṇḍala* measures one cubit.
(23) Having thus defined the measurement in cubits, he demonstrates the sequence for the division of the sections of the *vāstu-maṇḍala*: "Now," (*atha*).
The connection is that one should divide that maṇḍala into sixty-four squares (padas) in such a manner.
Now, [it may be asked]: "In the eighth chapter of the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*, it is stated:
'One should always [use] sixty-four [squares] for a temple and eighty-one for a house.'"
In the *Devīpurāṇa*, as upheld in the *Śrī-Vāstuyāgatattva*:
"In a temple, there are sixty-four [squares], and in a house, eighty-one squares."
Likewise, in the *Somaśambhu* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"One should construct a Vāstu-maṇḍala of sixty-four squares for a temple;
however, for a house, one should fashion the Vāstu with eighty-one squares."
Since such statements as these declare that the sixty-four-square *vāstu-maṇḍala* pertains solely to a temple,

how can the sixty-four-square nature of the *vāstu-maṇḍala*— which serves as a component for the construction of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) that is an auxiliary to initiation (*dīkṣā*)— be justified here? It is said in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*, as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
Having divided the site into eighty-one squares for houses and the like,
the Vāstu deity is prescribed by Brahmā as consisting of sixty-four squares for palaces.
Having said this, it was stated:

"I shall describe the excellent pavilions (maṇḍapas) in accordance with the temple. And thus, since the Vāstu-maṇḍala of the temple consists of sixty-four squares, [the pavilions] are proportionate to that.
Since it is also appropriate for this mandala within the pavilion to consist of sixty-four squares, it is well said: "just as [it is] sixty-four squares.

Here, he clearly states the sequence for the division into sixty-four squares in the eighth chapter of the *Ādikāṇḍa* of the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "When the field has been made square and divided eightfold on both sides..."
"Then, having drawn the diagonal lines, one should determine the portions for the deities.

Thus, having first made the ground square, one should divide it eightfold on both sides. In that division, nine lines extending eastward and nine extending northward must be drawn. When this is done, there are sixty-four squares.
They are completed. By the phrase "at the base, sixty-four squares as follows," this very sequence for the division of the squares is shown.
Furthermore, the designations for these lines, which extend east-west and north-south, have been demonstrated by Viśvakarman.
Among them, for those extending east-west, in order from north to south:

Śrī, Yaśomatī, Kāntā, Supriyā, Parā, Śivā, Suśobhā, Saghanā—these are to be known; likewise, the ninth is remembered as Ibha. (Viśva0 5.22–23). These are the names [of the eastern directions]. Now, the names for those extending northward, in order starting from the west, are as follows:
"Dhanyā, Dharā, Viśālā, Sthirā, Rūpā, Gadā, Niśā, Vibhavā, Prabhavā, and another, Saumyā; these veins are situated in both gentle and ungentle [locations]. (Viśvakarmaprakāśa 5.23–24).
Likewise, for the square-shaped Vāstu-Rākṣasa, these lines extending from east to north are the veins, and they are as follows:

It is stated that [the deities] must certainly be installed within the body of the site (vāstu) which is the very nature of the mandala. One should draw two corner-threads from Īśāna to Rākṣasa and from Agni to Prabhañjana; thereafter, one should worship Brahmā. (24)
In the four central compartments, one should likewise worship Aryaman in each of the four compartments starting from the east in the four cardinal directions.
Then [place] Vivasvat, then Mitra, and after that Mahīdhara;
again, in the squares of the two half-corners starting from the southeast (Agni) direction.
The best of mantra-knowers should worship in the sequence from top to bottom:
Sāvitra, Savitṛ, Śakra, and again Indrajaya.
The practitioner, being wise, should place Rudra, Rudrajaya, Āpa,
and Āpavatsaka on both sides of the ear-line within the pairs of squares.
Then one should worship Śarva, Guha, Aryaman, Jambhaka, Pilipiñjaka,
Carakī, Vidārī, and Pūtanā.

24–29 | "From Īśāna," etc. In the previously mentioned sixty-four-square mandala, one should apply two diagonal lines (*karṇasūtra*)—one from Īśāna to Nirṛti, and the other from Agni to Vāyu—one by one; this is the remainder [of the sense]. The word *karṇa* is well-known in the treatises on architecture (*śilpaśāstra*) as denoting a corner.
Having thus described the application of the diagonal lines, he instructs on the sequential worship of Brahmā and the others starting from the center of the mandala:

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): one should worship Brahmā in the central group of four squares. Next, he states the locations for the deities of the directions with the words "pūrvādi" (starting from the east).

Thus, the meaning is that one should worship Aryaman in the eastern group of four squares adjacent to the central group of four squares occupied by Brahmā; Vivasvat in the southern group of four squares; Mitra in the western group of four squares; and Mahīdhara in the northern group of four squares.

Regarding the phrase *koṇārddha* (half of the corner): one should worship Sāvitrī and the others in the pairs of half-corner squares starting from the positions of Agni and the rest, following the sequence of above and below. Thus, outside the four Brahma-squares, in the four first corner squares divided by the previously drawn corner lines, the worship of Sāvitrī and the others is prescribed here according to the sequence of above and below. And so it is said:

In the upper half of the two halves of the southeast corner, one should place Sāvitra; in the lower half, Savitṛ. Likewise, in the upper halves of the two halves of the southwest cell, [one places these deities] in the four directions starting from the east, within the first and last steps plus a half.
The wise one should [worship] eight by eight in their respective divisions, in sequence, up to Īśa.
One should worship Īśāna and Parjanya, Jayanta, Śakra, and Bhāskara;
then Satya, Vṛṣan, Antarikṣa, and likewise Agni and Pūṣan.
Vitathāśramasaṃjña, Gṛharakṣakasamjñaka, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, Mṛga, and likewise Nirṛti; || 32 ||
The gatekeepers are named Sugrīva, Varuṇa, and Puṣpadantaka;
and the Asura, Śoṣa, and Roga, along with the chief ones known as Vāyu and Nāga. (33)
Soma, Bhallāṭaka, the one called Vargalā, Uditī, and Aditi. || 34 ||

The meaning is that one should worship Indra in the upper half of the eastern square (Indra-jaya), Rudra in the upper half of the northern square (Rudra-jaya), Āpa in the upper half of the western square, and Āpavatsa in the lower half; thus one should worship them.
Now, he describes the procedure for the four corner squares situated above those: "In the corners," etc. This also is according to the previously stated method.
This should be arranged within eight compartments divided by diagonal lines. Thus, it results that one should worship Śarva above and Guhya below in the southeast (Āgneya);
Aryaman above and Jambhaka below in the southwest (Nairṛta); Pilipiñja above and Carakī below in the northwest (Vāyavya);
and Vidārī above and Pūtanā below in the northeast (Aiśāna).

Although no specific distinction is stated here, since it was previously mentioned that [the sequence] begins from the word "fire" (vahni), the worship of Śarva and the other deities must also be performed according to the sequence starting with fire.

(30–34) Now, he describes the procedure for the compartments (koṣṭha) of the directions beginning with the east, starting with the words "pūrvādi" (beginning with the east). Regarding the phrases "sārddhādyantapadeṣu"—"ādi" (beginning) and...

The compound is to be analyzed as follows: *anta* (end) and *ādyanta* (beginning and end), and *ardha-ādyanta* (half, beginning, and end); [the phrase refers to] those words which exist together with these. Thus, in the words located at the ends and middle points of the corners divided by the previously mentioned corner-lines, as well as in the other words, one should place the eight [mantras] to be described hereafter, sequentially in each direction from the East up to the Northeast (*īśāna*).
The meaning is that one should worship the deities beginning with Īśāna.

Accordingly, one should worship these: Īśa in the eastern half of the northeast corner; then Parjanya; then Jayanta; then Śakra; then Bhāskara; then Satya; and then Antarikṣa in the eastern half of the southeast corner. Thus it has been stated:
In the third chapter of the *Śāradā-tantra*, it is stated: "In order, Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Śakra, Bhāskara, Satya, Vṛṣa, and Antarīkṣa are situated in the eastern direction."
(The filling of the squares of the mandala with powders and the commencement of the offering of oblations:
Having filled the squares of even those deities already mentioned with five kinds of powders, one should then offer oblations to them with these [verses]. (35)

Likewise, in the southern direction, in the half of the southeast corner, one should worship Agni, and then in sequence Pūṣan, Vitatha, Aśman (Yama), Gṛharakṣaka, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga. As it is stated in that very same source:
"Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Yama, and Gṛharakṣaka..."
The Gandharva, the Bhṛṅgarāja, and the Mṛga are situated in the southern direction.

Thus, in the western direction—from the middle of the southwest corner up to the middle of the northwest corner—one should worship in sequence these [deities]: Nirṛti, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Varuṇa, Puṣpadanta, Asura, Śoṣa (Śeṣa), and Roga (Rāga).
It is stated in that very same [text]:

"Nirṛti and Dauvārika, then Sugrīva and Varuṇa, Puṣpadanta and Asura, Śeṣa and Roga—these are situated in the western direction. Thus, in the north—from the middle of the northwest corner to the middle of the northeast corner, in sequence: Vāyu and Nāga.

"Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should construct an auspicious pavilion.

It has been stated that one should then construct the pavilion on an auspicious lunar day as prescribed in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). "It is praised for him, but not at all praised for him by whom it blazes;

Having placed a single unbaked clay vessel at each of their mouths and filled those vessels with ghee, he should light a wick in each one and observe the flame. If the lamp-flame in the east is bright, the construction of a pavilion and so forth is auspicious for a Brāhmaṇa; if it is so in the southern and other directions, it is likewise for a Kṣatriya and the others respectively; and if all the flames are equal, [it is auspicious for all].

"For all. Here, "bestowing all desires" (*sarvakāmapradā*) means bestowing the desires of all. It follows that a ground where a distinction in color occurs or where the flame of a lamp is extinguished is not auspicious for that particular color.
Regarding the statement that water does not digest quickly, he clearly describes the method of testing it in that very same place:
At dusk, having filled a pit with water,
the wise preceptor should carefully examine it at sunrise to determine whether it is of the highest, lowest, or middling quality.
"If the earth remains moist with water, it is excellent; if it is damp, it is middling; if it is dry and cracked, it is inferior. Such ground should indeed be avoided with great effort.
Having thus caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, the wise man should construct the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
(Regarding the nature of the cubit for the purpose of determining the dimensions of the mandala:
"Either with a lotus-hand or with the hand as previously described according to the rule. (2)
(Regarding the actual form of the lotus-hand: "If the māna-hand should be provided with four aṅgulas, that itself shall be the padma-hand; so the experts in Tantra know. (3)
(Various dimensions of the pavilion:
The pavilion may be sixteen cubits, or even twelve cubits.
(The nature of the pavilion, as well as the number, measurement, and positions of the pillars.)
It is quadrangular, with four gates, and provided with a railing and other features. || 4 ||

2. Regarding the phrase "or sixteen cubits" (*hastaṣoḍaśaka*) and so forth, he states the measurement of the cubit (*hasta*) in order to define the dimensions of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) that will be described:

"By the lotus-cubit" (*padmahastena*). The connection is that one should construct the pavilion with either the previously mentioned "lotus-cubit"—defined in the third chapter as "consisting of twenty-four finger-breadths" (*caturviṃśatyaṅgulāḍhya*) and so on—or with the [standard] hand (*kara*).
3. Regarding that, he states what the nature of the *padmahasta* (lotus-hand) is: "māna... and so forth.
A *mānahasta* consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), measured by the standard unit of measurement for the right hand of the practitioner.
If that [measurement] is augmented by four finger-breadths, then those learned in the Tantras know it as a *padmahasta*. By this—

It is indicated that the construction of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and other ancillaries for Tantric worship must be carried out strictly according to the measurements of the cubit (*hasta*) as previously defined.
4. He describes the nature of the pavilion with the words "hasteti": the pavilion is either sixteen cubits or twelve cubits [in size].
By this, the superior and inferior dimensions of the pavilion are demonstrated; therein, the sixteen-cubit pavilion...

The maximum measurement is twelve cubits, and the minimum measurement is [twelve cubits]. Here, by the word "api" (also), the pavilion consisting of fourteen cubits—the intermediate measurement—is also included. For this very reason, Rāghavabhaṭṭa states:
"This small [pavilion] is twelve cubits; from that, it increases successively by two [cubits each]."

Having thus stated the words of the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*, by this it is declared that a [maṇḍapa] of fourteen cubits is of middle size, while one of sixteen cubits is of the highest size. By this, it is established that among the maṇḍapas of twelve, fourteen, and sixteen cubits, their status as inferior, middle, and superior sizes follows sequentially through a doubling of the first measurement. Likewise:
Having stated that it is the same elsewhere as well:
"It is joined with sixteen pillars, four of which are situated in the middle;
the altar stands all around, eight cubits in height. (5)
Measuring five cubits and straight on all twelve sides,
the best of teachers should bury one-fifth of them in the earth according to the procedure for planting stakes. (The sequence for staking.)
"A wise man should have a pavilion constructed in the northeast corner of the house, measuring twelve, eight, six, or sixteen cubits on all sides. Thus it is said.
Here, "eight or six cubits" means fourteen cubits. And so, in the present case as well, sixteen cubits is the superior measurement.

The smallest measurement is twelve cubits; by the word "api" (also), the intermediate measurement of fourteen cubits is included, and thus it should be understood that the pavilion is of three types, which is also the view of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Pūrṇānanda.
As for what is stated in the third chapter of the Śāradā-tantra:
The distance between them should be measured by five, seven, or nine cubits;
it is joined with sixteen pillars, four of which are situated in the middle.

Thus, the characteristics of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) have been stated; by that as well, the three previously mentioned measurements were indicated by the teachers. For instance, in that context, by the conjunction of "five" and "seven," the number twelve is obtained; likewise, by the conjunction of "five" and "nine," the number fourteen is obtained; and similarly, by the conjunction of "seven" and "nine," [the number sixteen is obtained].

The number sixteen is thus understood. Consequently, in the opinion of the venerable Lakṣmaṇācārya as well, by the phrase "that which has a measurement of five, seven, or nine mantras," it is stated that the pavilions possess the dimensions of inferior, middling, and superior sizes according to the method previously described.
It is precisely with this intention that Rāghavabhaṭṭa has combined [the numbers] "five" and "seven. Likewise...

It has been stated that [the number] follows as five and nine, and likewise as seven and nine. By the phrase "the altar and so forth" (*vedikādi*), the inclusion of the flagstaff (*dhvaja*) and other such items is intended. The characteristics of the door, the altar, and so forth will be explained later.
Regarding the word "sixteen": the meaning is that the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is joined with sixteen pillars. Of these...

He describes the spatial distribution of the pillars with the words beginning "at the crossroads" (catvara): among those sixteen pillars, four are situated in the middle—that is, located in the central region of the pavilion—at the four corners of the altar; these have a height of eight cubits.
The meaning is that the height of the four pillars standing at the corners of the altar is eight cubits.

6. Regarding "five": the twelve outer pillars are five cubits in measure. Regarding "straight": the meaning is that those sixteen pillars themselves must be taken as straight and without curvature. This is also stated in the third chapter of the *Śāradā-tantra* concerning the location of the twelve outer pillars and the measurement of the door.
Two [pillars] on each side of the door and four at the corners;
the wise one should construct the door with a measurement of two cubits.
"...four of them are to be placed in the middle;
they should be twelve [in total] around [the perimeter], eight cubits in height.
They should be five cubits in measure, without gaps, straight, and auspicious. Thus it is said.

In this context, since trees and other materials for the construction of the pillars have not been prescribed in the root text, they are demonstrated from another source. Thus, in the *Pañcarātra* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"One should make the pillars firm, straight, and equal, fashioned from heartwood."
Specifically, Rāghavabhaṭṭa states in the *Kriyāsāra*:
"For the work of constructing a pillar, the sacrificial tree, bamboo, or the *kramuka* tree [should be used];
or other pure trees may be used, but not trees of any other kind."
Even though it is prohibited for a pillar, a tree is taught in that very same context, as follows: "A tree that is a thorn in the house, one that is withered on its own, crooked, ancient,
or produced from inauspicious ground must be rejected in the work of making a pillar."

In that regard, the measurement of the pillars stated as being eight cubits externally and five cubits internally refers to the best-sized pavilion (*maṇḍapa*); for the medium and inferior sizes, however, the measurement should be determined accordingly.
It is with this very intention that Rāghavabhaṭṭa also prescribes the measurement of twelve pillars for the medium and inferior types.
It has been stated that this is to be calculated by the rule of three proportions (*trairāśika*).

Here, the placement of the pillars, both externally and internally, must be performed precisely according to the sequence beginning with Agni (the southeast). To this effect, there is a statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
One should place pillars, which have the nature of the Vedas, at the corners of the altar, following the sequence starting from the southeast (āgneya), as follows... ||
By this, it should be understood that the placement of the twelve pillars outside the altar (*vedi*) is also according to the sequence starting from the southeast (*āgneya*).
"A fifth part of that" means a fifth part of those pillars measured by their respective dimensions previously mentioned. Thus, having divided the height of the pillar into five parts—
Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that one should bury [the remainder] one-fifth deep in the earth.

(7) Regarding what was stated as "twelve on all sides," he demonstrates its sequence with the words "of the door. This means two [units] in each direction [from the ground level of the pavilion]. (The height from the site is the elevation of the maṇḍapa floor.)
The site for the pavilion is said to be raised twelve finger-breadths above the ground.
(Regarding the enclosure of the pavilion:
One should enclose it on both sides of the entrance with bamboo poles and coconut leaves.
(Resolution on the Doors) It has four doors aligned with equal lines and is adorned with four archways. (The distinctions of the archways according to the directions)
A gateway made of nyagrodha wood is prescribed for the east, and one of udumbara wood for the south.

In the west, a gateway made of *aśvattha* wood; in the north, a gateway made of *plakṣa* wood (to be constructed in the absence of the previously mentioned *nyagrodha* and others). Alternatively, one may place a *plakṣa* in the east and likewise a *nyagrodha* in the north.
(Regarding the height and circumference of the archway pillars: In the absence of these very trees, the Śamī tree, Jambu, Khadira, Sāra, or Śāla wood is prescribed for the archway. || 11 ||
The meaning is that there are eight pillars in the four directions and four in the four corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya), making twelve pillars in total.
Regarding the phrase "two cubits" (hastadvaya): here—
In the smallest [size], the door should be two cubits; from there, it increases by four finger-breadths for each of the middle and largest sizes.
Thus, according to the authority of the *Pāñcarātra* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, the measurement of two cubits for the door applies to the pavilion of the lowest dimension;

however, for the middle and highest dimensions, it is understood that there is a difference in measurement through an increase of four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each. Therefore, even though there is no specific mention here [of the door], by virtue of its syntactic unity with the previously cited *Pāñcarātra* statement, the phrase "by the measure of two cubits" refers to the door of the pavilion of the lowest dimension.

Regarding the measurement of the door: for the middle and superior [mandapas], the determination of the door's dimensions should be made by increasing [the size] by four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each.
This appears to be indicated by the word "expert" (*vicakṣaṇa*).
(8) Regarding the phrase "from the ground": the meaning is that the height of the mandapa floor from the ground is twelve finger-breadths.

9–11 | The connection is that one should construct the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) according to the rule beginning with "of equal dimensions" (*samasūtram*). In that regard, he states the arrangement of the arches (*toraṇa*) according to the different directions, beginning with "the *nyagrodha*," etc. *Nyagrodha* is the banyan tree (*vaṭa*). *Plakṣa* is the *parkaṭī* tree. The rest is clear. He states another alternative: "or in the east. These two alternatives have been demonstrated by Somaśambhu, as recorded in the *Vaidikasarvasva*: [The Sanskrit text follows... ...Thus, these two options have been shown.

"One should install the arches (toraṇa) of Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa, arranged starting from the east; or else, there may be a reversal of the beginning and the end. Here, by the phrase "reversal of the beginning and the end," the first option—namely, the Vaṭa arch in the east and the Plakṣa arch in the north—is that which is stated in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi*.
The ritual procedure has been shown. Furthermore, there is another statement held as the very essence of the Vedic tradition:
"One should place a *nyagrodha* tree in the eastern direction, likewise an *udumbara* in the southern, a *pippala* in the western, and a *plakṣa* in the northern direction."
In the third chapter of the *Śāradā-tilaka*, it is stated:
"At each door there should be arches (*toraṇa*) made, in order, from milky trees (*kṣīri-mahīruha*).
Thus, only one method is prescribed. Regarding the explanation of the phrase "from milky trees" (*kṣīri-mahīruhām*), Rāghavabhaṭṭa [comments] on this term...

It has been stated that this is because of the definition: "The *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa*— namely, the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa*— are the milky trees (*kṣīrimahīruha*)."

Regarding the phrase "of these": the meaning is that in the absence of these previously mentioned trees such as the *nyagrodha* and others, only the *śamī* tree is to be employed for all the archways (*toraṇa*). Here, by the use of the plural number in the word "sarveṣām" (of all), it is indicated that the rule for employing the *śamī* tree applies only when even one of the four previously mentioned types is unavailable. It should be understood that if even a single one of them is obtained, the archways must be constructed using that very one.

For this very reason, Somaśambhu, as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, stated: "In the absence [of all], one should install even just one of these in all directions. Here, by the restrictive indication "even just one" (*ekameva*) in Somaśambhu’s statement, [the possibility of installing] two or three is excluded.
It is indicated that even if all of these [materials] are available, one should not employ them [all], but rather construct all the archways (*toraṇas*) using just one of them.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"If none of these are available, there may be just one; in its absence, the *śamī* tree [is used]."
"Jambu, khadira, sāra, and tāla are prescribed for the archway (toraṇa).
By this, it is stated that in the event of the unavailability of the śamī tree, jambu, khadira, and the others are to be employed in the archway in their respective order.
The specific characteristics of the archway are described in detail in the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*:
The Aśvattha, Udumbara, Nyagrodha,
and Plakṣa are prescribed for the purpose of the archways (toraṇa) in the directions starting from the east, respectively.
One should place one cubit [of the base] upon the ground and likewise raise it four cubits;
the measurement of the horizontal plank should be half the measurement of the pillar's height.
16. Śrī.
(The height and circumference of the pillars of the archway: The height of those pillars is prescribed as seven cubits each; their circumference is stated to be ten finger-breadths.
One should arrange the archways at intervals of two cubits from one another,
covered with pairs of white cloths and provided with bundles of *darbha* grass.
One should fashion archways encircled by garlands of flowers,
whether circular or square, measuring twelve or sixteen finger-breadths.
The archway (toraṇa) should be made six, four, or two aṅgulas [in height], free from blemishes, and level;
at the bases of the pillars of the archway, one should place water-pots (kalaśas) and auspicious sprouts (maṅgalāṅkura).
One should place [the image] above; then one should give the Sudarśana discus, or one should fashion a water-pot or a vardhamāna vessel using an eighth part of the materials.

"The archways (toraṇas) should be established and worshipped with the mantra 'Syonā pṛthivī'. Here, in this statement from the *Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra*, the instruction "one should place the Sudarśana discus" refers specifically to the Vaiṣṇava pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Following that, the names of these archways are also specified:
"Suśobhana shall be in the east, likewise Subhadra in the south;
Sukarman in the western part, and likewise Suhotra in the north.
Here, the deities named Suśobhana, Subhadra, Sukarman, and Suhotra are [to be placed] in the form of the four archways (toraṇa) starting from the east.

Because they stand there for the purpose of warding off obstacles to the sacrifice, the archways (toraṇas) are designated by the names of those respective deities, since they are presided over by them. As it is stated in the Mahākapilapañcarātra cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"The gods are stationed in the form of archways within the sacrificial pavilion."
"For the purpose of destroying obstacles and for the protection of the sacrifice.
For this very reason, the worship of these deities at the archways (toraṇas) is taught in that same [text]:
"That most beautiful [archway] in the east, consecrated with excellent mantras from the Ṛgveda and other [Vedas]..."
And with the mantra "īṣe tvā," one should place the one named Subhadra on the right.
"One should place [the deity] called Sukarma in the western direction with the Sāmaveda and so forth, using the mantra 'śanno devī'; one should install Suhotra in the north.
(12) Thus it is said. He indicates the height of the pillars of the arches with the word "stambha" (pillar).

"Seven cubits" refers to the dimensions of the arches (*toraṇa*) for the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) of the highest grade; by the phrase "separately," [the text indicates] the pillars of the arches for the pavilions of the middle and lowest grades (including the placement of the wooden planks upon the arch-pillars and the installation of the tridents therein).
The measurement of the horizontal plank should be two and a half cubits in length;
one should fashion tridents in the middle of the archway according to the measure of one cubit.
The fact that their dimensions differ by five or six cubits is indicated in sequence. It is stated clearly in the *Vāstuśāstra*:
"They are five cubits in measure in width, two cubits [in height];
those of medium size are said to be six cubits, and likewise those of superior quality are seven cubits."
Here, by "two cubits in width," the measurement of the horizontal plank is stated. Thus, in a pavilion of the highest dimension consisting of sixteen cubits, [the planks] are seven cubits in measure;
in a pavilion of the middle dimension consisting of fourteen cubits, they are six cubits in measure.

It should be understood that in a pavilion (maṇḍapa) of the lowest dimension, measuring twelve cubits, the arch-pillars (toraṇastambha) are five cubits in measure. Regarding the thickness of the pillars, he says: "ten," etc.; "parīṇāha" means width.

By the previously cited statement from the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*, "Whether circular or square, measuring twelve or sixteen finger-breadths," two options are seen for the pillars— either circularity or squareness—
as well as various measurements of width starting from twelve finger-breadths.

13. Regarding the term "horizontal" (*tiryak*): the meaning is that the measurement of the horizontal plank (*phalaka*) in the form of a lintel (*dehalī*) situated above the two pillars of the archway (*toraṇa*) should be two and a half cubits (*sārddhakaradvaya*) in length. This measurement refers to the horizontal planks of the archway according to the supreme dimension mentioned in the rule, "the height of those pillars is said to be seven cubits. However, the measurement for the horizontal planks of the archway according to the middle and inferior dimensions is as follows:

It should be conceived as gradually decreasing by six finger-breadths [at each stage]. To demonstrate this very point, Rāghavabhaṭṭa, in his commentary on the third chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*, states: "The measurement of the horizontal plank should be half the measurement of the pillars. This measurement of the horizontal plank applies only to the best [type of pavilion].

It should be understood that for the other two [sizes], there is a reduction of six and six *aṅgulas* respectively. Thus it has been stated. And so, it follows that for the largest-sized archway (*toraṇa*), the plank should be measured at two and a half *karas*; for the medium-sized one, it is reduced by six *aṅgulas* from that; and for the smallest-sized one, it is reduced by four *aṅgulas* further than that, resulting in a plank measuring exactly two *karas*.

As for that which is stated in the twenty-fourth chapter of the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*, concerning the pillars of the archway (*toraṇa*) measuring five cubits: "The central prong should be straight, and those on the two sides should be slightly curved."
That is declared to be both; one should then plant it at a depth of two finger-breadths.
One should place one cubit [of the base] on the ground and raise it four cubits;
the measurement of the horizontal plank should be half the measurement of the pillars.
Thus, the fact that the plank's dimension is half that of the pillar has been stated.

It should be understood that the maximum [height] remaining after its burial is four and a half cubits (*caturhastārddha*). Consequently, even in the case where the pillar is five cubits, it results in the wooden plank being exactly two cubits; thus, everything is beyond dispute.
Regarding the term "spikes" (*śūlāni*): the meaning is that one should fashion or install spikes in the middle—that is, in the central region—of the aforementioned wooden plank. This...

A trident (śūla) must be fixed at each archway (toraṇa) individually. This has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa in his commentary on the *Śāradātilaka*: "The plural number in the word 'tridents' refers to the number four; the singular number in the word 'archway' is used in the sense of a genus. Therefore, one trident should be made for each archway. Regarding this:
Having constructed the archway, one should place three tridents upon its summit.
And in the middle portion of the two foremost [ends], there are tridents upon the fillet.

Thus, according to two passages from the *Kriyāsāra* and *Mantramuktāvalī* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, there is also an alternative ritual procedure (*kalpāntara*) for the installation of three tridents upon each crossbeam of the arches. Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that the circumference is one-sixth [of the length], and that this applies equally to all three pavilions (*maṇḍapa*).

14. He describes the nature of the tridents (*śūla*): "straight," and so forth. Tridents have three prongs; among them, the middle prong should be straight and not curved, while both of those prongs on the sides—that is, at the flanks of the middle prong—should be slightly curved. Of those tridents, one should fix them at a distance of two finger-breadths (*dvyaṅgula*) [from the edge], as is understood from the context that they are for the arch-panels (*toraṇaphalaka*). This has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
The central peg has a sharp point and is straight; on both sides of it are two curved pegs with sharp points, their curved portions facing the area of the central peg.
As stated in the *Piṅgalāmata* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"The regions of the door-frames should be marked with tridents at their respective tops."
"The central prong should indeed be straight, while those on the two sides should be slightly curved;
both of these have been described, and one should then fix them at a distance of two finger-breadths.
In this regard, whichever archwood has been prescribed for a particular direction, the tridents (śūla) in those respective places should likewise be [fixed] with that very same [measure].
It should be understood that these [rites] are to be performed; thus indeed says Rāghavabhaṭṭa. (Herein lies the distinction for Vaiṣṇavas:
Now, the specific distinction regarding the Vaiṣṇava tantras is being declared here. || 15 ||
On the head, with a twelfth part [of the measurement], one should place the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
made from their respective woods, according to the sequence starting from the east.
One should place jars provided with perfumes, flowers, and garments into them;
there, one should worship Dhruva, Dharā, Vākpati, and Vighneśa.
These [deities] are to be worshipped in sequence in the jars situated at the corners of the pavilion.
At each and every door, one should place two golden or other metal jars, filled with water from a spring and adorned with mango leaves.
One should worship these in sequence with mantras and offerings of perfume, flowers, and so forth: Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārtha, and likewise Maṅgala. || 19 ||

Indra and the other deities should be worshipped in the pitchers placed at the doors with their respective mantras; one should then fix banners, radiant like the world-protectors, in the cardinal directions.

15–19 | Having thus described the procedure of the Śaiva Āgamas regarding the installation of the trident (*śūla*), he states the procedure of the Vaiṣṇava Āgamas with the words "In the Vaiṣṇava [tradition]": Here, at the previously mentioned location of the trident, one should install on the tops of the beams (*phalaka*)—in the sequence starting from the east—a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus made of wood from one's own tree, consisting of the wood for the arches (*toraṇa*). Thus, one installs a conch on the eastern arch.

One should place the discus on the southern arch, the mace on the western arch, and the lotus on the northern arch. "By the twelfth part" means by the twelfth part of the pillar of the arch. This specific detail for the Vaiṣṇavas is not mentioned in the *Śāradā-tantra*;
however, Rāghavabhaṭṭa [states as follows]:
In the Vaiṣṇava [temple], one should install the conch, discus, mace, and lotus using the twelfth part [of the measurement],
made from their own respective woods, arranged in order starting from the east.

Having cited this statement from the *Vāstuśāstra*, it is stated that because these [architectural elements] are said to be made of one's own wood (*svadāruja*), the status of being "made of one's own wood" is attained precisely through the installation (*nyāsa*) of the *śūlas* occupying these positions in the Śaiva tradition. The conclusion is that in both Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava archways (*toraṇa*), the *śūlas*, conch shells, and so forth must be constructed exclusively of wood.

20–22 | He describes the hoisting of the banner with the verses beginning with "In the directions" and ending with "possessing auspicious marks": "In the directions starting from the east, banners five cubits long should be made, two cubits in width;
or the banners may be seven cubits long and twelve finger-breadths in width. (21)

The staff for them should be made of bamboo and measure ten cubits in length; the mantra-practitioner should draw the elephants of the quarters, endowed with auspicious marks, in the middle of the banner.

The meaning is that one should fasten eight banners, possessing a radiance equal to that of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), in sequence at the midpoint between the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and the archway (*toraṇa*).
This is stated in the *Hayaśīrṣa* as cited in the *Vaidikasarvasva*:
"Likewise, in the outer region of the archway and within the pavilion..."
"Eight banners are to be established according to the sequence starting from the east. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the statement "having a splendor equal to the world-protectors," the *Śāradātilaka* states the colors of the world-protectors in its fourth chapter:
"Yellow, red, black, smoke-colored, white, smoke-colored, and both white."
"These are proclaimed in order by color as fair (gaura) and reddish (aruṇa).

This means these are the world-protectors (lokapālas). In this statement, the colors of Ananta and Brahmā are described by the terms "fair" and "reddish," but those are irrelevant to the present context. Here, however, the colors of the deities beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna are to be described by the passage ending with "both white."

And thus it results that there is a yellow banner in the east, a red one in the southeast, a black one in the south, a smoke-colored one in the southwest, a white one in the west, a smoke-colored one in the northwest, and white ones in the north and the northeast.
However, in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*—
Dawn-colored, resembling fire, black, white,
yellow, red-colored, as well as white, and likewise possessing all colors.

By this statement, the colors of some of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) are described differently from those previously mentioned. Such being the case regarding this difference of opinion, the underlying intention is that one or the other position should be adopted in accordance with the established tradition (satsampradāya).
21–22. He states the dimensions of the banners: "five," etc.; by "vyāyāma" is meant the width.

He states another measurement: "seven. He states the measurement of the flagstaff: "and the staff. The meaning is that the flagstaff, made of bamboo, should be ten cubits in length. Rāghavabhaṭṭa also says:
"They are considered to be joined with five-twos (ten) bamboo staffs."
Thus this statement has been cited in accordance with the context. In that regard, "with ten cubits" (dvipañcahastaiḥ) means with ten cubits.
All that is performed by the wise, such as worship, fire-oblations, and so forth, beginning with the sacrifice, [is accomplished thereby]. || 23 ||
Just as a field belonging to its owners perishes without protection, so too a temple always perishes without a banner. (24)
Then, indeed, banners should be made together with a flagstaff;
the banners should be seven cubits long and one-seventh as wide.
Regarding the "elephants of the quarters" (*diggaja*):
Amarasimha states— "Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka are the elephants of the quarters. Thus it is said.
Thus, the meaning is that one should draw the eight auspicious directional elephants (diggajas), beginning with Airāvata, in sequence upon the eight banners starting from the east.
However, Rāghavabhaṭṭa [states]: "An elephant, a rat, a goat, a deer, a lion, a fish, an elephant, and a horse..."
One should draw a bull in the middle of the banner according to the prescribed rule,
or else the eight elephants of the quarters, headed by Airāvata.

By this statement from the *Kriyāsāra*, two alternatives are shown: one should either [depict] Mātaṅga and the other elephants of the quarters (*diggaja*) in the center of the banner, or [as stated previously].

(23) Regarding "worship" (*pūjā*): the connection with what precedes is that one should fasten the banners in the various directions at that very place where the worship, fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth were performed.

24. Regarding the fault incurred by not performing the raising of the banner (*dhvajāropaṇa*), he states an illustration: "rakṣaṇa... and so forth. 25. He speaks of the raising of the pennant (*patākā*): "tataḥ" and so forth. "Tataḥ" means immediately after the raising of the banner. The pennants should be made accompanied by, that is, following, the banner itself. By this [it is implied] whatever rule applies to the staff and other components, as well as the colors, applies to the banner.

It is indicated that the same procedure demonstrated for the hoisting of the banner should also be observed for the erection of the flagstaff; therefore, [the sequence for accomplishing the decoration of the pavilion is as follows]:
it is richly adorned with garlands of mango sprouts and graced by canopies.
