It was adorned with variegated garments and provided with beautiful jars. || 26 ||

One should decorate the pavilion with water-pots, small jars, mirrors, and chowries; it should be adorned with various kinds of fruits, foods, sprouts, incense, and lamps, and made radiant with jewels and flowers.

By the statement beginning with "the banners should be seven cubits long," only the measurement of the cloth for the banners has been mentioned. Regarding this measurement, the *Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra*, in its *Ādikāṇḍa*, states a specific detail: "They should be seven cubits in length and twelve finger-breadths in width."
"One should fix the banners on staffs of two or five cubits.
Regarding the specific colors of the banners, the *Kāpila*, cited in the *Vaidikasārvabhauma*, states:
"Now, therefore, I shall describe the characteristics of the banners according to the prescribed rule."
One should hoist a banner of golden-yellow hue in the eastern direction.
In the southeast she has the luster of red, in the southern region she has a black luster;
in the southwest she has the luster of blue, and likewise in the western direction she is white.

One should place a banner of smoky color in the northwest, one of yellow color in the north, and one of all colors in the northeast direction; one of white color in the [direction of] Ananta, and one that is red in the direction of Brahmā. Thus it is said.

Here, from Kapila’s statement that the determination of the colors applies specifically to ten [objects], it is clearly understood that ten banners, representing the deities of the ten world-protectors (lokapālas), are to be installed. However, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, as cited in the *Vaidikasārvabhauma*, also mentions the installation of four banners—each measuring either one or two cubits—upon the four panels of the archway (*toraṇa*). As follows:
"Those [pillars] for the purpose of the arches (toraṇa) shall be one cubit in measure, while those two cubits long shall be placed at each arch, variegated with various colors.
Regarding this, the *Vaidikasarvasva* states that by the word "arch" (*toraṇa*), the horizontal beam (*tiryak-kāṣṭha*) forming a part of the arch is meant.
(The Characteristics of the Altar): On that ground divided into three parts, one should construct the altar in the central portion;
it should be one cubit in height, square, and level.
The altar, made either of bricks or of clay, should be like a mirror.
28. In the *Kriyāsāra* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"A [line] that is crooked, with a moist middle, rough, or unsightly;
or one that is deficient or excessive in measure—such destroys the work of the performer."

By this [statement], since it is heard that a sacrificial altar (*vedikā*) defiled by faults such as being crooked on its sides yields undesirable results, he describes the construction of an altar conducive to achieving the desired result: "That" (*tat*).
The meaning is that one should construct the altar in the middle portion of a space measured by a third part—that is, the third division—of that pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).

The third part, although situated in the cardinal directions, ought to exist; in order to exclude that [possibility], he says: "the middle part. Thus, by tripling the thread of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and omitting one part each from the east, west, south, and north, the construction of the altar (*vedikā*) in the remaining middle part is taught by this. Its height—that is, the elevation of that altar—[is to be determined].
One should make it one cubit in measure, square, four-cornered, and level; the meaning is that no variation in height (utsedha) should be made.
(29) "With bricks" refers to the primary method; in its absence, an altar (vedī) should be constructed from clay, resembling a mirror and free from defects such as unevenness.
Thus it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "Having divided the pavilion into three parts, the middle part shall be the altar (*vedikā*);
its height should be one cubit, and it should be square and level."

"Whether with bricks that are baked or even unbaked, the excellent altar (vedikā) should be made as firm as possible; or, in the absence of those, it may be made even with clay. Its sides must be straight, very smooth, and resemble the surface of a mirror."
In the twenty-ninth chapter of the *Tantrarāja*, immediately following the description of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), it says:
"... there, one should construct an altar (*vedī*) from the center, measuring one-third [of the pavilion] and one cubit (*kara*) in height."
The middle [of the altar] should resemble the surface of a mirror...
Thus the characteristics of the altar have been stated.
(The rite of sowing seeds/aṅkurārpaṇa.)

In the consecration of a temple, in initiation, in the installation [of an image], as well as in a festival, in the ritual sprinkling for the sake of peace, in marriage, and in the binding of the sacred girdle; || 30 ||
One should perform the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) upon entering a new house, during the ceremony of consecration, and in all rites involving auspicious characteristics.
(The Time for Depositing the Sprouts): The depositing of sprouts should take place on the ninth, seventh, fifth, or third day prior to the day of the consecration,
or it may be done immediately.

30–31. Now, regarding the description of the offering of the seed-syllable (*aṅkura*) for the purpose of examining whether an action is auspicious or inauspicious, he first states its objects with the words beginning "In the consecration" (*pratiṣṭhāyām*): in the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of tanks and the like; in the installation (*sthāpana*) of deities and the like; in a festival (*utsava*), namely a festival for the procession of a deity; in the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*), such as an ablution (*abhiṣeka*); in rites for pacification (*śānti*), such as pacificatory sacrifices (*śāntikayāga*); and in the *mauñjavaghana*.

In the *Śāradā-tantra*, the third chapter also states: "In initiation (*dīkṣā*), in consecrations (*abhiṣeka*), upon entering a new house, in the investiture ceremony (*upanayana*), in the consecration of kings, in all rites concerning auspicious marks, and in all auspicious acts, one should perform the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) according to the sequence to be described hereafter. This is the implied meaning.
"And one should perform the rite of *aṅkurārpaṇa* (the sowing of sprouts) during festivals and upon prosperity.

(32) By the phrase "installation and so forth" (*pratiṣṭhādityādi*), there is the inclusion of initiation (*dīkṣā*), consecration (*sthāpana*), festivals (*utsava*), and the others previously mentioned. However, since it is initiation alone that will be discussed in the present context, [one should perform it] on the ninth, seventh, fifth, or third day prior to the aforementioned days for initiation and so forth.

The meaning is that the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) should be performed either on the day before or immediately [on the day of initiation]. Among these five ritual options (*kalpa*), if the preceding one is not possible, the succeeding one should be adopted. Regarding this, he states by the word "previously" (*pūrva*) that in the first option, the offering of the sprouts must be performed in such a way that the day of initiation becomes the tenth day. This is also stated in the third chapter of the *Śāradā*: [The text continues with the citation from the Śāradā.]

"Seven days before the day of initiation, according to the prescribed rule"—here, by the phrase "before the day of initiation," the eighth status of the day of initiation is indicated. In his commentary on this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa also states: "By this it is said that it should be performed in such a way that the day of initiation becomes the eighth. And therefore:
The days for the offering of the ritual sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) are to be determined according to this sequence: on the ninth or the seventh day prior to the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Thus it has been stated.
(The construction of the hall for the offering of the ritual sprouts.)
To the north of the pavilion, one should construct a hall extending from east to west,
ten cubits wide and five cubits deep;
it should be enclosed, and then the wise man should fashion the mandala within it.
(The Procedure for Constructing the Mandala): One should lay down five threads measuring five cubits each;
they should extend from east to west, with an interval of twelve finger-breadths between them. (34)
In that same manner, one should lay down eleven threads from south to north;
forty squares will thus be produced there, which one should then erase.

33. Regarding the construction of the hall which is an ancillary part of the ritual for sowing the seedlings, he says: "Of the pavilion. To the north of the previously mentioned pavilion, one should construct a hall that is oriented from east to west, very wide with a span of ten cubits in length, and five cubits wide, measuring five cubits in its extension, and covered with mats and the like.
One should construct a hall that is not susceptible to the entry of wind; as stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa in his commentary on the third chapter of the Śāradātilaka:
"On the northern side of the pavilion, the wise man should construct a secret hall extending from east to west, and then he should arrange the pavilion within it."

Having cited this statement, it is said in the context of its commentary: "One should construct [the site] in the form of a long square, concealed, surrounded on all sides by mats and the like, provided with a single door to the south, and protected from the wind. Regarding that, he describes the construction of the mandala with the words "Then," etc.
(vv. 34–35). He describes the sequence for constructing the *aṅkura-maṇḍala* with the words beginning "five cubits," according to the traditional injunctions.

By this much [is the procedure completed]. One should lay down five threads extending from east to west, measuring five cubits each and separated by twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas). Likewise, immediately after laying down the threads extending from east to west, one should lay down eleven threads extending from south to north.
"In that same manner" means they are separated by twelve finger-breadths. Thus, by the laying down of the eleven threads separated by twelve finger-breadths—
Five cubits measured from east to west should be taken. Regarding the "squares": thus, by drawing lines extending east-west and north-south, there will be forty squares in that mandala.
The word "should wipe" is to be connected with what follows later. And so, this sequence results as follows:

In the central portion of the width of the hall mentioned previously, one should lay a single thread measuring five cubits in length, extending from east to west; then, on its southern and northern sides, at intervals of twelve finger-breadths, [the division of the squares is made].
By means of rows, four paths are formed at the end on both sides of the four squares;
thus, two paths remain, leaving only three sets of four squares.
(The deposition of powders: One should color those squares with white, yellow, red, and black [powders]. || 37 ||
Following the sequence beginning with Īśāna, the practitioner of mantras, knowing the traditional injunctions, should fill the pathways with powders of dark color.
One should drop two threads each; then, one should drop eleven threads intersecting those [first] threads, extending from south to north.
However, in the *Prayogasāra* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, it says: "Having stretched out the thread, one should snap it so that it extends from south to north."
One should cause two [lines] to be drawn on each side with a measurement of five cubits.

"In the same way, according to the previously mentioned measurement, one should cast eleven lines sequentially— twelve finger-breadths each— equally toward the east and the north, and toward the west; [one should place the points] at the intervals between those lines and the end of the eastern line."

In this regard, five lines extending north-south and eleven extending east-west are seen according to the sequence stated in the root text; thus, a specific difference is observed at the intersection of these lines. Therefore, since such a specific difference is observed at the intersection of the lines here, the established conclusion is that one should adopt either of the two views in accordance with one's own respective tradition. For this very reason, [it is said] "according to the prescription of the tradition."
Thus he will say [in verse 36].

Regarding those squares, he describes the construction of the pathways (*vīthī*) and so forth with the words "by rows" (*paṅktyā*). The connection with the preceding [verse] is: "one should clear away four pathways by means of rows.
Since it will be stated later that "[inside]," it should be understood that these are the outer pathways. And thus, previously...

It is stated that one should make one path (*vīthī*) consisting of four squares on the south, another of eight squares on the west, another of four squares on the north, and the remaining one of eight squares. Now, he describes the two inner paths with the word "antar" (inside):
the meaning is that within the three sets of four [squares], one should clear away two paths on both sides, each consisting of two squares. When this has been done...

He states the result: "only three sets of four squares remain" (verses 37–38). Now, he describes the filling of the three inner sets of four with colored powders (*rajas*) with the words "the squares" (*padāni*). Those squares—specifically the four squares located within each of the four inner sets of four—should be filled in sequence, starting from the northeast (*īśāna*), with white, yellow, red, and black powders respectively.

The meaning is that one should fill [the squares]. And thus, for every group of four, it is stated that the northeast (Īśāna) square is white, the southeast (Āgneya) is yellow, the southwest (Nairṛta) is red, and the northwest (Vāyavya) is black.
This is stated in the third chapter of the *Śāradā-tantra*:
One should color those squares with white, yellow, reddish-brown, and black powders;
then, one should fill the pathways with dark blue powder.
By this statement, only the filling of the squares with dust-particles is expressed, but the sequence for the placement of those particles is not specified.
Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa explains as follows:
"Yellow, red, white, and black, at every step, beginning with Fire (Agni) and ending with Śarva."

Having cited this portion of the *Prapañcasāra*, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the colored powders— yellow and so forth— in the sequence beginning with fire (*vahni*) has been established as authoritative.

According to this view, it is understood that the southeast position (*āgneyapada*) is yellow, the southwest position (*nairṛtapada*) is red, the northwest position (*vāyavyapada*) is white, and the northeast position (*aiśānapada*) is black.

Nor should the placement of yellow and other colors in the sequence starting with fire (Agni) be conceived as occurring during the drawing of the five lines extending from west to east— on the basis of the previously cited *Prayogasāra* statement, "one should not stretch and strike the thread"—
when, in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi*, the placement of yellow and other powders is prescribed in the sequence starting with Īśāna during the drawing of the five lines extending from east to west.
It should not be argued that because it is specifically mentioned here, the sequence must begin with Īśāna;

for this is contradicted by a portion of the previously cited *Prapañcasāra* passage beginning with "yellow, red, white, and black," which states: "Others among his mantra-practitioners declare [the mandala] to be extended from south to north. Thus, upon examining the other verses, both types of ritual procedures (kalpa) are established as being based on lines.

Since the venerable Ācārya-pāda has prescribed the deposition of the colored powders (*rajonnyāsa*) precisely according to the sequence beginning with Fire (*vahni*), one should perform the deposition of the yellow and other powders in either the Īśāna-first sequence or the Fire-first sequence in both types of mandalas, following the tradition and by reflecting upon the words of the previously cited *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* and *Prapañcasāra*. It is for the purpose of making known both these traditions that [this] is stated in the root text.
Since it has been stated, "according to the traditional injunction," everything is now clear.

Regarding the phrase "and by Śyāmala": the meaning is that one should fill in the paths (vīthīs)—which are situated externally in the four directions and internally from east to west—with two squares each, using the color black (śyāmala-varṇa).
In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*, however, it is said:
"One should lay down ten threads measuring five cubits each;
when the field is divided ninefold, there will be eighty-one squares."
One should erase two middle streets and the group of six on both sides of the corners;
for the sake of beauty, one should fashion a lotus in the center using exactly nine [squares].
(Regarding the vessels for the offering of sprouts:
They say there are three kinds of vessels for the rite of offering sprouts:
*pālikās*, five-mouthed vessels, and shallow bowls, in that order.
They are declared by those learned in all the Tantras to be of the nature of Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva.
(Regarding that mold: The width of the mouth of the mold is said to be sixteen finger-breadths;
its neck-opening should be eight finger-breadths wide. (40)
One should subsequently color the squares with white, yellow, red, and black powders;
then, one should fill the pathways with dark-colored powder.
By this, the maṇḍala consisting of eighty-one squares has been described. It should be understood that this, too, is another tradition.

(39) Now, he teaches the vessels for the sprouts—referring to the word "pātrāṇi" (vessels). The connection is as follows: they say that three kinds of vessels—namely, *pālikās* (small pots), *pañcamukhīs* (five-mouthed vessels), and *śarāvas* (bowls)—are prescribed for the rite of depositing the sprouts. Regarding those, the meanings of *pālikā* and the others are as follows:

This has been demonstrated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "Large, high shallow bowls (*śarāva*) are denoted by the term *pālikā*. Those same *pālikās*, when somewhat lower and provided with five openings, are called *pañcamukhī*. The *śarāvas* are well known.

In his commentary on this passage from the *Śāradātilaka*, which follows the same sequence of words, [he explains] the phrase "by those who know all the Tantras": ...by this [phrase], [it is meant that] those who know all the Tantras...

Rāghavabhaṭṭa maintains that there is no distinction between vessels (*pātra*) in rites such as the initiation of the five deities (*pañcadevatādīkṣā*). By the phrase "according to the fourfold sequence" (*catuḥkramāt*), it is stated that within each of the three groups of four, four vessels—such as the *pālikā* and others—should be placed. He himself will later state that this placement follows the sequence starting from the west. Regarding the phrase "consisting of Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva," the *pālikās* are forms of Hari, while the five-faced [liṅgas] are...

The meaning is that the *brahma*-forms are the vessels (*śarāva*) and the *śiva*-forms are the bowls; by this it is stated that Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva are to be worshipped in these vessels respectively.
This has been stated in the *Kāpila* [text] cited in the *Vaidikasārvabhauma*:
"The *pālikā* is to be known as belonging to Viṣṇu, while the *ghaṭikā* is said to belong to Brahmā;
the *śarāva* belongs to Śaṅkara—these three have the three deities [as their presiding divinities].
(40–41). Now, he states the definition of the *pālikā*, which follows in sequence, beginning with the word "pālikā": the *pālikā* is a shallow bowl (*śarāva*).
The width of the footstool is said to be six aṅgulas;
its height should be four aṅgulas, and its joint should be one aṅgula.
Alternatively, that joint may be two [aṅgulas], or even half of the footstool's height. || 41 ||
The five-faced vessel indeed bestows all desires;
its five faces are said to be four finger-breadths in width.
And four [cups] in the four directions and one above, according to the rule;
the height and width of the small vessel (ghaṭikā) is said to be twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula). || 43 ||
Some teachers say it should be exactly sixteen finger-breadths.
The specific measurement is as follows: the width of that mouth is sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); the width of the cavity at the neck is eight finger-breadths;
and the width of the lower part of the footstool is six finger-breadths. The height is four finger-breadths. Regarding "its joint" (*tatsandhi*):
the meaning is that the joint of that footstool is the place of connection between the shallow bowl (*śarāva*) and the footstool. This is the measurement of the joint.

"It ought to be either two finger-breadths or three finger-breadths," he says with the words beginning "its joint" (*tatsandhiśca*), etc. Here, it should be understood that it is two finger-breadths by half the height of the footstool (*pādapīṭha*), or three finger-breadths by half its width.
(Verses 42–44). He states the characteristics of the five-faced [liṅga] with the word "it should be" (*bhavet*): the five faces of this five-faced [liṅga] are as follows...
And all [the faces] are four finger-breadths in width. He states the location of those faces with the word "four":
there are four in the four directions and one in the center, making five. "Ghaṭikā" is another name for this.

The meaning of "pañcamukhī" (five-faced) is that the ghaṭikā itself is endowed with five faces. For this very reason, [it is stated] in the passage beginning with "the width of the ghaṭikā. Regarding the five-faced [image]:

Thus, the length and breadth have been explained. The length (*āyāma*) of the *ghaṭikā*—meaning its height—and its breadth (*vistāra*), that is, its width, are both measured at twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Nor should it be argued that because the word "breadth" (*vistāra*) is in the singular, it must be a genitive compound meaning "the breadth of the length" (*āyāmasya vistāraḥ*);
for otherwise, the height would not be established by any other statement.

Furthermore, because of the corroborating statement from the *Saṅkarṣaṇakāṇḍa* of the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "The *ghaṭikā* [should be] twelve finger-breadths in both length and width," which establishes that both the length (*āyāma*) and the width (*vistāra*) have the measurement of twelve finger-breadths; therefore, the meaning is simply that the width is accompanied by [equal to] the length.
(Regarding the *śarāva*): The mouth of the *śarāva* is traditionally said to have an extent of twelve finger-breadths;
its base at the bottom is said to have an extent of four finger-breadths. || 45 ||
Regarding the specific measurements of the *pālikā* and other vessels, it is stated that they may be made according to whatever measurement is available, or even by anyone at all. (46)
"Correctly. "Some teachers" means that certain teachers state that the width and length of the *ghaṭikā* (water-clock) are sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

(45) He describes the nature of the *śarāva* (shallow bowl), which follows in sequence, with the words "twelve," etc. The mouth of the *śarāva* measures twelve finger-breadths, and its base is four finger-breadths.
The height of these is taught in the third chapter of the *Śāradā* [Tantra]:
"In the rite of offering sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), they say there are three kinds of vessels:
the *pālikās*, those with five openings, and the shallow bowls (*śarāvas*), in that fourfold order."
"It is taught in all the Tantras that [the deities] consist of Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva;
their height should be inferred as sixteen, twelve, and eight [aṅgulas] respectively.
Thus, the height of the *pālikā* is sixteen aṅgulas, and that of the *pañcamukhī* is twelve aṅgulas.
"Eight finger-breadths for the *śarāva*.

(46) "According to possibility" means that if it is impossible to achieve the specific measurements previously stated for the *pālikā* and other vessels, one should make them according to what is possible.
Thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"Or one should perform [the rites] with vessels such as the *pālikā*, according to what is available.
In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*, in the *Saṅkarṣakāṇḍa*, the vessels for the sprouts (*aṅkura*) are described as follows: [The text continues with the description of the vessels.]
Three types of vessels are prescribed for the rite of the auspicious sprout: the shallow bowl, the small jar, and the vessel; their characteristics are now described.
The mouth of the śarāva vessel should be twelve finger-breadths in width;
its base, even for that which is sixteen finger-breadths [in height], should be four finger-breadths.
The five-faced water-clock (ghaṭī) should be known as the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
one face should be directed upwards, and the remaining ones should be arranged toward the cardinal directions.
The wise person should fashion the materials for the *pālikā* and other vessels out of gold, silver, copper, or clay.
(The sequence for placing the vessels:)
One should wrap the auspicious items three times with a triple-stranded thread.
Having washed those places where rice has been placed, the preceptor should,
beginning from the west, set them down upon bunches of fragrant *darbha* grass.
One should fashion the openings measuring four finger-breadths;
the water-clocks (ghaṭikās), however, should be twelve finger-breadths in both length and width.
The *ghaṭikā* is said to be sixteen finger-breadths in both length and width;
the *pālikās* are declared to be sixteen finger-breadths in width.
Her face is remembered as being well-covered with half a mātrā;
it is six aṅgulas in height at the lower part and likewise wide.
The footstool should be of that same measurement and four finger-breadths in height;
its joint should be known as one finger-breadth, and its thickness should be three finger-breadths.

Regarding this, the meaning is as follows: based on the statement, "It should be known that [the pedestal] is four *aṅgulas* high and its joint (*sandhi*) is one *aṅgula*," when a joint of one *aṅgula* is made for a footstool (*pādapīṭha*) that is four *aṅgulas* high, the height of the footstool becomes three *aṅgulas*.
As for the word "suvarṇa" (gold): using gold is the primary rule (*prathamaḥ kalpaḥ*); in its absence, [it may be made] with silver, or copper, or clay.

Or one should arrange the vessels; by this sequence, it is demonstrated that there is a progressive reduction (*apakarṣa*) of the subsequent materials. Furthermore, by the term "wise" (*sudhīḥ*), it is indicated that when the preceding [materials] are available, the taking up of any subsequent materials should never be performed. And thus says the citation recorded by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"They may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even new earthenware.

(47–48). Regarding the phrase "tripled": this means that those vessels should be auspicious, free from black discoloration, blemishes, and so forth. Having washed the vessels, one should wrap them three times with a tripled thread. It should not be said that the wrapping occurs first and the washing afterwards.

According to Rāghavabhaṭṭa, since it is stated that "first there is washing and afterwards the wrapping with thread," the washing is to be performed prior to the wrapping with thread. Consequently, in the case of the "placed rice" (*āhitaśāli*)— that is,

in the twelve squares located within the previously mentioned circle of sprouts (*aṅkuramaṇḍala*), which are joined with grains and provided with fragrant substances and *darbha*-grass tufts— the vessels [are to be placed] in order from west to east.

The meaning is that one should place [them]. As for the definition of the *darbhakūrca* (a bundle of *darbha* grass), it will be explained by the author himself in the fifth chapter, beginning with the words, "a braid of twenty-seven *darbha* blades adorned with knots," and so forth.
One should fill those vessels with dried cow-dung, sand, and clay.
In those vessels thus described, one should worship Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva.

This is what is meant: having first placed grains, perfumes, *darbha* grass, and *kūrca* bundles within the previously mentioned twelve squares, one should then place a set of four *pālikās* in the western group of four squares, a set of four five-mouthed vessels (*pañcamukhī*) in the central group of four squares, and a set of four *śarāva* bowls in the eastern group of four squares.

Here, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the vessels and other implements is performed in groups of four, following the sequence starting from the southeast (*āgneya*). As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra* as cited in the *Prāṇatoṣaṇī*:
"Having done this, the practitioner should place the vessels there."
"In each of the four [corners], from the southeast (vahni) to the northeast (īśāna).

(49) Regarding the filling of those vessels, he says: "With dried cow-dung" (*karīṣa*), etc. *Karīṣa* is dried cow-dung; *vālukā* (sand) and *mṛd* (clay) are well known. By this [verse], for each vessel, first [one places] dried cow-dung, then sand upon that, and then clay upon that—following this sequence.
The filling is taught as follows. It is stated in the *Ādikāṇḍa* of the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*:
"One should fill [the vessel] successively with dried cow-dung, sand, and earth.
Also, in the *Prayogasāra* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"One should fill the vessels from above with earth, sand, and cow-dung. Thus it is said.

Rāghavabhaṭṭa has also stated that one should fill all the vessels in this successive manner. This too must be performed in the same order as the placement of the vessels, starting from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in those mentioned"—[one should worship] Hari in the four western vessels.
The meaning is that one should worship Brahmā in the central group of four [squares] and Śiva in the eastern group of four.
Regarding the specific procedure for fetching the earth, Rāghavabhaṭṭa quotes the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"On another day, having worshipped the spade with perfumes and other offerings..."
Accompanied by song and dance, and provided with elephants and horses.
The preceptor and the others, some mounted on chariots and others likewise mounted on elephants,
went to the bank of a pond, a river, or a flower grove.
There, having swept a pure portion of the ground with *darbha* grass using the Weapon mantra (*astramantra*),
and having sprinkled it with water for the guest-offering (*arghyatoya*) while recollecting the respective mantras;
Having invoked the Earth with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should worship her with scents and flowers;
then, having dug the ground with a spade while reciting the weapon mantra, [one takes] the earth.
139) (The necessity of performing the previously mentioned rites during the day:
A wise person should perform this rite during the daytime; not at night. || 50 ||
(The necessity of performing the sowing of seeds at night:
"The task of sowing the seeds, however, should be performed at night by those most skilled in the Tantras;
for the Moon, the friend of the night-lotus, is the eternal lord of seeds. (51)
(The sowing of the seeds):
Having washed the seeds with water and milk, the knower of mantras, preceded by the five sounds, consecrates them with the recitation of the root mantra. (52)
Preceded by auspicious customs and the benedictions of the twice-born,
he should pour [the offerings] into those vessels while facing either southward or northward.
Having taken it with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should fill a bronze vessel;
having cleansed the clay with the Hṛdaya mantra and wiped it with a cloth, one should hold it.
"Having circumambulated the Guru with all auspicious sounds [proceeding] from the town or even the city, one should then lead him to the pavilion.

(50) Regarding this: one should perform this ritual—beginning with the mandala which is a subsidiary part of the rite of offering the germinating seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) and ending with the worship of Hari, Hara, and Śiva—during the day alone, and not otherwise.
The meaning is "at night.

(51) He states that the act of sowing seeds must be performed at night with the words "bīja... (seeds...). Here he provides the reason with the words "bījānām... (of seeds). And thus, since the moon alone is the lord of the night, seeds which have it as their presiding deity [should be sown] right there.

The intention is that shaving leads to auspiciousness. (52–53) He describes the sowing of seeds with the words "in water" (*jale*). With the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, *vaṃ*, [one should wash]—the ellipsis being that the seeds to be mentioned later [are washed]. They are consecrated by the root-mantras, that is, by the respective mantras of the deities to whom they are offered.

The recitation (*japa*) should be one hundred and eight or one thousand and eight times; for it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "When no number is specified, there should be one hundred and eight or one thousand [recitations] in rites such as *japa*. Regarding the phrase "preceded by the five sounds":
The five grains (to be sown as seeds),
however, are rice, *śyāmāka*, *āḍhakī*, mung beans, *niṣpāva* beans, and sesame seeds.
Kulattha, kaṅgu, and māṣa are seeds for the purpose of producing sprouts. || 54 ||

(Regarding the worship of the ten deities beginning with Skanda among these [grains]): one should worship Skanda in *kaṅgu* and Vāyu and Agni in *niṣpāva*; Nirṛti in *kulattha*, Soma in *āḍhakī*, and Vaivasvata in *mudga* and sesame.
One should worship Prajāpati in a grain of rice and Ananta in a mustard seed;
one should worship Indra in a Śyāmāka grain and sacrifice to Varuṇa in a bean.
One should worship Soma daily, beginning from the day of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa). || 57 ||

Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that [the instruments] are the *paṭaha*, *kāṃsya*, *mṛdaṅga*, mouth-instruments (*mukhavādya*), and conch shells (*śaṅkha*). Regarding "auspicious rites" (*maṅgala*): these are practices such as the sound of the *hulahula* drum and so forth. Regarding "he should offer" (*nirvapet*): the meaning is that, facing either east or north, he should sow the seeds into those vessels, such as the *pālikā* and others. This is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
Facing either the east or the north, one should sow all the seeds, beginning with the primary seed, into the *pālikās* and other vessels in due order;
since Soma is the lord of seeds, one should perform the sowing at night. Thus it is said.

54. Regarding "śālī" and so forth: *śālayaḥ* are winter grains; *śyāmākaḥ* is the grain well known in Vaṅga as *śāmā*; *āḍhakī* is a specific type of legume (*dvidala*) well known in Vaṅga as *aḍahara*; *niṣpāvāḥ* are *rājamāṣāḥ* (kidney beans); *kaṅguḥ* is *kāunī*, which is also known in Vaṅga as *kā an*.

55–56 | He teaches the sequential worship of the ten deities, beginning with Skanda and ending with Varuṇa, within these ten seed-vessels (bīja), by means of the passage beginning with "Skanda" and ending with "one should worship Varuṇa.
57 | Regarding "Soma": "constantly" (nityam) means from the day of the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) until the day of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
The meaning is that one should worship Soma.
This has been stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"One should worship Soma daily until the day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*)."
"When the day of the *adhivāsa* has arrived, the Guru should perform the dismissal (*udvāsana*) of Soma.
Thus [it is said]. (The ritual of the offering): Having sprinkled [the image] with turmeric water and covered it with cloths, the Preceptor...
One should cast the bali offering for the three types of vessels into the directions starting from the east,
using mantras beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ," and at night, using the names of the Lords of Night.
(The lords of the seven nights:
The Bhūtas, the Pitṛs, the Yakṣas, the Nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva, and Hari are declared to be the deities of all seven nights. (59)
58. "With turmeric water" means having sprinkled [the seeds]—the word "seeds" being understood—with water mixed with turmeric powder.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"To Tryambaka, to Śarva, to Śaṅkara, and to Śiva..."
Homage, repeated homage, to the eternal one, the foremost in all the worlds.
Having scattered [the seeds] with this mantra, one should rain down water mixed with turmeric powder upon them, sprinkling them every day.

Here, "day by day" (*dinaṃ prati*) means every single day. Regarding "with cloths" (*vastraiḥ*): having covered [the vessels] with new cloths. Here, by the use of the plural number in *vastraiḥ*, the threefold nature of the cloths is indicated. Thus, the meaning is that each set of four [vessels] is to be covered with one [cloth].
This very point is indicated by the word "the teacher" (*deśika*). Regarding "the offering" (*bali*): [it refers to the offering] for the three types of recipients.

The meaning is: [the offering] for the previously mentioned *pālikās*, the five *sukhīs*, and the *śarāvas*; and the *bali* for the spirits (*bhūtādīn*) that will be described hereafter. Regarding the phrase "from the east, etc.": although the placement of the vessels (*pātranyāsa*) begins from the west, one should nevertheless perform the *bali* according to the sequence starting from the east. Regarding the phrase "beginning with the *praṇava*": [one should recite] the mantras of the Lords of Night (*rātrīśān*), whose characteristics will be described later—starting with "the spirits" (*bhūtāni*) and "the two ancestors" (*pitaraḥ*)—preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should offer the oblation (*bali*) with their names; this is the connection. And thus, the sequence of the oblation begins with "Oṃ, obeisance to the *bhūtas*," and so forth.
(Verse 59) Since it was stated, "with the names of the Lords of Night" (*rātrīśa*), and there being the inquiry as to who those Lords of Night are, he says: "the *bhūtas*," and so on. And thus...

The *bhūtas* are the deities of the first night, and the *pitṛs* are the deities of the second night; in this sequence, seven deities are the lords of the seven nights. The meaning is that their *bali* offering must also be performed in sequence from the first night up to the seventh night.
(Various materials for the bali-offering:
For the spirits (bhūtas), there should be parched grain (lāja), sesame seeds (tila), turmeric (haridrā), curdled milk (dadhi), and roasted flour (saktu).
For the ancestors (pitṛs), rice grains (taṇḍula) mixed with sesame seeds (tila) are prescribed.
To the Yakṣas, [offerings of] parched grain mixed with curd and coconut water; to the Nāgas, groats and flour; and to Brahmā, lotuses and unbroken rice grains (akṣata).
The food for Śarva should be rice with cakes, and for Viṣṇu it should be rice with jaggery.
(In this regard, there is a distinction:
according to the ritual for the nine nights, the practitioner of mantra [should offer] milk-rice and again kṛśara.
In this manner, one should offer [the oblation] to Viṣṇu and likewise to all [the deities] with milk-rice (pāyasa).
(The offering to the Guardians of the Quarters:
Thereafter, one should present the bali-offering to the World-Protectors with milk-rice and cooked rice.

60–61. Now, he states the different materials for the *bali* offerings according to the different deities, beginning with the words "to the *bhūtas*": *Karambha*—according to Amarasimha, *karambha* is curd mixed with parched grain (*dadhiśaktava*).
Parched grain (*lāja*) mixed with that [is the offering]. *Sāpūpam* means accompanied by cakes (*piṣṭaka*); according to Amarasimha, *pūpa*, *apūpa*, and *piṣṭaka* are synonyms for a cake.

63–64. Regarding the ritual procedure for the nine nights (*navarātra*) mentioned previously in the verse *pūrvaṃ navame saptame 'pi vā* (4.32), he states the specific detail concerning the offering (*bali*): "In the ritual of the nine nights," and so forth. Therein, having performed the offering according to the previously described sequence up until the seventh night, one should offer milk-rice (*dugdhānna*) to Viṣṇu on the eighth night, and on the ninth night, one should likewise offer rice-and-pulse porridge (*kṛśara*) to Viṣṇu alone.

This has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "When the offering of the *bali* occurs during the nine nights (*navarātra*), then the materials for the *bali* and the deity are declared by the teachers [to be]: milk-rice (*dugdhānna*) for Vaiṣṇava and *kṛśara* for the Vaiṣṇaveya, if the *bali* is said to follow the sequence of the nine nights.

Regarding the phrase "to all": in the event that the previously mentioned *bali* materials are unavailable, one should likewise offer milk-porridge (*pāyasa*) to all, beginning with the spirits (*bhūta*s) and so forth.
The meaning is that one should offer the *bali* according to the sequence previously described.

Regarding the phrase "then" (*tataśca*): after that—that is, immediately following the offering of the *bali* to the spirits (*bhūta*) and others—one should present the *bali* to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) with milk-rice (*pāyasa*). This *bali* follows the sequence starting from the east. Among them, the *bali* for Ananta is between Nirṛti and Varuṇa, while that for Brahmā is between Īśāna and Indra.
The distinction: (Examination of the Sprout) Now, the sacrificer should examine the sprout for its auspicious or inauspicious nature. (65)
"In that regard, auspicious sprouts are those that have grown straight upward, tender, and white;
people who know the mantras say that such sprouts are auspicious. (66)

One should avoid inauspicious [trees] that have deformed sprouts, which are smoke-colored, incomplete, or growing horizontally; likewise, those that are dark-green, crooked, and otherwise inauspicious.
66. Now, in the examination of the sprouts, he describes the auspicious ones with the words "properly" (*samyak*) and so forth. "White" (*sitāni*) means bright.

In the reading *mitāni*, the meaning is that they have equal-sized tips. 67. He describes the inauspicious sprouts with the verse beginning "smoky" (*dhūmra*) and so forth. "Incomplete" (*apūrṇāni*) means having a sparse arrangement; "transverse" (*tiryaggatāni*).
"Curved," "humped," and "bent in the middle. Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa, citing the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, states the examination of the auspicious and inauspicious sprouts:
"One should examine the sprouts for the sake of the prosperity of the patron (*yajamāna*)."
They grow straight upward, tender, and white.
One should avoid those that are smoke-colored, incomplete, or similarly distorted; as well as those that are dark-brown or crooked, for these are inauspicious.
"It causes drought, blackness, a smoky appearance, as well as strife;
it brings about incomplete harvests, loss of people, famine, and dark sprouts.
When [the wind] moves horizontally, there will be disease; likewise, when it is crooked, there is fear of enemies. Thus it is said.
(There is peace when the sprout of the inauspicious has emerged.
And for the sake of pacifying those defects, one should perform a *śānti*-oblation;
the preceptor should offer oblations with the root mantra either a hundred or a thousand times.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa.

(68) Regarding the remedy for the arising of inauspicious sprouts, he says: "taddoṣa... and so forth. "By the root" means by the mantra to be given. "A hundred or [a thousand]" means that if the fault is slight, one hundred [recitations] are required, and if it is abundant, a thousand. This is also stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"When an inauspicious sprout has arisen, one should perform a pacifying *homa*;
the Guru, together with those who bear the [deity's] forms, should offer oblations with the root mantra, or with the *aghorāstra* and *astra* mantras, a hundred or a thousand times. Thus it is said.
The Fifth Chapter: (The Ritual for the Consecration of the Limbs of Initiation and the Ritual of Initiation) (The Necessity of Performing the Consecration on the Day Preceding the Initiation)
Then, prior to the day of initiation, the Guru should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), which includes the worship of the five deities beginning with Gaṇeśa:
Gaṇeśa, Savitṛ, Śaṅkara, and the beloved of Śaṅkara (Pārvatī). || 1 ||
One should worship the Lord of Kamalā with the sixteen types of offerings.
(In that regard, the sequence of worship for Śiva in the Pañcāyatana initiation:
When one worships Śaṅkara in the center, one should worship Śrīpati in the northeast. || 2 ||
Likewise, having worshipped Haṃsa in the southeast and the son of Pārvatī in the southwest,
one should fully worship Bhavānī, who is affectionate toward her devotees, in the northwest.

1. Having thus described the rites up to the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) in the fourth [chapter], and desiring to explain the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣākrama*) in the fifth, he first states the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), which is an ancillary part of that, beginning with the words "Now" (*atha*). In that context, one should first worship the five deities beginning with Gaṇeśa.
2–3. Regarding the worship of the aforementioned [deities] in the initiation of the five abodes (*pañcāyatanadīkṣā*), he states the specific rule with the words "But when" (*yadā tu*). Here...

One should worship the principal deity as the object of adoration in the center, and the other four in the four corners. Thus, when a devotee of Śaṅkara worships Śaṅkara primarily in the center, he should then worship Śrīpati in the northeast (aiśānī), Sūrya in the southeast (āgneyī), Gaṇeśa in the southwest (nairṛtī), and Ambikā in the northwest (vāyavī). In this manner...
Furthermore, regarding the worship of Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Ambikā, and Heramba which will be described hereafter, the worship shall be performed specifically according to the sequence starting from Īśāna.

In this case, having established four *kalaśas* in the four directions and one *kalaśa* in the center, the worship should be performed upon them. However, in a place where initiation (*dīkṣā*) for a single deity is performed, one should install only a single *kalaśa* and worship the deity therein. Therefore...
Thus it is stated in the *Prapañcasāra*:
"When one should worship Govinda in the center and Śaṅkara in the northeast of Viṣṇu..."
The practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should worship Gaṇanātha in the southeast, Tapanas in the southwest, and Ambikā in the northwest.
When [the sun] has a thousand rays at midday, one should worship the beloved of Pārvatī in the northeast,
the One-tusked [Ganesha] in the southeast, and Acyuta in the southwest.
In the northwest, one should worship the Goddess, who is the sole ground for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"Thus, by the statement 'either by the single procedure for the jar as described,
or by many jars,' the masters have established the installation of either one or multiple jars."
In the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī* commentary on the *Tantrasāra*, the synthesis of all [deities] within a single [mandala] is observed. As it says:
"When Śambhu is in the center, Hari, Hara, Bhū, and Devī are established; when Hari is in the center, Śaṅkara, Āgāsuta, Ravi, Hara, Gaṇeśa, Aja, and Ambikā are established."

"In the [directions] of the Goddess, Viṣṇu, Hara, Ekadanta, Aravaya, Lambodara, Aja, and Īśvara— the [deities] starting from the portion of Śaṅkara bestow great happiness when placed correctly, but they cause loss when reversed. Here, by the statement "one should worship Śrīpati in the northeast," etc., it is shown that all the limb-deities (aṅgadevatās) follow the sequence starting from the northeast (Īśāna).
The worship has been described. However, in the *Tantrasāra*, the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*, and the *Gautamīya*, it is stated:
"When, having worshipped Govinda in the center, Gaṇanāyaka in the southeast (āgneyī), Haṃsa in the southwest (nairṛtī), one should worship Śivā in the northwest (vāyavī)."
And one should worship Śaṅkara in the northeast for the attainment of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.

By such statements, the worship of the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) in the sequence beginning with Āgneyī and so forth has been described. This being the case, since there are two systems (prasthāna), one must adopt either one according to the tradition of one's own school. For this very reason, the authors of the *Tantrasāra* state that, in reality, these are optional (vaikalpika).
When one worships Bhavānī in the center, one should worship Mādhava in the northeast,
Pārvatīnātha in the southeast, and Gaṇanāyaka in the southwest.
Or rather, one should worship Pradyotana there as the Ācārya of the Vāyavya quarter. || 6 ||
(Regarding Gaṇeśa:
One should worship Heramba in the center, Acyuta in the northeast,
the Five-faced one in the southeast, and Jagadambikā in the southwest.
And in the northwestern direction, the practitioner, composed and concentrated, should worship the Sun.
(There is a fault in worshipping these [deities] in a location other than their assigned place): "Deities deprived of their own proper places bestow sorrow, delusion, and fear.
This opinion has been stated here as an incidental discussion from the *Mantraratnāvalī*. (8)

8. Regarding "mantra": [the word] "incidentally" (prasaṅgāt) is used because the previously mentioned sequence of worship was prescribed specifically for the initiation into the Five Abodes (pañcāyatana-dīkṣā); however—O Bhairavī, [this applies] to Śyāmā, Bhairavī, Tārā, and Chinnamastā.
Likewise, for Mañjughoṣa and Raudra, the five-limbed [mantra] is not accepted by the wise.

Thus, it was stated [in the previous passage] that "because of the lack of utility for the initiation of the five abodes (pañcāyatanadīkṣā) here," based on the statement from the *Tantrasāra* and the *Rudrayāmala*.

And so, although there is no utility for it here, since it is useful elsewhere and elsewhere, it is entirely appropriate for the author to describe even those specific features of the initiation of the five abodes that pertain to the definition of the nature of initiation; such is the intention of the authors of the text.
With a concentrated mind, meditating upon the deity of the mantra,
one who is skilled in the tantras and mantras should perform the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).

Thus, in his commentary on the fourth chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*, Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that regarding the phrase "the deity of the mantra" (*mantrasya devatām*), in the case of initiation into a single mantra, one should install five jars (*kalaśa*) in the case of the system of initiation into five deities (*pañcāyatana-dīkṣā*) and invoke the respective deity into each jar. Consequently, the procedure involving the five ancillaries (*pañcāṅga-prakriyā*) has no application in the context of initiation into a single deity.
Even according to the opinion of Rāghavabhaṭṭa, the phrase "in this context" (*prasaṅgāt*) is appropriately consistent.
(In these [cases], there is a difference in the sequence of worship based on the distinction between the primary and the secondary:
Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the primary [deity], one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others.
If Gaṇeśa alone is the principal deity, then the sequence of the Sun [deities] should follow there.
(Regarding the fault of not worshipping these:
A man who fails to worship them goes to hell; there is no doubt about this. || 10 ||
(The Offering to the Guardians of the Quarters:
Next, the most excellent preceptor should present the bali offering to the deities who are the guardians of the quarters. (11)

9. Regarding the word *mukhya* (principal): the meaning is that having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the principal deity—the primary object of worship—one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others as prescribed in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*). On this point, some maintain that one should first offer a handful of flowers to the principal deity, then complete the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others, and finally perform the worship of the principal deity. Others, however, [hold a different view] here...

By the term *puṣpāñjali*, they refer to the handful of flowers that should be offered at the conclusion of the worship (*pūjā*). Accordingly, they say that having completed the worship of the principal deity and having offered a *puṣpāñjali* to it, one should perform the adoration of Gaṇeśa and the other deities. Such being the case, since the statement admits of both interpretations, one or the other alternative should be adopted according to one's own tradition (*sampradāya*).
This is the point to be understood. For this very reason, Rāghavabhaṭṭa stated: "And this should be known according to the respective traditions of one's own guru.

However, the author of the *Tantrasāra* maintains that the worship of the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatā*) occurs after the worship of the deities of the seats (*pīṭhadevatā*). Thus, it is said in the *Santkumāra-tantra*:

The worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the worship of the limbs (*aṅga*), the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), then the invocation (*āhvāna*), the fashioning of one's own mudrās, meditation (*dhyāna*),

and the worship of the Lord— by this [sequence], after the worship of the pedestal of the principal deity, the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others is prescribed. [Then] the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) upon the principal [deity].
It has been established that statements such as "having given" (*dattvā*) refer to consecrated images, yantras, and the like; this was demonstrated by the passage ending with:

"Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the principal deity, one should worship the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadeva*); that, however, refers to consecrated images, yantras, and so forth."

11. Now, having completed the worship and other rites—the sequence for the offering to the guardians of the directions will be explained in the ninth chapter—[then follows] the teacher’s duty toward the disciple:
"Then, having brought the disciple, who has bathed well and is properly adorned..."
One should perform the placement of the Mātṛkās upon his body, as well as the placement of the Ṛṣi and the other [limbs].
One should recite his own deity-mantra one hundred and eight times over his head;
then, with water from a conch shell, one should sprinkle the child while reciting those same mantras.
(The Duties of the Disciple:
Then, having offered flowers and other such items, the child should prostrate before the guru. || 14 ||
(Then, the duty of the Guru toward the disciple: Having bestowed his blessing along with the Brahmins and the practitioners, the Guru,
having prepared a bed of Darbha grass, should cause the disciple to lie down upon it.
The knower of mantras should bind the child's topknot with the sleeping mantra. || 15 ||
(At the time of the disciple's sleep, the recitation of the mantra of the person granted by the venerable Guru in a dream:
At the time of sleep, the disciple, having fasted and subdued his senses, should recite that mantra three times while meditating upon the sandals of the venerable Guru. (16)

12. He states what must be done immediately thereafter: "Then [he should initiate] the disciple," etc. It should be noted that all this ritual action, ending with the self-surrender (*ātmasamarpaṇa*), must be completed before proceeding. Regarding "the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth": the placement of the seers and other elements as taught in this *Kalpa* will be explained in the sequence of worship (*pūjākrama*).
15. "With the sleep-mantra" means with the mantra of the Dream-Manava which is to be mentioned later. Here, the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandhana*)...
It is stated in the *Svapnamānava-mantra*. Furthermore, in the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
"Having tied the topknot with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should then cause the child lying on the bed to sleep, relying upon the *Svapnamānava*, with the head facing east."

By this root mantra, the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandhana*) is taught; by the *svapnamānava* mantra, the act of inducing sleep (*svāpana*) is taught. This being the case, although there is a difference in the sequence [of these rites], it should be noted that one or the other sequence must be adopted according to the tradition of one's own guru.
(The *svapnamānava* mantra:)
Tāra, followed by two *hilits*, then *śūlapāṇaye* twice, and *dhiṭha*—this is declared to be the mantra of Svapnamānava, proclaimed by Śambhu. (17)
(The Prayer Mantra:
Homage to the unborn, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;
homage to the one who is favorable, whose form is the universe, the Lord of Dreams. 18.
"O Maheśvara, tell me the truth in my dream regarding all matters without exception; by your grace, I shall bring about the accomplishment of the task. (19)
(The disciple’s sleep preceded by a prayer: Having prayed to the Lord with this mantra, the good disciple may sleep.
(In the morning, the inquiry regarding the vision of dreams directed toward the disciple.)
In the morning, the teacher should ask the child about whatever auspicious or inauspicious things were seen in the dream.
(The vision of those things to be described below in a dream brings about success):
a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a palace, a forest, a river, an elephant, a bull, a garland, the ocean, a serpent, and a tree. (21)
Having seen a mountain, a horse, pure raw meat, a temple of the gods, and all such things as these, one shall attain perfection.
17. He states the mantra of the Dream-Man: "The Tāra," and so forth. *Tāra* is the Praṇava (*oṃ*); *dviṭha* is *svāhā*. Thus, the mantra of the Dream-Man is:
*oṃ hili hili śūlapāṇaye svāhā*. He states that one should recite this mantra three times at the time of sleep, by means of the phrase "three times" in the preceding statement.

18–20 | He states the prayer-mantra (*prārthanā-mantra*) to be recited immediately after the recitation of this mantra: *namaḥ* etc. Even in the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*, the statements beginning from here up to "one shall attain success" (*siddhim avāpnuyāt*) are seen to be identical.
22 | Here, by the passage beginning with "a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot" and ending with "one shall attain success," [the text indicates] auspicious omens in a dream.
(Regarding the fire-oblation for the pacification of seeing inauspicious dreams:
Having discerned what is auspicious or inauspicious, the Guru should perform one hundred oblations in the case of the inauspicious with the Astra-mantra;
thus is the procedure for the preliminary consecration of the disciple described in due order.

Only the auspicious [rites] have been explained; however, since the inauspicious ones are also required— as indicated by the upcoming passage stating that "the Guru, having known the auspicious and inauspicious"— they are now demonstrated, as it is said in the twenty-sixth chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:

"Upon seeing a *cāṇḍāla*, a donkey, a crow, one afflicted by disease, anything inauspicious, a man anointed with oil, a naked man, a withered tree with thorns, or a palace without a floor, a person shall incur illness. Thus it is said.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, after describing auspicious omens consistent with the root text— such as a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, and so forth—
it continues: "A Caṇḍāla, a young camel, a craftsman, a pit, an empty space, and inauspiciousness..."
Having seen a naked man smeared with oil, a dry tree covered in thorns,
or the upper story of a palace, a person shall incur disease.
By this, the inauspicious [rites] are also demonstrated.

(23) "With the Astra-mantra" means that one should offer a hundred oblations with the mantra *phaṭ svāhā*. This preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) should be performed on the night preceding the reception of the mantra. However, in the *Piṅgalāmata* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, immediate consecration (*sadyo'dhivāsana*) is also mentioned.
For example:
"Or one should perform the consecration (adhivāsa) immediately according to the prescribed rule.
Also, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"The wise one should perform the rite of initiation in just two days;
or there may be an immediate consecration (*adhivāsana*) if it is done in a single day.
Regarding the meaning of the word *adhivāsa*, Rāghavabhaṭṭa cites the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
When the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *adhi* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*),
this usage "adhivāsa" attains its grammatical validity.
"Staying together with the guru and others at night according to the prescribed rules—
this is indeed considered the meaning of the particle *vā*, given its polysemous nature.
Thus [ends the section on] the duties for the day of initiation.
Then, on the day of initiation, the practitioner of mantra, having bathed according to the tantras with a conch full of water in his hand, should proceed to the place of sacrifice.
One should wash one's hands and feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rules.
(The general preparation of the arghya offering:
One should arrange the arghya near the archway at the eastern gate. 25.

24. "Then" (*atha*) means immediately after the *adhivāsa*. "Having bathed according to the *tantra*"—the author himself will explain this ritual bathing (*tāntrika-snāna*) in the fifteenth chapter. "With water, a conch, and hands" refers to the purpose of establishing the *arghya* offering. 25. "One should wash"—this is the washing of the hands and feet which is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). As it has been said:
Having washed his hands and feet, with his hand in the shape of a cow's ear,
he should drink water that has been inspected three times, in a quantity sufficient for a bean to sink.

And so forth. Regarding the phrase "one should sip water according to the prescribed rule" (*ācāmed vidhipūrvakam*): here, by the term "according to the prescribed rule," the sipping of water (*ācamana*) as taught in the *Śrīvidyā* tradition is being instructed.
This is stated in the *Bhairavatantra*, as cited in the *Haratattvadīdhiti*:
"Having drunk [the water] with the three *bālā* seed-syllables, one should wipe the lips with two."
Having wiped both hands twice with the *durgā* mantra, one should wash the hands with the *māyā* mantra.
With the Śrī-māyā-vāk-parā, the Kāma, and the Tripuṭā-yoni circles,
as well as with the Kāmakalā and the goad (aṅkuśa), [one should worship] the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears.
"One who touches the arms above the chest is not authorized for recitation (*japa*) and other rites.

Regarding this: "with the *bālā* seeds" refers to *ai*, *klīṃ*, and *sauḥ*. "With the two *durgā*s" refers to *dū* and *dū*. "With *māyā*" refers to *hrīṃ*. The *śrī* seed is *śrīṃ*. The *vāc* seed is *ai*. The *parā* seed is *hrīṃ*. The *kāma* seed is *klīṃ*. "The *tripuṭa*" is *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *klīṃ*. The *yoni* is *ai*. The circle is the *bindu*.

By the word "spherical" (*vartulaiḥ*), the previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bījas*) are specified: *kāmakalā* (the digit of desire) is *ī*, and the goad is *kro*. Thus, the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: having drunk water three times with the triad of seed-syllables *aiḥ*, *hrīḥ*, and *sauḥ*; having wiped the lips with *dūḥ*, *dūḥ*; one should wash the hands with *hrīḥ*. [One should wash] the face with *śrīḥ*, the right nostril with *hrīḥ*, the left nostril with *aiḥ*, and [the left nostril again] with *hrīḥ*.

*Klīṃ* in the right eye; *śrīṃ* in the left eye; *hrīṃ* in the right ear; *klīṃ* in the left ear; *e* at the navel; *ī* on the chest; *kroṃ* on the right arm; and *kroṃ* on the left arm—this is the radiance of the principle of Hara.
(The procedure for the general *arghya*).
Having washed the vessel with the Astra-mantra, one should fill it with water using the Hṛdaya-mantra;
then, having invoked the sacred waters (tīrtha), one should pour in the perfumes and other offerings with the Praṇava.
One should indeed display the dhenu-mudrā; this is remembered as the general arghya.
(The performance of the door-worship: One should perform the worship of the door according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual. || 27 ||
(The Entrance into the Maṇḍapa for the Gorocanā Sacrifice): Touching the left branch slightly, the Guru should step over the threshold;
contracting his body, he should enter within with his right foot. 28.
(Pūjā) One should worship Vāstveśa and Brahmā in the south-western direction.
(Sprinkling of the pavilion)
One should sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with the five products of the cow and with water for the guest-offering (arghya).

(The measurements for the five products of the cow: There should be one *prastha* of urine, and half as much cow dung or milk. [This is done] with the weapon-mantra *phaṭ*, and with the heart-mantra *namaḥ*.

27–28 | The worship of the doors will be explained in the sequence of the worship of the root deity. Regarding the phrase "a little": touching slightly the left jamb of the pavilion door, he then [worships] Vighna and Kṣetreśa at the end of the right jamb.

Thus, according to the statement in the fifth chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*, regarding the southern branch, the general measure for the Vighneśa-kṣetra is proclaimed to be half the quantity of clarified butter;
the knower of mantras should then prepare the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with their respective mantras. (30)
Because the worship of the guardians (pālas) is prescribed, one is instructed to proceed by touching the left branch in order to avoid contact with them.
The same applies to crossing the threshold (dehalī):
"One should worship the Weapon-mantra (astra) at each door," according to this sequence.

Thus, according to the words of Śāradā. For this very reason, Rāghavabhaṭṭa also stated in his commentary on the passage from Śāradā beginning with "touching slightly" (*kiñcit spṛśan*) that these three [actions] beginning with "touching" (*ataḥ spṛśan*) have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), because the Deity is worshipped even at the threshold (*dehalī*). "The limb" (*aṅgam*) means contracting the left limb. The contraction of the limb is for the sake of providing space for the obstacles (*vighna*) as they depart.
While clearing away the obstacles that had been uprooted, he gave way by contracting his left side as they were departing;
thus, by the gesture of contracting his left limb, he granted a path to those who were creating hindrances as they went forth.

This is because it is stated thus in the verse cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, beginning with "ityādi. Regarding the phrase "with the right foot": the meaning is that one should enter the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) placing the right foot foremost. This is exactly the same in the *Tantrasāra* and other such works. As for what was said by the author of the *Haratattvadīdhiti*:
"Touching slightly the left branch, preceded by the left foot... [the above explanation clarifies the correct procedure].
Recalling the lotus feet of the Goddess, the wise practitioner should enter the pavilion.
Thus says a statement from another tantra;
and "placing the left foot forward, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion," thus says a statement from the *Tripurārṇava* cited in the *Śivārcanacandrikā*.
One should enter the temple of the deity placing the right foot forward;
however, a follower of Śakti [should do so] with the left foot... [omitted].

Having thus cited the words from the fifth chapter of the *Merutantra* in support of his own view, and having established that one should enter the temple of the male deity with the right foot foremost,

while entering the temple of the Śakti with the left foot foremost, [he addresses] what was stated by the author of the *Tantrasāra*: "Entering with the right foot foremost, touching the left branch, and contracting the right limb..."
Within the maṇḍapa (the nature of the prastha): four palas shall constitute a kuḍava, and four of those are said to be a prastha.
(Regarding the purification of the pavilion:
One should perform that purification, extending to the four-way junction, by means of inspection and other rites. || 31 ||

Beholding with the root mantra and sprinkling with the weapon mantra are prescribed; striking with *darbha* grass by means of that same [mantra] and sprinkling with water by means of the armor mantra are prescribed. || 32 ||

Having stated "having entered" in general terms, [the author] is now intent on inflicting punishment upon the author of the *Tantrasāra* by means of the words "without even considering that statement," and so forth; yet we maintain that even this is done without even considering the statement from the *Gandharva-tantra*:
"Contracting his limbs, he should enter within with his right foot."
Then, one should dispel the obstacles that have entered the sacrificial hall.

Thus, because the statement in the seventh chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra* prescribes that even in the case of a female consort (*śakti*), one should enter the pavilion preceded by the right foot, it cannot be argued that there is a contradiction with the previously cited statements from other tantras; for while the *Gandharva-tantra* teaches exclusively the Śrīvidyā, the statements from those other tantras apply to cases of consorts other than the Śrīvidyā.

Because its purpose has been fulfilled. And thus, it is established that entry into the Śakti-maṇḍapa for those other than the Śrīvidyā system is preceded by the left foot, whereas for the Śrīvidyā, entry into the maṇḍapa is prescribed as being preceded by the right foot alone. For this very reason, the venerable Pūrṇānanda stated, "one should enter with the right foot. As for what was stated by the author of the Tantrasāra—that [entry] is preceded by the right foot—[that refers to a different context].
Intending that the previously cited statement from the *Gandharva-tantra* refers generally to the power (*śakti*) alone, [it applies] by way of commonality to both female and male deities.
However, it is not thereby prohibited anywhere that one enters the pavilion of the female deity (*strī-devatā-maṇḍapa*) preceded by the left foot.
Regarding entry into the pavilion of the Power (*śakti-maṇḍapa*), in some cases there is precedence by the left foot, while in others there is precedence by the right foot.

The summary is as follows: because the *Darśana* of Dakṣapāda concerns deities common to both women and men, and because the *Tantrasāra* teaches deities common to both women and men, the precedence of Dakṣapāda therein is stated in a general sense.

31. He states the purification of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) with the words "as far as the crossroads" (*catuḥpathāntām*). Here, by the term "crossroads," a space measuring only one cubit extending from the pavilion outwards in the four directions, up to the gate-pillars, is indicated. Thus, the meaning is that one should perform the purification of that [space], namely the purification of the pavilion, up to the crossroads by means of the [rites] to be described, such as inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth.

32. Regarding "inspection" (*vīkṣaṇa*): this means it should be performed with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), the mantra to be given (*deyamantra*), and the arrow-mantra (*śara*), namely the *astra-mantra* with the syllable *phaṭ*; and with the armor-mantra (*varman*), namely the *kavaca-mantra* with the syllable *hūṃ*.
The wise one [should perform this] between each step with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
One should scatter the sacrificial offerings there, having consecrated them seven times with the weapon-mantra.
(The characteristics of the scattering ritual:
Parched grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and kuśa grass—these are designated as the *vikira* offerings, which destroy the entire multitude of obstacles. (34)
(Cleansing):
One should cleanse them with a handful of *darbha* grass consecrated by the recitation of the *astra-mantra*.
(The worship of the Guru, etc.)
The rites beginning with the worship of the Guru should be performed according to the rules of the tradition. || 35 ||
(Recitation of the Auspicious Day, etc. Having caused the recitation of the auspicious day and having satisfied the Brahmins,
(the construction of the Cakrarāja).
Or else, with the powder of vermilion or with saffron. || 36 ||
Upon the altar, the mantra-practitioner should draw the enchanting king of wheels.
First, one should draw a hexagon; in its center, a triangle;
then a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, a twelve-spoked wheel, and two [other] eight-petaled lotuses.
33. By the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) "śarāṇunā phaṭ," the meaning is that [the materials] have been consecrated seven hundred times.

36. Regarding the construction of the *cakra* for the purpose of worship during initiation (*dīkṣā*), he first states the substances required for the equipment of the *cakra*’s construction: "sindūra... [and so on]. "On the altar" (*vedikāyām*) means upon the central altar within the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
38. He describes the construction of the Cakrarāja: First, draw a hexagon; inside it, a triangle.

Outside the hexagon, a circle; then an eight-petaled lotus; then a circle and a twelve-petaled lotus; then a circle, a sixteen-petaled lotus, and a twenty-petaled lotus. Having drawn these, one should then draw an eight-petaled lotus.
One should draw a square on the outside, provided with four gates. || 39 ||
(Therein, another method:
Alternatively, one should draw a nine-cornered figure joined with a square. || 40 ||

(The Arrangement of Ritual Substances): Seated in the bound lotus posture, the mantra-practitioner intent on the worship of the deity should place the beautiful ritual substances on the right side. (41)
To the left, one should place a beautiful jar filled with well-scented water,
and behind it, one should set down a vessel for washing the hands.
The preceptor should place auspicious lamps ignited with ghee all around;
he should also place a mirror, a fly-whisk, an umbrella, and a beautiful palm-leaf fan, as well as vessels containing auspicious sprouts, in the various directions.
There is a lotus, and outside that a circular twenty-petaled lotus, and outside that a circular eight-petaled lotus,

and outside that a square provided with four gates. Here, it should be noted that because of the rule regarding the construction of the petals following the circles, one circle must be made at the base of each petal for the purpose of establishing the boundary.
40. Regarding those unable to perform the previously mentioned wheel-construction (*cakra-karaṇa*), he states another sequence with the words "Alternatively" (*athavā*).

In this ritual manual (*kalpa*), first a nine-cornered figure (*navakoṇa*) is made, and then a square (*caturasra*); furthermore, that square must be provided with doors (*sadvāra*), because the square takes the form of the earthly abode (*bhūgṛha*), and it is appropriate for it to have doors, as is seen in the aforementioned King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*).

41–43 | Regarding "having assumed the bound lotus posture" (*baddhapadmāsana*): Rāghavabhaṭṭa, citing another Tantra, describes the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) as follows: "Having taken the left foot, one should place it upon the right; likewise, one should place the right foot above the left."
Pressing the heels against the hips with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose—
this is the lotus posture (padmāsana), honored by all.
(The Bringing and Seating of the Disciple):
Then, having brought the disciple, he should seat him on the right, adorned with various ornaments and provided with a pair of washed garments. (44)
(The Offering of Sesame and Gold):
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the disciple, with his senses conquered, should offer sesame and gold for the sake of expiating the sins committed since birth. (45)
(Choosing the Preceptor preceded by the Recitation of Auspicious Verses, etc.

Having sat down to the left of the preceptor and having performed the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) preceded by auspicious recitations, the wise man, endowed with devotion, should choose the preceptor according to the prescribed rule. (46)
(Regarding the worship of the Guru:
He honored him with cows, land, gold, garments, and the like, as well as with radiant earrings and other ornaments, without stinting his wealth.
One should worship the guru with devotion, preceded by joining the palms in reverence;
having circumambulated the guru, one should offer oneself to him. 48.
(Prayer before the Guru:
Now, therefore, O Blessed One, O Supreme Self, O Most Compassionate Guru, please grace me by means of the initiation and consecration for the knowledge that accomplishes all human goals.

Thus [it is said]. The materials for worship (*pūjā-dravya*) are flowers and so forth. However, the vessel for the *arghya* offering, the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and so on, should be placed specifically to the left.

As for the lamps, mirrors, chowries, and the like, the meaning is that one may place them in whichever directions one desires. The vessels for the auspicious sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura*) are those employed when the rite of offering sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) was previously performed.

46 | Regarding the phrase "having sat down": first, having sat down to the right of the Guru and offered a mark of honor (tilaka) and gold, one should then rise, sit down on the left, and perform the recitation of auspicious benedictions (*svastivācana*) and so forth; this is the meaning.
Having spoken thus, the humble disciple should remain for a long time on the right side of the Guru.
The disciple should recite the Gāyatrī or the name of the deity one thousand times. (The Gāyatrī Japa and its Count) 49.
(The performance of the purification of the elements, etc.
Having performed the purification of the elements and so forth, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as prescribed in the Kalpa.
(The consecration of the mantra)
Alternatively, one should consecrate the supreme mantra by means of the previously mentioned path.
(The Pīṭha-nyāsa):
Thereafter, the best of practitioners should perform the pīṭha-nyāsa upon his own body. (51)
One should then place Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya, respectively,
upon the pair of shoulders and thighs by moving clockwise.

49. "Or the name of the deity" refers to a distinction in eligibility: a twice-born man (*dvija*) should recite the *gāyatrī*, whereas women, *śūdras*, and others, being ineligible for that, should recite the name of the deity they worship.
