Alternatively, by the phrase "or the name of the deity," it is stated that while a twice-born man should recite the *gāyatrī*, if he lacks the capacity for that, he should recite the name of his own chosen deity.

50. *Kalpeti*. Here, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the ritual placements (*nyāsa*), and so forth as taught in the *Tripurākalpa* will be explained in the sequence of worship (*pūjākrama*). "Or else" (*athavā*) means that one should purify the mantra according to the previous path—that is, by the sequence stated in the second chapter—and perform the consecrations (*saṃskāra*) for the mantra to be given, such as its birth (*janana*), infusion of life (*jīvana*), and so forth.

This procedure for the purification of mantra (*mantra-saṃskāra*) applies specifically to those cases where the purification of mantra was not prescribed on the day prior to the initiation (*dīkṣā*). However, there is no requirement for a further purification of mantra even when it has already been performed previously. For this very reason, it is stated in the commentary (*pāda-ṭippaṇī*) on manuscript B:
"If the purification of mantra was not performed before the day of initiation, then one should perform it at this time"—thus the word "or" (*vā*) is used.

51–52 | Regarding "the placement of the seats" (pīṭhanyāsa): by this it should be understood that, having performed the placement of the seats as prescribed in one's own ritual manual (kalpa), one should then place the [principles] beginning with Dharma as they are about to be described. This has been clearly stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"One should place Adharma and the others, in sequence, on the face, the two sides, and the sides of the navel."
Dharma and the others are remembered as the feet, while the others are the limbs of the pedestal.
Within the heart-lotus, one should place the infinite lotus and the sun, moon, and fire, preceded by their respective seed-syllables and the letters of their own mantras. (54)
Having thus assigned the three qualities, beginning with sattva, the supreme guru should likewise assign the Self (ātman),
the inner self (antarātman), the supreme self (paramātman), and the knowledge-self (jñānātman).
(Contemplation of the chosen deity upon the seat consisting of the body):
Having properly placed the seat-mantra, one should contemplate the chosen deity.
(Displaying the mudrās and the installation of the arghya and other offerings).
Having displayed the mudrā according to the rule, one should begin the ritual placement of the arghya offering.
"One should mentally construct a throne within one's own body in due order with Dharma and the other [virtues].

Regarding this statement from the fourth chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*, [the procedure is as follows]: one performs the placement (*nyāsa*) of Maṇḍūka with "Salutation to Maṇḍūka" at the *ādhāra*; Kālāgnirudra with "Salutation to Kālāgnirudra" at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*;
and Kūrma with "Salutation to Kūrma" at the navel. Then, having performed the placement of Ādhāraśakti and the others in the heart...

By this passage, "the subsequent placement of Dharma and the others," [it is meant that] "in a clockwise direction. Thus, one should place Dharma on the right shoulder, Jñāna on the left shoulder, Vairāgya on the left thigh, and Avairāgya on the right thigh. Regarding "on the face":
likewise, one should place Adharma on the face, Ajñāna on the left side, Avairāgya on the navel, and Anaiśvarya on the right side.

"Beginning with Dharma," etc.: the connection is that the four beginning with Dharma are the feet of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the other four beginning with Adharma are the limbs (*gātra*) of the pedestal.
(56) "The pedestal-mantra": the ellipsis is "having properly placed the pedestal-mantra upon one's own body"; [this refers to] the body.

This arrangement of the seats (pīṭha) is for the purpose of the mental sacrifice. With this very intention, in the fourth chapter of the Śāradā-tantra, immediately after the description of the ritual placement of the seats, it says:
"In this manner, one should contemplate the chosen deity within the seat consisting of the body."
Thus it has been said:
"The general *arghya* [offering] is on one's left, while the special *arghya* is directly in front of oneself;
to the north of the *arghya* should be placed the *pādya*, the *ācamana*, and the honey. (57)
(The eightfold offering for the Goddess):

The tips of *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), barley, *vrīhi* rice, and sesame seeds, along with clarified butter, white mustard seeds, and flowers—this is another offering for the Goddess. (58)
(The eightfold arghya common to all deities:
With flowers, fragrance, unbroken rice, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and dūrvā grass—this is declared to be the arghya for all deities. (59)
(The water for washing the feet: Uśīra and sandalwood, as well as milk, are excellent for the water for the feet;
the water for the feet is also said to consist of śyāmāka, dūrvā grass, lotus, and viṣṇukrāntā. (60)
(Regarding the water for sipping):
Having ground together nutmeg, karpūra, kakkola, mango root, and tamālaka, one should add them to the water for sipping; as for the other [ingredients], it is as follows. 61.
The water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) consists of water infused with nutmeg, cloves, and kakkola.
(The Madhuparka:
Honey, sugar, clarified butter, curd, milk, and unbroken rice;
or alternatively, honey, clarified butter, water, and curd combined as "madhu."
Having prepared the madhuparka, he should offer it according to the prescribed ritual.
57. Regarding "the general *arghya*": this has already been explained in the context of the worship of the door (*dvārapūjā*).
58. Regarding "tips of *kuśa* grass": the specific details for placing the *arghya* will be stated by [the author] himself in the eighteenth chapter:
"In every respect, honey is superior to *kṣadra*; ghee and sugar are equal."
If there is only a very small amount of water available from all sources, it is declared to be *madhuparka*.
(Once more, the water for sipping: But the water for sipping once more is with pure water alone. (The rule regarding the vessels for the presentation of offerings.)
Alternatively, one may prepare the water for washing the feet and the other offerings in a single vessel. || 65 ||
(Regarding fragrance: Sandalwood ground with *nameru* and *śavala*, as well as *aguru* and the like, together with *mṛgamada*. 66.

65 | Regarding the phrase "in one": if it is asked how the word *athavā* ("or"), which indicates an alternative option, is appropriate here given that the distinction of vessels was not previously mentioned, it is said in response: in the fifth chapter of the *Sammohana-tantra*:
"For the purpose of offering the *arghya* and *pādya*, and also for the purpose of the *madhuparka*..."
In the same manner, one should place four vessels for the purpose of ritual sipping (ācamana).

By this, the rule for providing each individual vessel has been stated; however, if that is impossible, all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*) may be arranged in a single vessel. Thus, there is a statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"Or else, one should arrange the water for the feet, the respectful offering (*arghya*), and so forth, in a single vessel."
The venerable Pūrṇānanda, having kept in mind the sequence previously stated in the *Sammohanatantra* and with reference to that very text, said "or else" (*athavā*).
And thus, when there is capacity, separate vessels for the offerings (*upacāra*) should be prepared; in the case of incapacity, all the offerings should be given in a single vessel.
As for that which—
When possible, there should be three vessels; otherwise, one should proceed with two.
O Maheśānī, in the case of the water for the feet and other offerings, one vessel must never be used.
Thus, by this statement from the *Svatantra-tantra* cited in the *Śyāmārcana-candrikā*, the prohibition of a single vessel refers to vessels of the same material:
"One should present, in sequence, a copper vessel for the water for the feet (*pādya*), a conch for the respectful offering (*arghya*), and a bell-metal vessel for the water for sipping (*ācamana*)."
Thus, because the *Mahānīlatantra*, in its tenth chapter, acknowledges the distinction of vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings:
"Fragrance gathered from equal parts of saffron, agallochum, musk, and camphor is pleasing to Tripurā; it is not so with any other substance. (67)
(Seat-worship in one's own body):
Then, by means of the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should worship Dharma and the other [qualities] within the bodies;
with flowers and other offerings, up to the end of the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*), and upon that [seat], the Supreme Deity.
(Offering the Fivefold Handful of Flowers):
With one-pointed mind, one should again offer five handfuls of flowers in succession to the head, the heart, the navel, the feet, and all the limbs. (69)
(The Worship of the Mandala and the Worship of the Pīṭhas within the Mandala):
The mantra-practitioner should worship the previously described mandala with perfumes and other offerings. (70)
Having spread *darbha* grass there together with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) upon a *kūrca*,
one should perform the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) there according to the sequence prescribed in one's own ritual manual.
(The characteristics of the *kūrca*:
A braid made of twenty-seven *darbha* grasses, adorned with knots;
that which is wrapped [with thread] in all sacrifices is proclaimed to be the *kūrca*. 72.
(The sequence for the worship of the deity within the yantra; therein, the worship of Tripurā in the center):
One should first worship Tripurā, the ornament of the Kula, in the center of the yantra.
(The sequence for worship in the hexagon):
Then, one should worship the six limbs in the hexagon, and within that, in the triangle. || 73 ||

73–74. Now, he introduces the worship of the deities in the previously mentioned King of Mandalas (*cakrarāja*), beginning with the word "yantra": [One should place] Rati in the front corner, Prīti in the northern corner, and Manobhavā in the right corner.
(Outside the hexagon, on the eight-petaled [lotus]—) then, on the eight-petaled [lotus], the Mothers. || 74 ||
The best of practitioners should worship these goddesses in sequence: Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and thereafter Mahālakṣmī. (75)
On the twelve-spoked wheel outside of that, one should likewise [worship] Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī; then Ambikā, Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Kubjikā. (76)
Then, the mantra-practitioner [should place] Vicitrā, Viṣaghnikā, and Bhūcarī,
as well as Ānandā, in due order (outside of that, on the sixteen petals).
Then one should worship on the petals of the lotus. || 77 ||
Nityā, Nirañjanā, Klinnā, Kledinī, Madanāturā, Madadrāvā, Drāviṇī, Rucirā, and then Rāgavatī. (78)

"In the center" means that one should first worship the root deity Tripurā in the middle of the triangle. Then, after the worship of Tripurā, one should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the root deity in sequence within the hexagon. Next, in the triangle situated inside the hexagon, one should worship Rati, Prīti, and Manobhavā in sequence; specifically, Rati in the corner facing the [practitioner], Prīti in the northern corner, and [Manobhavā] in the southern corner.
He says "born of the mind" (*manobhavām*) and so forth, beginning with "in the presence" (*sammukha*).
Regarding "the Mothers": the meaning is that one should worship the Mothers who are about to be described in the eight petals above the *vṛtta* (circle), starting from the east in due order.
(75) He points out the eight Mothers with the words "Brāhmī" and so forth.

76–79 | Having thus described the procedure for the eight-petaled [lotus], he indicates the deities to be worshipped on the twelve petals in the order starting from the east, with the verse beginning "The twelve-spoked" and ending with "and Ānanda in due order":
Kāmeśvarī, likewise Kāmadīpanī, and Vāmakeśvarī.
Lalitā, Kṣobhaṇī, Kṣudrā, and Svacchandalalitā are the sequence. (79)
(Outside of that, on twenty petals):
Then one should worship on the twenty petals, starting from the east in order:
Māyāvatī, Mahākṣī, and then Sarvavaśaṅkarī. (80)
Jhaṅkāra, Īśabhāvā, Kamalā, Kamaleśvarī, Nīlagrīvā, Viśālākṣī, Bheruṇḍā, and Ḍāmareśvarī. || 81 ||
Samayā, Samayeśānī, Nityānandā, Mahodarī, Sarvasaubhāgyadā, Ānandā, Candrikā, and Candraśekharā. || 82 ||
And Sarveśvarī should be fully worshipped;
[on the petals outside of that] are the seats on the eight-petaled lotus.
(The Eight Seats:
Kāmarūpa, Malaya, Kolagiri, and Kulāntaka. || 83 ||
Then the Mantrin [should visit] Cauhāra, and after that Jālandhara;
Uḍḍīyāna and Devikoṭṭa—this is remembered as the group of eight sacred seats (pīṭha). || 84 ||

Now, he describes the worship of the sixteen goddesses beginning with Nityā on the sixteen-spoked [wheel], starting with the words "kalāpatre" and ending with "kramāt. "Kalāpatre" means on the sixteen petals.
(80–84) Now, outside of the sixteen-petaled [wheel], on the twenty petals, [he describes] Māyāvatī and the others in the order starting from the East.
The worship of the twenty deities is taught by the passage beginning with "Māyāvatī" and ending with "and Sarveśvarī should be fully worshipped.
Regarding the "seats" (pīṭhas): outside the twenty-petaled lotus, on the eight-petaled lotus, one should worship the eight seats, such as Kāmarūpa and the others, in the order starting from the east.
He describes the eight seats with the words beginning "Kāmarūpaṃ ca... and so forth.
In the subterranean chamber outside the twenty-petaled lotus, the best of practitioners should worship Tripureśānī. || 85 ||
(Another Yantra and the Arrangement for Worship therein): In the case of the Śeṣa-maṇḍala, however, one should worship the six limbs starting from the fire [corner].
One should worship Rati and the others in the triangles, and worship everything in the center.
The eight seats are in the underground chamber, and Tripureśī is in the center.
(The characteristics of the vessel to be established:
Whether it be made of gold, silver, copper, or fashioned from clay,
the practitioner of mantras should wash the vessel preceded by the Śara mantra.
It was auspiciously perfumed with the incense of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor. || 87 ||
85 | Regarding the worship of Tripureśvarī outside the eight-petaled lotus within the *bhūgṛha* (earth-house), he says: "In the *bhūgṛha*.

86 | Having first described the sequence of worship for the maṇḍala previously mentioned—beginning with "one should first draw a hexagon"—or else, regarding the worship in the maṇḍala consisting of nine corners as stated in "but [there is] a nine-cornered [figure],"...

He teaches the sequence with the words beginning with *śeṣa* and so forth. The meaning is that one should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the root deity starting from the fire-corner (*agnikoṇa*).

Then, within the inner triangle, one should worship Rati and the others—namely Rati, Prīti, and Manobhavā—in order at the corners facing oneself, the right, and the left. In the center, "all" refers to what was previously mentioned, from Brāhmī and the other eight Mothers up to Sarveśvarī. This is called the "earth-house" (*bhūmigṛha*).
Outside the hexagon, within the enclosure of the ground, are the eight seats (*pīṭhas*) previously mentioned. "In the center" means that one should worship Tripureśī in the middle of the triangle.
(87) Regarding "golden": here, if each preceding material is unavailable, one should take the next succeeding one. Preceded by the *śara* mantra...

[This is] preceded by the utterance of "phaṭ. Here, the reading "śivamantra" is erroneous, because in the fourth chapter of the *Śāradā-tantra*, the washing is specified by means of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) itself, as in: "A pitcher fashioned from gold and other materials, its interior washed with waters [consecrated] by the weapon-mantra... [The word] "śubham" means having a beautiful form.
The width of the pitchers should be fifteen finger-breadths and their height sixteen finger-breadths;
the opening at the mouth should be eight finger-breadths.
(Wrapping with thread: One should wrap the water-pot with thread spun by a maiden; one should wrap it evenly all around with thread consisting of three strands. (89)
Having wrapped it three times, it is said by someone: "By whom? (90).

(Installation of the Vase) One should place the vase in the center while reciting the syllable *Tāra*; it has been honored with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, is provided with a tuft of grass and unbroken grains, and its interior contains gold and jewels. 91.
Then, the mantra-practitioner, regarding the shared base as a pedestal (pīṭha),
should further conceive of the unity between that pedestal and the water-pot (kalaśa).
(The measurement of the nine jewels: Pearl, lapis lazuli, ruby, agate, diamond, coral, ruby, emerald, and sapphire—these are the nine. (93)

87–90 | *Kanyā* refers to a young girl who has not yet reached marriageable age. Regarding the phrase "consisting of the three qualities" (*guṇatrayātmaka*), it means wrapping [the thread] once and then tripling it.
Regarding the phrase "three times," according to the ritual manual (*kalpa*), one should wrap it three times with a single strand and then triple it.
91 | Regarding "with a *kūrca* and unbroken rice": this term *kūrca* is technical and was explained previously. It is [an object] whose interior contains gold and jewels.
The connection is that one should place the common *kalaśa* (vessel) in the center—within the previously mentioned *yantra*—with the thought that it is a pedestal (*pīṭha*).
Regarding the phrase "having a belly of gold and jewels," here the word "jewel" (*ratna*) refers to the nine gems;
the practitioner, reciting the mantra, should place [the vessel] with its interior filled with the nine gems.
Thus, according to the fourth chapter of the *Śāradātilaka* [verse 92],
the meaning is that it is impossible for the Goddess to reside within the jar (*kalaśa*) without first conceiving of the jar as the seat (*pīṭha*) of the Goddess.
(The filling of the jar.)
With a decoction of milky trees, or with a decoction derived from the bark of the *pāśa* tree,
or even with special waters scented with the fragrance of camphor.
The practitioner, reciting the root mantra with the thought that it is the deity itself, should fill the jar while reciting the Mātṛkā letters in reverse order. (95)
(Placing the Śrīcakra in the jar: One should place the cakra of the illustrious Tripurasundarī therein. || 96 ||
(Herein is the worship of the sixteen Kāmakalās:
Śraddhā, Prītī, Rati, Bhūti, Kānti, Manobhavā, Vimalā, Modinī, Ghorā, Madanotpādinī, and Madā. (97)
Regarding the phrase "with the decoction of milky trees" (kṣīrivṛkṣakaṣāyeṇa): here, the meaning is "with the decoction of the bark of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa.

Rāghavabhaṭṭa maintains that, according to the method prescribed in Āyurveda, the decoction should be taken when reduced to one-fourth. Here, by the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and with that produced from the bark of the Palāśa," it is understood that the filling is to be done with the combined decoctions produced from the barks of the four milky trees and the Palāśa.

Regarding the statement in the fourth chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*, "with a decoction of milky trees or with that produced from the bark of the *palāśa* tree," the word "or" (*vā*) instructs that if a decoction of milky trees is unavailable, one may fill [the vessel] with a decoction of *palāśa* bark. This has also been stated by the author of the *Tantrasāra*: "with a decoction of milky trees or with that produced from the bark of the *palāśa* tree."

It has been stated, "either with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha) or with water well-scented with perfumes and flowers. Thus, since the word *vā* is seen in the authoritative *Śāradātilaka* and *Tantrasāra* as indicating alternative ritual procedures (*kalpāntara*), it should be understood that the word *ca* here functions in the sense of *vā*. [The phrase] "with special waters" refers to waters from sacred fords.
This is stated in the fourth chapter of the *Śāradā*:

"Or with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha), well-scented with camphor, fragrance, and flowers. Thus, "the Mātṛkā in reverse order" means reciting the Mātṛkā in reverse (viloma-mātṛkā) and likewise reciting the root mantra (mūlamantra).
Verses 96–98. The wheel of the venerable Tripurasundarī, however, will be described in the seventeenth chapter. In that regard—

He teaches the worship of the sixteen digits of passion (*madanakalā*) with the passage beginning with "Faith" (*śraddhā*) and ending with "the practitioner" (*sādhaka*). These [deities], beginning with Faith, joined with the sixteen vowels,
are Mohanī, Dīpanī, Śodhanī, and Śāṅkarī.
The practitioner should worship these—Rañjanī and Madanakalā—conjoined with the sixteen vowels, using perfumes and flowers. 98.
One should worship the digits (kalās) of Fire, Sun, and Moon with their respective mantras;
there are five digits of the Praṇava according to the fifty-fold division of phonemes.
One should pour a small amount of water from a conch shell, which consists of the [sixteen] digits (kalās), into the pitcher.
(The procedure for placing sprouts and other items in the water-jar:
Likewise, with the sprouts of mango, jackfruit, holy fig, banyan, and udumbara;
and with the tender sprouts of kinnāśa, jackfruit, holy fig, and mango.
The Guru [honored them] with the thought that they were celestial trees, bound together like Indravallī vines.
Having covered the mouth of the jar with this cup,
one should place it according to the ritual rules with the thought that it is a fruit, as if it were the fruit of the wish-fulfilling trees.
Then, the wise person should wrap the water-pot with two clean cotton cloths;
one should place curd, unbroken rice, fragrant flowers, and vermilion on its exterior. (103)
(The Installation of the Corner Vases): One should designate four water-pitchers, joined with water and sprouts, upon heaps of rice at the four corners of the altar. 104.
(Regarding the specific procedure for placing the flask in the second mandala ritual:
However, in the case of the remaining mandalas, one should place a very beautiful new flask, endowed with gold, jewels, and other such items, within the ninefold matrix. 105.

The meaning is that one should worship the arts of love (*madanakalā*). And so it is: *aṃ* salutation to Śraddhā; *āṃ* salutation to Prīti; *iṃ* salutation to Rati—thus the sequence of worship is concluded.

(101–102) Regarding the word "likewise" (*tathā*): here, because of the separate mention of "with tender sprouts" (*pallavaiḥ komalaiḥ*) and because of [the subsequent] mention of "likewise" (*tathā*) and so forth, as well as "kinnāśā" and so forth...

It should be noted that two alternatives have been stated. *Indrabalī* is a specific type of *indravāruṇī* creeper. A *caṣaka* is a vessel such as a shallow bowl or the like, belonging to the same category as a *kalasa*.
(The worship of the Root Power).
Then, having arrived at the time prescribed in the Kalpa, the best of practitioners should worship the Supreme Goddess,
having invoked her into the shade of this wish-fulfilling tree.
And with the sixteen primary offerings and various other charming substances,
he should present the food offerings and so forth, individually, together with the retinue.
(The specific procedure for the ritual of placing nine jars:

Furthermore, in the case of the nine-jar arrangement, the knower of mantras should worship the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī in the eighth jar, using water for the feet and other offerings. 108.
(The Homa):
Then, the wise practitioner should fashion a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the right of himself,
or he should prepare an altar (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit, according to the prescribed ritual.
Having duly installed the fire, the practitioner of mantras should worship the Goddess there and offer oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter one hundred and eight times in sequence.
(The Bringing of the Disciple): Then the wise [teacher] should bring the disciple near to the fire-offering. || 111 ||

(Contemplation of the six paths within the body of the disciple): Having beheld him with divine vision, the wise one should contemplate the six paths here in sequence upon the feet, the navel, the heart, the forehead, and the head. (112)

112. Now, while the purification of the paths (*adhva-śodhana*) is to be described, [the author] first states the manifestation of the six paths within the body of the disciple, beginning with the words "having beheld with divine vision" (*vilokya divyadṛṣṭyā*).
"Divine vision" (*divyadṛṣṭi*) is the unblinking gaze (*animeṣadṛṣṭi*). As it is stated in the second chapter of the *Viśvasāra*:
"Vision with an unblinking eye is proclaimed as divine vision."

Thus [it is said]. The six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) will be explained further on. He states the locus for contemplating the paths with the word "pāda" (foot): "Andhu" means a well; [the six paths] are the path of *kalā*, the path of *tattva*, and the path of *bhuvana*—these three.
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), and the path of mantras (mantrādhvan)—this is another triad. || 113 ||
(Therein lies the path of the kalās:
Nivṛtti, Supratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti immediately following, and Śāntyatītā—these are to be known; thus they declare it to be the path of the kalās. 114.
The path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) belonging to Prakṛti consists of the five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, as well as Bindu, Kalā, Nāda, Śakti, and Sadāśiva. (115)

The meaning is "the anus. And thus, one should contemplate the path of kalās on the disciple’s feet, the path of tattvas at the anus, the path of bhuvanas at the navel, the path of varṇas at the heart, the path of padas on the forehead, and the path of mantras on the head; such is the meaning.

113–114 | He states the six paths (adhvan) with the words "kalā" etc. Here, by dividing the six paths into two groups of three each, it is indicated that the first three paths—consisting of *kalā*, *tattva*, and *bhuvana*—are of the nature of objects (*artha*), while the other three—consisting of *varṇa*, *pada*, and *mantra*—are of the nature of sound (*śabda*). He states this explicitly:
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"These three [terms] are here stated to be the roots (dhātu), while their meanings (artha) are three.
Another statement expressing this same meaning has also been shown by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"The path of mantra, the path of word, and the path of phoneme are [the paths] from the perspective of sound;
the path of world, the path of principle, and the path of limited power are [the paths] from the perspective of meaning, in sequence.
Herein lies the secret: at the beginning of creation, when the desire of Paramaśiva—"May I become many, may I procreate"—has arisen...

From that, the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) arises from the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), and from that, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Through the conjunction of these three powers, the creation of objects (*artha-sṛṣṭi*) and the creation of words (*śabda-sṛṣṭi*) are accomplished. Here, in the root text, the creation of objects is shown by the triad beginning with "the path of the *kalās*," and the creation of words is shown by the triad beginning with "the path of the phonemes (*varṇa-adhvan*). And thus, from the path of the *kalās* comes the path of the principles (*tattva-adhvan*); from the path of the principles comes the path of the worlds (*bhuvana-adhvan*); from the path of the worlds...

The path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), from the path of phonemes to the path of words (*padādhvan*), and from the path of words to the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*)—this is the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*). From the path of mantras to the path of words, from the path of words to the path of phonemes, from the path of phonemes to the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), from the path of worlds to the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*), and from the path of principles to the path of energies (*kalādhvan*)—this is the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). The purification (*śodhana*) of these principles follows the sequence of withdrawal.

Having brought [the elements] into dissolution in Paramaśiva through the process of withdrawal, there is again birth through the process of emanation. This is stated in the fifth chapter of the Śāradā-tantra:
"In the sacrificial pit of the Ācārya, with sesame seeds thoroughly purified and saturated with clarified butter..."
"I purify this path; Svāhā!"—thus for each individual path separately.
One should cause those [elements], beginning with Tāra, to dissolve in sequence by means of eight oblations;
having caused them to merge into Śiva, one should generate [the universe] from the end of Śiva via the path of emanation.

Thus, the term *adhvaviśodhana* (purification of the paths) has precisely the meaning of "purification of the path of emanation. This body consists of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*); since purification of the body is impossible without the purification of the paths, a mantra bestowed upon a disciple whose body is impure does not serve any beneficial purpose.

Prior to the bestowing of the mantra by the Guru, one should perform the purification of the paths (*adhva-śodhana*). Among these, first is the purification of the path of *kalā* (*kalādhva-śodhana*).

The five *kalās*, beginning with *nivṛtti*, constitute the path of *kalā*. Regarding their purification, Rāghavabhaṭṭa states: "Having recollected the path of *kalā* in the feet, and having placed the *kalās*—beginning with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*)—in the secret place, heart, face, and head, one subsequently performs the purification of the path of *kalā*."
He himself will state this later with the words, "One should purify this path," and so forth. Now follows the purification of the path of the principles (*tattvādhva*).
Regarding the principles, the *Śāradā-tantra*, in its fifth chapter, states:
"The path of the principles is divided in many ways according to the differences among the scriptures of Śiva."
There are thirty-six Śiva-tattvas, and twenty-two Vaiṣṇava-tattvas.
Furthermore, twenty-four principles are said to be derived from primordial nature (prakṛti),
while seventeen principles are said to belong to that which consists of the three states (tripadātman).

By this, many divisions of the *tattvas* have been demonstrated according to the distinctions of Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and other systems. Among them, the Śiva-*tattvas* are threefold: by way of being pure (*śuddha*), both pure and impure (*śuddhāśuddha*), and impure (*aśuddha*). Therein, the pure *tattvas* are called the Śaiva [principles]: Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva.
Indeed, these five pure things, together with knowledge, belong to the Lord.
Regarding the pure and impure, as follows:
Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Kalā, and Vidyā are likewise mentioned;
Rāga and Puruṣa—these seven are both pure and impure.
But the impure [principles] are:

Nature (prakṛti), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), mind (manas), the organs of perception, the organs of action, the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the five gross elements— thus say the teachers.
"These twenty-four [principles] are said to be impure in the Āgama;
thus is the classification of the principles of the Śaivas presented here.
In this same manner, the principles of the Vaiṣṇavas and others are also to be understood.
(The Path of Worlds):
That which is called the path of worlds consists of the fourteen worlds. 116.
(The Path of Phonemes):
The path of phonemes is proclaimed to consist of the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*.
(The Path of Words)
A collection of phonemes ending in a case-suffix is called the path of the word (padādhvan). || 117 ||
The path of mantra, the mass of mantras, and the six paths are thus proclaimed. || 118 ||
Even among the Śaivāgamas, there is a specific distinction regarding the reality of Tripurā:
"The five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, then the Bindu, the kalā, the Nāda, the Śakti, Sadāśiva preceded by Sadyojāta, and Prakṛti— thus they know [the sequence]."
"Śiva is the knowledge of the Self, and thereafter Śiva is the Knowledge itself;
furthermore, the entire reality (sarvatattva) and the individual principles (tattvas) are declared to belong to the threefold nature.
Thus has this Path of Principles (tattvādhvā) been described by those who know the various Āgamas. Thus [it is said].
Since Tripurā herself is the subject under discussion in the root text, it is the principles (tattvas) pertaining to Tripura that are presented by the words "nivṛtti and so forth.
Even there, only seven are specifically mentioned by name; however, it should be inferred that other principles taught in the *Śāradā* [Tantra] are also included here.
In this regard, it should be noted: among the previously mentioned principles, some are insentient and impure by their very nature due to being products of Māyā.

Although Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, and the others are inherently pure, they possess impurity due to contact with a body, because they are endowed with the threefold impurities: *āṇava*, *kārmaṇa*, and *māyika*. The nature of these three impurities, beginning with *āṇava*, has been described by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: *āṇava* is the non-recognition (*anavamarśa*) of one's own true nature by Sadāśiva; *kārma* is the cognition "I am a possessor of merit and demerit"; [and *māyīya* is...]

The notion of "I" regarding the name, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth is what constitutes the idea of a self. Thus, by means of purifying the impure principles (*tattvas*), the purification of the body, the self, and so on is accomplished;
therefore, the purification of the paths (*adhvaśodhana*) is necessary for that purpose—this is the summary.
(Verses 116–118) Regarding the word *īrita* ("stated"): it means the fourteen worlds constitute the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*).

In the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "The path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) is proclaimed to extend from Ādhāra up to Unmanī. By this, the location of the path of worlds is defined. It is stated explicitly in the tenth chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*:
(The Sequence for Purifying the Paths):

Then, touching the disciple with the *kūrca* [grass-bundle], the Guru should offer oblations of clarified butter and sesame seeds, reciting eight times: "I purify this path of such-and-such a person."
One should [offer oblations] ending with *svāhā* and preceded by *tāra* (oṃ), for each of the paths in their respective order. || 119 ||
(The Application of Consciousness to the Disciple’s Body):
Having gazed upon the disciple, one should project consciousness into his body. (120)
(The Fivefold Worship preceded by the Offering of the Full Oblation):
Then, having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should worship the Goddess in the jar.
Having worshipped her with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should present an umbrella and a fly-whisk. 121.
"Therein are the seven netherworlds (pātāla) and likewise the seven heavens;
thus, in due order, all fourteen worlds reside within the entire body.

Regarding the term "beginning with 'a'": the meaning is that the phonemes of the Mātṛkā, from the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa', are situated in their respective locations within the body. Regarding the term "ending in case-terminations": [this refers to their manifestation as such].

The path of words (*padādhvan*) consists precisely of a collection of phonemes ending in a case-suffix that constitutes a mantra-component. As it is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"The path of words is a collection of words divided into many varieties."
"The Great Mantra exists as the constituent parts of the sub-mantras;
because it is the primary constituent, this [Mantra] is called 'Path' (adhvan) and is denoted by the term 'pada'.

Thus [it is said]. Rāghavabhaṭṭa, however, says that the "collection of phonemes" refers to the phonemes together with the bindu. Regarding the "Mantra-path" (mantrādhvan), there are seven: a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, and ya.
"The mantras are at the aperture of Brahmā" (verse 119).
Now, he states the sequence for the purification of the paths (*adhvan*) with the word "atha" (now). "With the *kūrca*" means with that which was previously defined. "I purify" means as follows:
one should offer eight oblations with the mantra "Oṃ, I purify the path of the digits (*kalā*) of such-and-such a person, svāhā. This is the meaning.

The sequence of purification through the process of dissolution, creation, and so forth, has already been demonstrated previously by the passage beginning with "by those purified in the preceptor’s fire-pit" (120).
Regarding the word "the disciple," it is clearly stated in the fifth chapter of the *Śāradā*:

"Beholding that child with divine vision, the supreme teacher should again unite that consciousness residing within himself with the disciple. (The offering of camphor and other substances to the Goddess).
Then one should offer camphor and betel leaf to that Goddess.
(Recitation:
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, one should offer it to the Goddess. || 123 ||
(The oblation to the Goddess with the *vyāhṛtis*, the self-surrender, etc.):
Having offered oblations to the Goddess with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should complete the rest of the remaining rites. || 124 ||
One should bind the eyes of the disciple with a cloth using the Netra-mantra.
(The bringing of the disciple for the instruction of the mantra:
Taking that disciple by the hand, one should lead him to the place of worship. 125.
(The Offering of a Handful of Flowers):
Having placed a handful of flowers into his hand while reciting the root mantra, the practitioner should cast them into the water-pot for the sake of pleasing the deity. (126)
(Ascertaining the auspicious and inauspicious through the falling of flowers, and the remedy for the inauspicious:
If the falling of the flower occurs in the directions of the West-North (Vāyavya), Rudra (North), or Indra (East), it shall be auspicious.
If it is inauspicious, the preceptor should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the Astra-mantra.
123. Regarding "aṣṭottara" (one thousand and eight): this recitation is prescribed for the purpose of protecting one's own power (*svaśakti*). As it was stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"One should perform the recitation one thousand and eight times in order to avoid the loss of one's own power.
Furthermore, in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: [text follows].
"Having given the mantra, the preceptor should indeed recite it a thousand times for his own accomplishment.
(125) "With the eye-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
(126) "A handful of flowers"—this refers to the disciple who is about to be initiated at that time.

The meaning is that, due to ignorance of the mantra, the recitation of the root-mantra must be performed by the preceptor; then, authorized by him, the disciple should offer a handful of flowers without [reciting] the mantra.
(127) Regarding "in the west": a falling of handfuls of flowers in the west, north, northeast, or east brings auspiciousness.
(The Removal of the Eye-Bandage):
Having removed the eye-bandage, the pure practitioner should sit upon a seat of kusha grass.
(The Procedure Following the Offering of the Handful of Flowers)
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, the preceptor should worship again.
One should bring the Goddess into one's heart according to the prescribed ritual procedure. || 129 ||
Having placed a water-pot together with its spout upon a blade of kuśa grass in the region of Śambhu, filled with water and wrapped in a pair of cloths; || 130 ||
In the midst of that, the practitioner of mantra should place the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three fruits (triphalā),
as well as ashes, dūrvā grass, clay, horse dung, and gorocanā.
Having protected the sandalwood, the saffron, and likewise the wheel-king with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should display the cow-seal (dhenu-mudrā) and the womb-seal (yoni-mudrā). || 132 ||
(The procedure for the worship of the weapon-deities, etc.
One should worship the deity of the weapon, who is seated upon a lion, exceedingly fierce, bearing a sword and a shield, of terrible form, and facing westward. 133.
Upon that, the knower of mantras should recite the root mantra ten times.

The meaning is that the falling of flowers in the directions of Vāyu, Nairṛta, Yāmya (South), and Agni brings inauspicious results. Thus, when the fall of flowers is inauspicious, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times;
"one hundred and eight" means one hundred plus eight. This is clearly stated in the Piṅgalāmata as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"Having filled the hollowed palms with flowers, one should cause them to be offered upon the Yoga-pīṭha."

"If the flower falls in the northwest, west, north, or northeast, it is auspicious; if in an inauspicious [direction], one should offer one hundred and eight oblations for pacification with the Astra-mantra.
(130) "In the midst of Kuśa grass" means in the region of Śambhu, in the northeastern quarter.
Alternatively, the practitioner, having filled a conch vessel with water,
should worship there the digits (kalās) of Fire, Sun, and Moon.
Then, having cast out the mantra, one should worship with the six limbs;
having fully worshipped with the weapon-mantra, one should recite the root mantra ten times.

(The seating of the disciple upon the yantra): Then one should draw a lotus on the left; one should write the vowels in the filaments in pairs, and then one should write the consonants beginning with *ka*. 137.
On the seventh and eighth petals, the wise one should write one hundred thousand syllables;
in the center, within the pericarp, the preceptor should establish the disciple.
(The placement of the Śrīcakra upon the disciple's head:
One should contemplate the Śrīcakra, which consists of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), upon his head. (139)

(The Bathing of the Disciple): Having covered the disciple's face with a cloth and risen, one should bathe the child with water poured from the mouth of the pitcher while reciting the root mantra. (140)

(Initiation of the Disciple) Having lifted the pitcher according to the ritual rules, reciting the mantra of the Mother-goddess in reverse order while gazing at the celestial trees situated at its mouth, he should place it upon the head of the child.

137–138 | Next, regarding "the lotus": this lotus corresponds to the lotus described in the *Mātṛkāyantra*. First is a circular pericarp (*karṇikā*), then a circle from which eight petals emerge. From the first circle, filaments arise at the bases of the petals; upon these filaments are the sixteen vowels, two by two, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise. Upon five of the petals are the five groups of consonants.

In the sixth [circle] are the four letters ya, ra, la, and va; in the seventh, śa, ṣa, sa, and ha; and in the eighth, the two letters la and kṣa. This is the sequence for the construction of the lotus. One should seat the disciple upon the pericarp of that lotus.
(140) The meaning is: "having taken the water-pot" (gargarī).
141. Regarding the word "mātuḥ" (of the Mother): "reciting the letters of the Mother in reverse order" means pronouncing the phonemes of the Mātṛkā from the letter *kṣa* down to the letter *a*.
Then, with that very "sprout"—that is, with the water containing the Tāraka-mantra situated within the jar—[one should perform the rite].
The knower of mantras should sprinkle the disciple three times with the root mantra.
In this very way, through the consecration, one becomes a foremost leader among teachers;
having wiped his body with a pure cloth, he should become adorned.
(The duty to be performed immediately after the Guru:
He should seat that disciple on a pure seat to his own left side;
having placed flowers and fruit in his hand, he should cast the fruit into the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*). || 144 ||
Then the Guru, being Brahmā himself, should speak these words:
"The instruction on the knowledge of the six cakras.
Thereafter, he should awaken the disciple to the knowledge of the six cakras. (Instruction on the Knowledge of the Six Cakras) || 145 ||
(The ritual placement of the sages and so forth upon the disciple’s body:
The Guru should perform the ritual placement of the Mātṛkā along with the sages and other elements upon his body. (The instruction on Tantric non-duality.)
One should reveal the section on non-duality spoken by Śiva only to one who stands in the place of a disciple.

(The Specifics regarding Kaula Initiation): If the disciple should be one who excels in vital energy and is devoted to the Kaula tradition, one should cause the purification of the principles (*tattva-śuddhi*) to be performed according to the rules by means of their respective mantras. (147)
(The Instruction on Mantras):
Then, one should recite the mantra of the Child (Bālāmantra) three times into the right ear.
As for what follows, the realization of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) he himself will explain in the sixth chapter.
(Regarding the offering of mouthfuls of water:
One should offer the *gaṇḍūṣa* tirtha into the hand of the disciple according to the prescribed rule. 148.
"May it be fruitful for both of us," the supreme guru should say;
then, contemplating "I am He," the best of disciples should receive [the mantra]. (149)
If a doubt arises in the disciple regarding the offering of the mouthful of water (gaṇḍūṣa), he shall achieve no success anywhere, and the Śrīvidyā will turn its face away from him. 150.
(Re-worship of the Root Deity): Then, having written the Vidyā upon the ground, one should worship it with flowers and other offerings. || 151 ||
(The duty to be performed immediately after the Guru:
Having placed his right lotus-foot upon the head of the disciple, he should reveal the Vidyā to the disciple; the best of practitioners should then recite it. 152.
If there should be great affection for the disciple and for the giver of life,
then one should mutter the supreme [mantra] into the right ear merely by means of its utterance.
Śrīvidyā, who is of the nature of Brahman and bestows both happiness and liberation. || 153 ||
One should reveal the classification of the seers (ṛṣi), meters (chandas), and deities;
thereafter, one should awaken the disciple who is a worthy vessel to the secret of the mantra. 154.

148. Regarding the term *gaṇḍūṣa*: "Then one should give the Vidyā to that disciplined [disciple] preceded by water"—in his commentary on this statement from the fifth chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*, Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that "preceded by water" (*ambupūrvakam*) refers to the rule for Brāhmaṇas.
Thus, *gaṇḍūṣatīrtha* means water. Furthermore, because of the mention that [the teacher] was previously engaged in the Kaula practice (*kaulakrama*), [this applies] to the Kaulikas.

It appears that the offering of a mouthful (gaṇḍūṣa) of wine as a cause [for the ritual] has been mentioned; however, since it will be stated later that "a Brāhmaṇa should never give wine to Mahādevī," this refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas. For this very reason, Rāghavabhaṭṭa stated that the phrase "preceded by water" (ambupūrvakam) pertains to the Brāhmaṇa.
154. The secret of the mantra will be explained in the section on mantras. (The procedure for designating the name of the Guru:
Then, O dear one, the disciple should touch something belonging to the venerable Guru.
Then, having assigned the letters of the Mātṛkā to his limbs, the supreme guru— || 155 ||
One should assign him a name consisting of two syllables, three syllables, or even four syllables, ending with the word "Ānandanātha."
(Prostration and Circumambulation of the Guru): Then, having circumambulated the guru three times, the disciple, performing a prostration with eight limbs, should offer himself. || 157 ||
(The Giving of the Fee): Thereafter, having worshipped the sandals of the Guru, one should give a fee—either one's entire property, half of it, or even a fourth part. (158)
(The method for the Guru’s self-purification:
Thereafter, for the sake of purifying his own self, the Guru should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
or the preceptor, having conquered his senses, may recite it one thousand times. (159)
(Prohibition of fasting for the Guru and the Disciple on the day of initiation:
If the Guru, having imparted the mantra, should observe a fast—whether out of delusion or even intentionally—he becomes a worm; it is not otherwise. (160)
If a practitioner of mantra, having performed the initiation, should observe a fast, the deity will always be enraged; having bestowed a curse, he shall return to his own city.

157. He describes the procedure for the eight-limbed prostration (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*) in the second chapter of the *Bṛhan-nīla-tantra*: "With the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the chest, the head, the eyes, the mind, and speech—this is declared to be the eight-limbed prostration. Thus it is said.
(The Brief Initiation) Now I shall explain the brief initiation that bestows accomplishment.
Whenever there is a desire, then the initiation [is performed] according to the command of the Guru. (162)

Neither the lunar day, nor religious observances, nor fire-offerings, nor ritual bathing, nor the practice of recitation is the cause of initiation; rather, it is the spontaneous arrival of a true guru. (163)

That alone is the auspicious moment, that alone is the excellence of the stars; that alone is the strength of the moon, that alone is the strength of knowledge and the strength of destiny; that alone is the true strength of the month and other such factors. (164)

(A Distinction Regarding Reception, etc. Alternatively, when the mere recitation of the mantra occurs at a time of reception, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a perfected field (siddhakṣetra), or in a temple of Śiva, that is called "instruction" (upadeśa). || 165 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 5 ||
163. Here, it appears that the reading "svecchāprāptiḥ tu sadguroḥ" (the attainment [of initiation] by one's own will, however, [occurs] through a true guru) is the correct one.

As for the reading "svecchāprāpte tu sadguroḥ," it may be explained in some way by taking *prāpte* as a gerundive (*bhāvaktapratyaya*), meaning that initiation is recommended when a true guru has been attained by one's own will.
